data:
People log in at their own university, through RENATER’s Fédération Éducation-Recherche or eduGAIN, and applications get an OpenID Connect token. The same login can also have an SSH key certified, an X.509 client certificate issued for NFS over TLS, an application password set for SMB and S3, or a WireGuard key registered. The provider can revoke what it issued, and it publishes signed lists of what it has revoked; an access token already handed out stays valid until it expires. Pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0, one binary. These pages describe v0.23.1.
go install github.com/go-authn/bridge/cmd/authn-bridge@v0.23.1 authn-bridge keygen --key /var/lib/authn-bridge/oidc.key --salt /var/lib/authn-bridge/salt authn-bridge metadata --config /etc/authn-bridge > sp.xml # register this with the federation authn-bridge check --config /etc/authn-bridge authn-bridge --config /etc/authn-bridge # serve Before v0.20.0 the command was bridge. That is also iproute2’s /sbin/bridge, installed on practically every Linux system, and whichever came first on PATH won. The module path is still github.com/go-authn/bridge.
data.what-it-is-not#What it is not: One process. With a state block, refresh tokens and the access tokens honoured at /userinfo survive a restart. Logins in progress, codes and device grants do not. The state is written through and read at start, so two instances on one database would each miss what the other wrote. No dynamic client registration, and no front- or back-channel logout. No users or groups to add. People exist because their institution vouches for them, and their groups are what it asserts.
data.what-it-prints-at-startup#What it prints: $ authn-bridge --config etc/bridge-admin.hcl authn-bridge v0.23.0: http://127.0.0.1:28473 on 127.0.0.1:28473 metrics on 127.0.0.1:28475 admin API on unix:///tmp/authn/run/admin.sock This is a test provider on loopback (an http:// issuer is accepted only on a loopback host). It fetches the federation’s metadata before it listens. A provider that cannot name a single institution is one nobody can log in through, so without the metadata it exits rather than starts.
data.where-to-go-next#Where to go next: Installing it the user, the directories, the systemd unit, the keys The configuration every block, check, and what is refused at startup The federation side metadata, its signer’s fingerprint, scopes, and what an IdP may assert Tokens ID tokens, access tokens, the device grant, application passwords, WireGuard keys Resource indicators a token for one of a client’s resource servers at a time (RFC 8707) Certificates SSH certificates, the EuroHPC profile, X.509 client certificates for NFS Revocation the signed KRL and CRL, and the Shared Signals transmitter The admin API disabling a person or an institution, health and metrics The lists it signs are read by authn-revokd for a plain sshd or a TLS server, and by go-fileshare, which checks them itself.
data.why-a-bridge#Why a bridge:
A research federation speaks SAML. Its members are hundreds of identity providers, one per institution, listed in a signed metadata document the federation publishes. Applications written today want OpenID Connect, and trust one provider. authn-bridge is that one provider: a SAML service provider on one side, registered once with the federation, and an OpenID provider on the other.
A gateway decides who everybody is for every application behind it, so most of this program is refusals. It refuses metadata the federation did not sign, an assertion that names somebody from another institution’s domain, groups an IdP has no authority over, and a configuration that would let any of these through. A configuration that cannot be served safely does not start.

Both are off unless the configuration asks for them, and neither is ever on the public listener.
admin { listen = "unix:///run/authn-bridge/admin.sock" # mode 0600 # or over the network, mutual TLS and nothing less (loopback included): # listen = "10.0.0.5:9443" # tls_cert_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/admin.crt" # tls_key_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/admin.key" # client_ca_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/operators-ca.crt" # reflection = true # for grpcurl; off by default } metrics { listen = "127.0.0.1:9101" } # /healthz /readyz /metrics disabled_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/disabled.json" The listener is grpc-transports/control’s, shared with go-fileshare. The socket is never reachable by another user, not even between bind and chmod, and is never taken from an instance still running. TCP without all three TLS files is refused, loopback included, since every local user can reach 127.0.0.1:
authn-bridge: admin: control: listen address "127.0.0.1:9443" is TCP, which requires mutual TLS (loopback included: any local user can reach it); missing TLSCertFile, TLSKeyFile, ClientCAFile A binary built with -tags nogrpc has no admin API, and refuses a configuration with an admin block rather than start without it.
data.disabling#Disabling:
$ grpcurl -plaintext -unix -d '{"username":"alice@univ-example.example","reason":"left the lab"}' $PWD/run/admin.sock bridge.admin.v1.AdminService/DisablePerson { "disabled": { "username": "alice@univ-example.example", "reason": "left the lab", "by": "uid=501", "since": "2026-10-11T09:48:39.136975Z" }, "revoked": {} } $ grpcurl -plaintext -unix -d '{"entity_id":"https://idp.univ-example.example/idp/shibboleth","reason":"compromised","until":"2026-10-12T08:00:00Z"}' $PWD/run/admin.sock bridge.admin.v1.AdminService/DisableIdP { "disabled": { "entityId": "https://idp.univ-example.example/idp/shibboleth", "reason": "compromised", "by": "uid=501", "since": "2026-10-11T09:48:39.192047Z", "until": "2026-10-12T08:00:00Z" }, "revoked": {} } revoked counts what each call ended (refresh families, access tokens, logins, application passwords, certificates); nothing was live here. Every call that changes something is logged with who made it, the peer’s uid= on the socket or the client certificate’s cn= over TLS:
disabled alice@univ-example.example (0 known identities) by uid=501 until enabled again: left the lab revoked alice@univ-example.example: 0 refresh families, 0 access tokens, 0 logins, 0 app passwords, 0 certificates disabled IdP https://idp.univ-example.example/idp/shibboleth by uid=501 until 2026-10-12T08:00:00Z: compromised revoked IdP https://idp.univ-example.example/idp/shibboleth: 0 refresh families, 0 access tokens, 0 logins, 0 app passwords, 0 certificates enabled alice@univ-example.example by uid=501 A person is disabled as who they are. Usernames compare without case, as eppn, uid, mail and subject-id all do, so the same call with "Alice@Univ-Example.example" lifts what was set for alice@univ-example.example ({"wasDisabled": true}). The entry also records the stable identity of everybody known under that name, so another spelling from their IdP does not let them back in. A name with no @ is also matched as a sub, for a person whose IdP releases no username.
The entry is recorded before anything is revoked, so a grant racing the revocation meets the entry.
Disabling is kept in disabled_file, and refused without one. Somebody disabled until the next restart would be let back in by the next deployment:
$ grpcurl -plaintext -unix -d '{"username":"alice@univ-example.example"}' $PWD/run/admin.sock bridge.admin.v1.AdminService/DisablePerson ERROR: Code: FailedPrecondition Message: disabling needs disabled_file in the configuration: without it, a restart would forget who is disabled A file that cannot be read stops the provider from starting, for the same reason. A disabled institution counts as not usable in Status, ListIdPs and check.
What disabling reaches beyond the provider is on revocation: the KRL and the CRL for certificates, Shared Signals for tokens. An application password removed here stops working in go-fileshare when it next reads its directory; call its ReloadDirectory after DisablePerson for the effect to be immediate.
What RevokePerson cannot end
An access token already handed out is a signed statement a resource server checks on its own, valid there until it expires (an hour by default). An SSH certificate already issued lasts its validity unless the server reads the KRL, which is why both are short.
data.health-and-metrics#Health and metrics:
go-net-health/endpoint’s, as in go-fileshare, on the metrics listener, which must not be the public one (a configuration that makes it so is refused):
/healthz up while the process answers /readyz ready while the federation’s metadata is loaded and within its validUntil, and no revocation is waiting to reach the state database /metrics Prometheus text, bridge_* families $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:28475/metrics | grep "^bridge_" bridge_build_info{version="v0.23.0",goversion="go1.27.2",revision="bd63c1f29a7d6897bb05dcbbf6539455cd989958"} 1 bridge_start_time_seconds 1791737439 bridge_ready 1 bridge_metadata_valid_until_timestamp_seconds 1792342188 bridge_metadata_idps 1 bridge_metadata_last_refresh_timestamp_seconds 1791737439 bridge_metadata_refreshes_total{result="failed"} 0 bridge_metadata_refreshes_total{result="ok"} 1 bridge_logins_in_progress 0 bridge_devices_waiting 0 bridge_refresh_families 0 bridge_access_tokens 0 bridge_disabled{kind="idp"} 0 bridge_disabled{kind="person"} 0 bridge_ssh_certificates_total 0 bridge_x509_certificates_total 0 The counters of logins by outcome (bridge_logins_total), of tokens by grant (bridge_tokens_issued_total) and of application passwords (bridge_app_passwords_total) appear only once they have counted something. No label names a person or an institution: which universities’ people use the service, and when, is not the provider’s to publish. Alert on bridge_metadata_valid_until_timestamp_seconds before the time it gives is reached: past it, nobody can log in.

data: A person who logged in can have an SSH public key certified, or an X.509 client certificate issued, for a few hours. A server that trusts the provider’s CA lets them in with no account file to edit there. Every certificate is recorded in certificates_file before it is handed out: one that cannot be recorded is not issued, since it could never be revoked, and revoked ones are published in the KRL and the CRL.
data.a-certificate-request-held-open-across-a: The token is checked when the request starts and the body read after, at whatever pace the client sends it. So a certificate is recorded first, and then the token and the person are checked again: if the person was disabled, or the token revoked, in between, the certificate just recorded is revoked and the answer is 401. Either the revocation saw the certificate, or the certificate sees the revocation.
data.ssh-certificates#SSH certificates:
certificates_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/certificates.json" ssh_ca { key_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/ssh-ca" # authn-bridge keygen --ssh-ca; Ed25519 validity = "12h" # the default; a week at most } client "sftp" { device = true ssh_certificates = true } authn-bridge ssh-cert --issuer https://login.example.org --client sftp logs in with a code, posts ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub (or --key) to /ssh/certificate with a token of the ssh scope, and writes -cert.pub beside it, where ssh and sftp find it.
The CA key must be Ed25519: an RSA CA key signs with SHA-1 unless told otherwise, which OpenSSH has refused by default since 8.8.
What the certificate says.
Exactly one principal, the person’s preferred_username unless the client’s profile says another claim. A certificate with no principal is valid for any user (PROTOCOL.certkeys), so a person with no username gets none. A name holding a comma, a space, a quote, a backslash or a control character is refused (403): sshd reads principals="a,b" and AuthorizedPrincipalsFile entries as lists, so one such name is two. Key ID sub= jti=: what sshd logs. No permit-* extension by default. SFTP needs none, and a certificate that permits no pty, no forwarding and no rc file grants file access and nothing else. The person’s groups in the groups@go-authn.org extension, one per line, when the token carries groups. OpenSSH ignores it; it is signed, so a server that authorizes by group can believe it. Valid from five minutes ago (for clocks that disagree) until validity from now, or until the IdP’s session ends if that is sooner. The key must be Ed25519, ECDSA P-256/384/521, a security key (sk-), or RSA of at least 2048 bits. A certificate is refused as a key.
data.the-eurohpc-ssh-ca-profile#The EuroHPC S:
The EuroHPC Federation Platform’s SSH CA (GÉANT / MyAccessID) issues Ed25519 certificates valid one hour, with one principal that names the person across the federation, and the hosts they are meant for in GÉANT’s ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org extension. A client can have its certificates issued in that shape. Every key is per client and optional; a client that sets none gets the certificate above.
client "efp" { device = true ssh_certificates = true ssh_principal_claim = "voperson_id" # the default is preferred_username ssh_validity = "1h" # never longer than ssh_ca's, nor the IdP's session ssh_extensions = ["permit-pty"] # none by default ssh_domain_grants = ["login.hpc.example.org"] # the hosting entity's hosts # ssh_source_address = ["192.0.2.0/24"] # the source-address critical option } key ssh_principal_claim preferred_username, sub, voperson_id or eduperson_principal_name. The last two are released by the eduperson scope, which the token must hold (authn-bridge ssh-cert --scope eduperson); otherwise, or when the IdP released no such attribute, the answer is 403 saying which ssh_extensions among permit-pty, permit-user-rc, permit-port-forwarding, permit-agent-forwarding, permit-X11-forwarding ssh_source_address addresses or CIDR prefixes, written canonically into source-address ssh_validity never longer than ssh_ca’s validity (equal is accepted), for this client ssh_domain_grants domain patterns, checked by go-authn/sshcert’s ValidatePattern and encoded by its EncodeDomainGrant
data.trusting-it-from-a-site#Trusting it from:
GET /ssh/config publishes the CA key in the shape EFP publishes its own, so a site follows EFP’s trust instructions with this provider’s URL:
$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/config {"PublicKey":"ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIBNOYvUrAPdRTB+38aml+twPN+2k1shD3l62v8NxrIje"} curl -s https://login.example.org/ssh/config | jq -r '.PublicKey' > /etc/ssh/bridge-ssh-ca.pub echo "TrustedUserCAKeys /etc/ssh/bridge-ssh-ca.pub" >> /etc/ssh/sshd_config sshd ignores the domain grant. The site filters by it with an AuthorizedPrincipalsCommand: sshcert-authorize, which refuses a certificate whose grant does not name the host, and one with no grant at all. The CA is not in the OpenID discovery document: no OpenID Connect metadata names an SSH CA.
What remains different from EFP’s own CA: with ssh_principal_claim = "voperson_id", as above, the principal is the subject-id the person’s institution released, in lower case, not a MyAccessID identifier; the groups extension is there when the token carries groups; and there is a KRL, GET /ssh/krl, listing the certificates of people disabled here.
data.what-the-profile-refuses#What the profil:
Each at startup, from authn-bridge check:
authn-bridge: client "efp": ssh_validity = 24h0m0s: longer than the ssh_ca validity, 12h0m0s authn-bridge: client "efp": ssh_extensions: "no-touch-required" is not one of permit-X11-forwarding, permit-agent-forwarding, permit-port-forwarding, permit-pty, permit-user-rc authn-bridge: client "src": ssh_source_address: "192.0.2.1/24" has bits set under its mask: 192.0.2.0/24? authn-bridge: client "x": ssh_principal_claim, ssh_extensions, ssh_source_address, ssh_validity and ssh_domain_grants shape SSH certificates: they need ssh_certificates = true no-touch-required is not offered: it waives the user-presence test of the person’s own security key, which is not the provider’s to give away for everybody of a client.
A domain grant is held to the specification’s syntax, then to this provider’s own policy: lower case, at least two labels, and a wildcard only under a registrable domain. What stays fixed to the right of the last wildcard must not be a public suffix (the Public Suffix List): *.ac.uk would grant every institution under it.
authn-bridge: client "efp": ssh_domain_grants: "*.ac.uk": a wildcard over the public suffix "ac.uk" grants every domain under it authn-bridge: client "efp": ssh_domain_grants: "Login.hpc.example.org": written in lower case, as hosting entities' domains are compared authn-bridge: client "efp": ssh_domain_grants: "login.hpc.*": sshcert: invalid domain pattern: pattern "login.hpc.*" has a wildcard in its rightmost label
data.x509-client-certificates-for-nfs-over-tl:
NFS over TLS (RFC 9289) can name the client by its certificate.
certificates_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/certificates.json" x509_ca { key_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/nfs-ca/ca.key" # authn-bridge keygen --x509-ca /var/lib/authn-bridge/nfs-ca cert_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/nfs-ca/ca.crt" # what go-fileshare trusts validity = "12h" # the default; a week at most } client "nfs" { device = true x509_certificates = true } authn-bridge nfs-cert --issuer ... --client nfs makes a P-256 key on the person’s machine, posts a certificate request to /x509/cert with a token of the nfs scope, and writes the certificate and the key. The CA key must be P-256, and its certificate a CA that signs certificates and CRLs.
What the certificate says. The request’s subject and extensions are ignored: what is certified is the token’s person, not what they asked for.
The person, user@domain, as one subjectAltName otherName 1.3.6.1.4.1.2238.1.1.1 holding a UTF8String, where FreeBSD’s rpc.tlsservd -u reads it. A username without @, or under three bytes, is refused. Each group as a URI name beside it: tag:go-authn.github.io,2026:group:. The CN is the username; past 64 characters the subject is empty and the subjectAltName critical (RFC 5280). Client authentication only, and a CRL distribution point: /x509/crl. Valid from five minutes ago until validity, the IdP’s session or the CA’s own certificate, whichever ends first. A P-256 or RSA (2048 bits and more) key, and a request signed by it. A certificate names the machine, not the user of it
RFC 9289: the server “cannot utilize the remote TLS peer identity to authenticate RPC users”. Linux sets the client certificate per mount, so everybody using that mount is the person it names. This is for a machine one person uses, and authn-bridge nfs-cert says so.

data:
One HCL file, or a directory of them: --config /etc/authn-bridge reads every *.hcl there in name order and merges them, and --config may be given more than once. The configuration is read at start and never again.
issuer = "https://login.example.org" # https; compared whole by every relying party listen = "127.0.0.1:8080" # the default: plain HTTP behind a TLS proxy signing_key_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/oidc.key" # authn-bridge keygen --key subject_salt_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/salt" # authn-bridge keygen --salt; never change it disabled_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/disabled.json" certificates_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/certificates.json" saml { key_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/saml.key" cert_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/saml.crt" metadata_url = "https://pub.federation.renater.fr/metadata/fer/idps.xml" metadata_cert_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/metadata-signature-2026.pem" metadata_fingerprint = "68:2F:20:58:41:9E:D0:79:EB:FE:3C:27:D6:A4:A4:09:39:6F:AE:3F:10:5F:22:EA:04:0F:04:F3:78:2D:5C:C0" } state { driver = "sqlite" # or postgres, mysql dsn_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/state.dsn" } client "my-app" { secret_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/my-app.secret" # absent: a public client redirect_uris = ["https://app.example.org/callback"] } What is required is issuer, signing_key_file, subject_salt_file, a saml block with the five keys above, and at least one client. Everything else has a default or is off.
data.a-client#A client: key default secret_file the client secret, at least 16 characters; absent, a public client redirect_uris compared exactly, except that a loopback URI may change port (RFC 8252); http only on loopback audience the client ID what its access tokens are addressed to; with several, a token for one can be asked for (RFC 8707) subject public or pairwise: a different sub for this client (OIDC Core 8.1) name the client ID shown on the device confirmation page device false the device grant (RFC 8628); such a client needs no redirect URI refresh_lifetime off refresh tokens, and how long after the login they end pkce required or or_nonce, for a confidential client only: a nonce instead of PKCE id_token_claims false copy the released claims into the ID token as well (opkssh needs it) access_token_groups true false leaves the person’s groups out of the access tokens, for tokens pasted into ssh (tokens); refused with ssh_certificates or x509_certificates ssh_certificates, ssh_* SSH certificates x509_certificates NFS client certificates app_passwords may set the person’s application password wireguard_keys, wireguard_peers WireGuard ssf_receiver, ssf_subject_format a Shared Signals receiver A client with no redirect URI must be a device client, an SSF receiver or a WireGuard gateway, or there is nothing it could do.
data.acme#acme: acme { accept_terms_of_service = true # the operator's agreement; no default cache_dir = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/acme" email = "noc@example.org" # directory_url = "..." # Let's Encrypt by default # eab_key_id = "..." # External Account Binding (GÉANT TCS / HARICA) # eab_hmac_key_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/harica-eab.key" # http_listen = ":80" # http-01, and a redirect to https # directory_ca_file = "..." # a private ACME CA's own TLS } The certificate is for the issuer’s host. cache_dir holds private keys, and the provider refuses to start on one another user could reach or re-point.
data.check-before-a-restart#check, before a r:
check reads the configuration the way the server does, loads every key it names, fetches the federation’s metadata, and says what would be served:
$ authn-bridge check --config etc/bridge.hcl issuer http://127.0.0.1:28473 SAML entity http://127.0.0.1:28473/saml tls none (a reverse proxy in front) federation 1 IdPs, 1 usable here, valid until 2026-10-18T09:46:24Z client sftp (public, public subject, audience [sftp]) client efp (public, public subject, audience [efp]) client nfs (public, public subject, audience [nfs]) Usable here leaves out an IdP that saml { idps } does not list, and one the admin API has disabled: with the institution above disabled, the same command prints federation 1 IdPs, 0 usable here. An idps entry the federation does not list is refused here, though the server would start with it:
federation 1 IdPs, 0 usable here, valid until 2026-10-18T09:46:24Z authn-bridge: idps names "https://idp.nowhere.example/idp", which the federation does not list authn-bridge metadata prints the SAML metadata to register with the federation. See the federation side.
data.state-what-a-restart-must-not-forget#sta:
state { driver = "postgres" # sqlite, postgres or mysql dsn_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/state.dsn" } Refresh token families, the refresh tokens and the retired ones, the access tokens honoured at /userinfo and for certificates, the SAML assertions already accepted and the logins already answered, the SSF streams and their undelivered events: written through to one table, bridge_state (created if missing), and read at start. A refresh token is kept as its SHA-256, never as itself. Without the block they live in memory, and a restart logs everybody out.
A login in progress is not in it. It travels in its own cookie, sealed with AES-256-GCM under a key derived from the subject salt, so the browser can neither read nor change it.
data.the-top-level#The top level:
key default issuer the provider’s name and the base of every URL. https, or http on a loopback host for testing; no query, no fragment; a trailing / is dropped listen 127.0.0.1:8080 the public listener cert_file, key_file serve TLS from these files, re-read when they change; together or not at all acme serve TLS with a certificate from an ACME CA instead (below); not with cert_file signing_key_file RSA, signs ID tokens (RS256); a P-256 key here is refused access_token_key_file the signing key a P-256 key that signs access tokens ES256; refused if it is the signing key retired_signing_key_files keys that signed before: still published at /jwks, never used to sign subject_salt_file at least 32 bytes code_lifetime 1m at most ten minutes (RFC 6749 4.1.2) token_lifetime 1h access tokens id_token_lifetime 5m ID tokens trusted_proxies addresses or prefixes whose X-Forwarded-For is believed requests_per_minute 120 logins, device grants and ACS posts an address may start a minute; 0 turns the limit off disabled_file where disabled people and institutions are kept; without it, disabling is refused certificates_file every certificate and WireGuard key issued; required with ssh_ca, x509_ca or wireguard The blocks:
block page saml, claims the federation side client below, and tokens state below ssh_ca, x509_ca certificates app_passwords, wireguard tokens ssf revocation admin, metrics the admin API acme below
data.what-is-refused-at-startup#What is refus:
Each of these is the output of authn-bridge check on a configuration that asked for it. The server refuses the same configurations: each is read from the configuration and the files it names. The one refusal check adds is the idps entry the federation does not list, above: the server fetches the same metadata before it listens, but does not hold idps to it.
An issuer, a redirect, a secret that leak:
authn-bridge: issuer "http://login.example.org": an issuer is https (http only on loopback, for testing) authn-bridge: client "web": redirect URI "http://app.example.org/callback": a code sent over cleartext http is a code anybody on the path has authn-bridge: client "web": a secret of 5 characters is a password somebody can guess authn-bridge: code_lifetime = 15m0s: an authorization code lives ten minutes at most A name any institution could claim:
authn-bridge: claims: username = "uid" is not held to an IdP's scopes, so any IdP of the federation could name anybody: it needs saml { idps } to list exactly one IdP; with more, use eppn or subject_id authn-bridge: claims: groups = "affiliation" carries no institution, so any IdP of the federation could grant any of its values: it needs saml { idps } to list exactly one IdP; with more, use scoped_affiliation Something issued that could never be taken back:
authn-bridge: ssh_ca: certificates_file is required with ssh_ca or x509_ca: a certificate that is not recorded can never be revoked authn-bridge: ssh_ca: validity = 200h0m0s: more than a week, and a certificate lives that long on every server its revocation has not reached authn-bridge: ssf: needs a state block: a queue a restart empties loses revocations A listener that should not be reachable:
authn-bridge: admin: control: listen address "127.0.0.1:9443" is TCP, which requires mutual TLS (loopback included: any local user can reach it); missing TLSCertFile, TLSKeyFile, ClientCAFile authn-bridge: metrics: listen is the public listener; metrics have one of their own A configuration that says one thing twice:
authn-bridge: saml: an external discovery service lists every IdP; with `idps` restricted, leave `discovery` out and this provider lists them itself authn-bridge: client "sftp" is declared twice The SSH profile’s own refusals are on certificates, and the federation’s on the federation side.

data:
On this side authn-bridge is a SAML service provider. It is registered once with the federation (RENATER’s Fédération Éducation-Recherche, or eduGAIN), and it trusts the federation’s metadata: one signed document that lists every member IdP, their signing keys, and the domains each may vouch for. The SAML code is go-authn/saml.
saml { key_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/saml.key" # RSA: IdPs encrypt assertions to it cert_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/saml.crt" metadata_url = "https://pub.federation.renater.fr/metadata/fer/idps.xml" metadata_cert_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/metadata-signature-2026.pem" metadata_fingerprint = "68:2F:20:58:41:9E:D0:79:EB:FE:3C:27:D6:A4:A4:09:39:6F:AE:3F:10:5F:22:EA:04:0F:04:F3:78:2D:5C:C0" discovery = "https://discovery.renater.fr/renater" # or leave it out for this provider's own list # idps = ["https://idp.univ-example.example/idp/shibboleth"] # restrict; one entry skips the choice names = { fr = "Passerelle OIDC", en = "OIDC gateway" } technical_contact = "admin@example.org" } key default entity_id the issuer + /saml this service provider’s name in the federation key_file, cert_file the SP’s RSA key and certificate metadata_url https://, file:// for a copy something else keeps, or http:// on loopback only metadata_cert_file, metadata_fingerprint the federation’s signing certificate and its SHA-256 fingerprint, both required discovery this provider’s own list an external discovery service to send people to idps every IdP of the federation restrict login to these entity IDs names, descriptions, information_url, privacy_statement_url, technical_contact the issuer’s host as the name what goes in the SP metadata
data.from-an-assertion-to-claims#From an asse:
claims { username = "eppn" # preferred_username: eppn, subject_id, uid or mail groups = ["entitlement"] # groups: entitlement, scoped_affiliation, affiliation, is_member_of } uid and mail are not held to any scope, and affiliation (staff, student) names no institution. So each needs saml { idps } to list exactly one IdP; with more, they are refused at startup.
sub. The identifier behind it is taken in this order: subject-id, then pairwise-id, then eduPersonPrincipalName, then eduPersonTargetedID, then a persistent NameID whose qualifier is the IdP itself. It is qualified by the IdP’s entity ID, and sub is an HMAC-SHA256 of it under the subject salt: stable, not reversible, not an address. public is the same for every client, pairwise differs per client. An IdP that releases none of these is refused, since nobody could be recognised twice. Mail is never an identifier, and there is no email_verified: an IdP asserting an address is not anybody having verified that the person reads it.
What the request asks of the IdP. prompt=none becomes IsPassive, and an IdP with no session answers login_required. prompt=login and max_age=0 become ForceAuthn; for any other max_age, a person whose IdP authenticated them longer ago than that is sent back with ForceAuthn. acr_values becomes RequestedAuthnContext, and an IdP that answers with another context is refused: a client that asked for a second factor is never told it got one when it did not.
data.refreshing-it#Refreshing it:
The metadata is fetched before the provider listens, then again at three quarters of the document’s cacheDuration, never sooner than five minutes nor later than twelve hours, and whenever the admin API’s RefreshMetadata asks. A refresh that fails keeps the last good copy, but only until its own validUntil. After that nothing is vouched for, every IdP disappears, and /readyz says the provider is not ready. A federation server briefly unreachable logs nobody out; one unreachable for days does not leave the provider trusting stale keys.
Within the document, an IdP is kept only if it speaks SAML 2.0 and publishes an HTTP-Redirect SingleSignOnService. An entity described twice is dropped altogether, since nothing says which description is right, and one member’s unreadable certificate leaves out that member, not the federation.
data.the-metadatas-signer-is-pinned#The metad:
The certificate that signs the metadata is a file on this host, and its SHA-256 fingerprint is written in the configuration. The certificate is checked against the fingerprint at every start, so a file replaced on disk is noticed rather than trusted:
authn-bridge: saml: fed/fed.crt is not the certificate with fingerprint 68:2F:20:58:41:9E:D0:79:EB:FE:3C:27:D6:A4:A4:09:39:6F:AE:3F:10:5F:22:EA:04:0F:04:F3:78:2D:5C:C0 A key that arrives over the same channel as the document it vouches for vouches for nothing. So the fingerprint comes from the federation’s web page, never from the download that brought the certificate:
openssl x509 -in /etc/authn-bridge/metadata-signature-2026.pem -noout -fingerprint -sha256
data.the-sp-metadata#The SP metadata:
authn-bridge metadata prints what to register with the federation, without fetching anything (the certificate is shortened here):
$ authn-bridge metadata --config etc/bridge.hcl <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> 127.0.0.1:28473 MIIE… 127.0.0.1:28473 Assertions must be signed (WantAssertionsSigned="true"), and are delivered to /saml/acs by HTTP-POST. The same document is served at /saml/metadata.
data.what-each-idp-may-say#What each IdP may:
A federation has hundreds of members, and any of them could otherwise say it is alice@another-university.example. Every member’s metadata lists its shibmd:Scopes, the domains it may vouch for; a regular-expression scope is ignored, not honoured.
Identifiers. A scoped value (subject-id, pairwise-id, eduPersonPrincipalName, eduPersonScopedAffiliation) outside the asserting IdP’s scopes is dropped, and a value with more than one @ is not in any scope.
Groups. With more than one IdP allowed to log in, an eduPersonEntitlement or isMemberOf value is kept only if its namespace is one of that IdP’s scopes or under one:
value its namespace urn:mace::... urn:geant::... (AARC-G002) https:///... anything else none: dropped Groups decide what a person may do, at every resource server and in every certificate, so a value nobody can place is not passed on. A community proxy that asserts groups for people of many institutions is named explicitly, by entity ID, with the prefixes it may assert:
claims { trusted_groups = { "https://proxy.eduteams.org/saml2/idp/metadata.php" = ["urn:geant:eduteams.org:"] } } With exactly one IdP in saml { idps }, that IdP is trusted for every value.
data.what-is-refused#What is refused:
At the ACS, everything go-authn/saml refuses: an unsigned or SHA-1 assertion, several assertions, a replayed one, an identifier in a foreign scope. Then this provider’s own refusals:
an IdP response delivered into another browser: the login is found through its own sealed cookie, never through the RelayState the response carries; otherwise anybody could send their own IdP response to somebody else’s browser and log that person in under the sender’s identity; an IdP that the configuration no longer allows, or that the admin API has disabled; a person or an institution disabled here, whatever the institution says. At startup, a list of IdPs together with RENATER’s discovery service, which lists them all and cannot be restricted:
authn-bridge: saml: an external discovery service lists every IdP; with `idps` restricted, leave `discovery` out and this provider lists them itself

data:
The repository ships the unit and the user it runs as: packaging/systemd/authn-bridge.service and packaging/sysusers.d/authn-bridge.conf. Everything below runs as root unless it says otherwise.
/usr/local/bin/authn-bridge the binary /etc/authn-bridge/*.hcl the configuration, read in name order; root:authn-bridge, 0750, files 0640 /var/lib/authn-bridge/ keys, the subject salt, the SQLite state, the certificates issued, the disabled list; authn-bridge, 0700 /run/authn-bridge/ the admin socket, when the configuration asks for one
data.changes-need-a-restart#Changes need a re:
The configuration is read once. The unit has no ExecReload=, so systemctl reload is refused rather than pretending. A SIGHUP (from logrotate, or habit) is caught, logged and ignored. Left to Go’s default it would kill the process, and systemd would count that as a clean exit that Restart=on-failure does not restart:
SIGHUP: ignored, nothing is reloaded; restart the service to apply a configuration change (TLS certificate files are re-read on their own) TLS certificate files are the exception: they are re-read when they change.
data.coming-from-bridge#Coming from bridge: The configuration is unchanged; only the command and the release assets were renamed. Change every unit, script, cron job and bearer_token_command that runs bridge. The log line and the error prefix now say authn-bridge, so an alert that matched bridge v0. must match authn-bridge v0.. Metric names (bridge_*), the bridge_state table and the user-side cache (go-authn-bridge in the user’s configuration directory, ~/.config on Linux) are unchanged, so authn-bridge token reuses the logins bridge cached.
data.port-443#Port 443:
The default listener is 127.0.0.1:8080, behind a TLS reverse proxy, and needs no capability. To serve TLS itself on port 443 (cert_file or acme), the provider needs CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE and must leave the private user namespace, since a capability held inside it does not apply to the host’s network:
# /etc/systemd/system/authn-bridge.service.d/port-443.conf [Service] CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE PrivateUsers=no
data.the-binary#The binary:
A release carries authn-bridge-- for Linux, macOS and Windows on amd64 and arm64, a SHA256SUMS manifest and a build provenance attestation per binary; verifying a download says how to check both. Or build it, which records the version in the binary:
$ go install github.com/go-authn/bridge/cmd/authn-bridge@v0.23.1 $ authn-bridge --version authn-bridge version v0.23.1 The path matters: from v0.20.0 the program lives in internal/app and the command in cmd/authn-bridge, so go install github.com/go-authn/bridge@... builds nothing.
data.the-keys#The keys:
Run keygen as the service’s user, so that it owns what it writes. It refuses to overwrite a file that is already there:
$ mkdir var/nfs-ca $ authn-bridge keygen --key var/oidc.key --salt var/salt --ssh-ca var/ssh-ca --x509-ca var/nfs-ca wrote var/ssh-ca; its public half, for go-fileshare's trusted_user_ca_file: ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIBNOYvUrAPdRTB+38aml+twPN+2k1shD3l62v8NxrIje go-authn-bridge-ca wrote var/oidc.key wrote var/nfs-ca/ca.crt and its key; the certificate is what go-fileshare trusts for NFS over TLS wrote var/salt -- keep it: a new salt is a new subject for everybody $ authn-bridge keygen --key var/oidc.key authn-bridge: open var/oidc.key: file exists On a server the paths are under /var/lib/authn-bridge, and the command is runuser -u authn-bridge -- authn-bridge keygen ....
flag writes for --key an RSA 3072 key ID tokens (RS256), published at /jwks --salt 32 random bytes every sub, which is an HMAC under it --access-token-key a P-256 key access tokens signed ES256 instead, much shorter --ssh-ca an Ed25519 key in OpenSSH format the SSH certificates and the KRL’s signature --x509-ca DIR DIR/ca.key (P-256) and DIR/ca.crt, valid ten years, path length 0 NFS client certificates and the CRL Back up the salt, and never change it
A new salt gives every person a new sub, and every relying party then sees a new person. The same goes for deleting it on uninstall.
The SAML key and certificate are made with openssl: they are what the federation registers and what every IdP encrypts to. The key must be RSA (IdPs encrypt to it with RSA-OAEP). It is not the TLS certificate, and does not change with it.
runuser -u authn-bridge -- sh -c 'umask 077; openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:3072 -nodes -days 3650 \ -subj "/CN=login.example.org" \ -keyout /var/lib/authn-bridge/saml.key -out /var/lib/authn-bridge/saml.crt' The federation’s metadata signing certificate comes from the federation, and so does its SHA-256 fingerprint: take the fingerprint from the federation’s web page, never from the same download as the certificate. See the federation side.
data.the-unit#The unit:
What it grants, in short:
Type=exec, Restart=on-failure, RestartSec=5s, TimeoutStopSec=20s. The provider shuts its listener down within ten seconds of SIGTERM. StateDirectory=, RuntimeDirectory= (both 0700) and ConfigurationDirectory= (0750), UMask=0077. With ProtectSystem=strict, everything else is read-only. No capability (CapabilityBoundingSet= and AmbientCapabilities= empty), NoNewPrivileges=, PrivateUsers=, PrivateTmp=, PrivateDevices=, PrivateIPC=, ProtectHome=, the kernel, clock, hostname and control groups protected. RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_UNIX AF_INET AF_INET6: TCP for the listener, the metadata, an ACME CA and a database; a socket for the admin API. SystemCallFilter=@system-service, minus @privileged @resources, refused with EPERM rather than a kill. It waits for network-online.target, because the metadata is fetched before the provider listens.
systemctl enable --now authn-bridge journalctl -u authn-bridge -n 20 The first line in the journal is the one shown on the overview.
data.the-user-and-why-it-is-not-a-dynamic-one: install -m 0755 authn-bridge-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/authn-bridge install -D -m 0644 authn-bridge.conf /etc/sysusers.d/authn-bridge.conf systemd-sysusers # creates the authn-bridge user and group install -m 0644 authn-bridge.service /etc/systemd/system/authn-bridge.service systemctl daemon-reload install -d -m 0750 -o root -g authn-bridge /etc/authn-bridge install -d -m 0700 -o authn-bridge -g authn-bridge /var/lib/authn-bridge The unit names User=authn-bridge, not DynamicUser=. The signing key, the subject salt, the SAML key and the certificate authorities are made before the first start, live for years, and must keep one owner across reinstalls and restores from backup. A dynamic user gets its UID when the service starts.
data.upgrading-and-going-back#Upgrading, and:
Back up /var/lib/authn-bridge first: it holds the keys and the salt, which cannot be made again. Keep the binary that works, install the new one, restart:
cp -p /usr/local/bin/authn-bridge /usr/local/bin/authn-bridge.previous install -m 0755 authn-bridge-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/authn-bridge systemctl restart authn-bridge Going back is the same with authn-bridge.previous. A newer release may ship a newer unit: compare it with yours, install it and systemctl daemon-reload before the restart.

data:
A client whose audience names several resource servers, such as a portal in front of several file servers, gets access tokens addressed to all of them. Any one of those servers can then take a token it received and present it to the others: RFC 8707 §3 says this is why an audience should be restricted. Since v0.21.0 the client can ask, with RFC 8707’s resource parameter, for a token addressed to one of them. This page describes v0.23.1; what v0.22.0 did differently is at the end.
Without resource, nothing changes: the access token is for the client’s whole audience, as the tokens page describes.
data.a-token-for-one-server#A token for one s:
The person logs in as usual (here, against a test federation, with the authorization request naming no resource). The client then names one server when it exchanges the code:
$ curl -s --netrc-file etc/portal.netrc http://127.0.0.1:28473/token \ -d grant_type=authorization_code -d code="$(cat code)" \ -d code_verifier="$(cat verifier)" -d redirect_uri=http://127.0.0.1:9/portal \ --data-urlencode resource=https://fs-paris.example.org/ \ -o tokens.json -w "%{http_code}\n" 200 $ jq -r .access_token tokens.json | cut -d. -f2 | tr "_-" "/+" | jq -R "@base64d | fromjson | {aud, client_id, scope}" { "aud": "https://fs-paris.example.org/", "client_id": "portal", "scope": "openid profile" } The aud is the value asked for, exactly as it was sent, and nothing else. A server that checks its audience, as go-authn/oidc does, accepts this token at Paris and refuses it at Lyon.
data.another-server-at-the-next-refresh#Anoth:
The refresh token keeps the whole grant (RFC 8707 §2.2), so the next refresh can ask for another server:
$ curl -s --netrc-file etc/portal.netrc http://127.0.0.1:28473/token \ -d grant_type=refresh_token -d refresh_token="$(jq -r .refresh_token tokens.json)" \ --data-urlencode resource=https://fs-lyon.example.org/ \ -o tokens.json -w "%{http_code}\n" 200 $ jq -r .access_token tokens.json | cut -d. -f2 | tr "_-" "/+" | jq -R "@base64d | fromjson | {aud, client_id, scope}" { "aud": "https://fs-lyon.example.org/", "client_id": "portal", "scope": "openid profile" } The scope is the same for both servers: the provider does not reduce it per resource.
data.departures#Where this departs from RFC 8: RFC 8707 authn-bridge v0.23.1 §2: “Multiple resource parameters MAY be used” at the authorization endpoint, as written. At the token endpoint, one: a second resource is invalid_request, which §3 allows (“an authorization server may be unwilling or unable to fulfill a token request with multiple resources”) §2.2: the parameter applies “for all grant types” only authorization_code and refresh_token. With client_credentials or the device grant it is refused with invalid_target, at the device authorization request as when polling §2: the value “SHOULD NOT include a query component” not checked. What is checked is that the value is absolute, has no fragment, and is in the client’s audience §2: the server “may map from that value to a more general URI or abstract identifier” no mapping: aud is the value asked for, compared with audience as a string §2.2: “the authorization server should downscope the scope value” for each resource not done: the scope is the grant’s, whichever server is named §2.1: a request without resource MAY be processed “by using a predefined default resource value” the default is the client’s whole audience §2.2: a refresh may be limited “to those [resources] that were originally granted”, and the refresh token “is bound to the full original grant” as written Before v0.22.1, v0.22.0 refused a repeated resource at the authorization endpoint with an error page, as it refuses any other repeated parameter, so a grant could not name two servers; and its device authorization request did not read resource, so a device that asked for one server got a token for the whole audience.
data.the-client#The client:
Nothing needs turning on. Every URI in the client’s audience can be asked for. The examples below use a confidential client with refresh tokens, and a device client with the same audience:
client "portal" { secret_file = "etc/portal.secret" redirect_uris = ["http://127.0.0.1:9/portal"] audience = ["https://fs-paris.example.org/", "https://fs-lyon.example.org/"] refresh_lifetime = "8h" } client "files-cli" { device = true audience = ["https://fs-paris.example.org/", "https://fs-lyon.example.org/"] } $ authn-bridge check --config etc/bridge.hcl issuer http://127.0.0.1:28473 SAML entity http://127.0.0.1:28473/saml tls none (a reverse proxy in front) federation 1 IdPs, 1 usable here, valid until 2026-10-18T15:48:27Z client portal (confidential, public subject, audience [https://fs-paris.example.org/ https://fs-lyon.example.org/]) client files-cli (public, public subject, audience [https://fs-paris.example.org/ https://fs-lyon.example.org/]) check lists the audience and says nothing more about it. In particular, it does not say which entries can be asked for: only an absolute URI without a fragment can be. A logical name such as fileshare, or a URI with a #, is accepted in audience and still goes into the token when no resource is named, but a resource naming it is refused.

data:
Disabling a person or an institution (the admin API) ends everything that comes back to the provider: refresh tokens, /userinfo, new certificates, application passwords. What it has already handed out is checked elsewhere, against keys, and three mechanisms reach it:
credential taken back by an SSH certificate this CA signed the KRL, GET /ssh/krl, with its signature at /ssh/krl.sig an X.509 client certificate the CRL, GET /x509/crl an access token, an opkssh certificate, anything a server verifies alone a Shared Signals session-revoked event Revocation is permanent. Enabling a person again does not bring their certificates back; they get new ones. A list a revocation could be taken out of is a list somebody who reaches the admin API could edit.
data.shared-signals#Shared Signals:
An access token or an opkssh certificate is checked where it is used, and no list can name it. So the provider is an OpenID Shared Signals transmitter: on DisablePerson, RevokePerson and DisableIdP it queues a CAEP session-revoked event (everything issued to this subject before the event’s time is void) for every receiver that asked.
state { ... } # required: a queue a restart empties loses revocations ssf {} # event_retention = "192h" by default client "fileshare-ssf" { # a receiver: client credentials, scope ssf secret_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/fileshare-ssf.secret" ssf_receiver = true audience = ["fileshare"] } $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:28473/.well-known/ssf-configuration | jq . { "issuer": "http://127.0.0.1:28473", "jwks_uri": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/jwks", "delivery_methods_supported": [ "urn:ietf:rfc:8936" ], "configuration_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssf/streams", "status_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssf/streams/status", "add_subject_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssf/streams/subjects:add", "remove_subject_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssf/streams/subjects:remove", "verification_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssf/streams/verify", "spec_version": "1_0", "authorization_schemes": [ { "spec_urn": "urn:ietf:rfc:6749" } ] } Poll delivery only (RFC 8936): the receiver asks; nothing here dials out. A receiver authenticates with an access token from the client credentials grant, for an ssf_receiver client with a secret, scope ssf. It sees its own streams only, ten at most. Events are SETs (RFC 8417) signed with the ID token key, with no exp and no sub. The subject is the account, acct:, by default: a sub may be pairwise, one per client. A receiver configured ssf_subject_format = "iss_sub" gets instead the issuer and the public sub. An institution disabled is one event per person the provider has a trace of there, and one whose subject is the tenant, the institution’s entity ID, with its scopes, which covers the people the provider has forgotten. Streams and undelivered events are kept in the state database until acknowledged or event_retention passes. An event a receiver reports in error is handed out again, up to ten times. The SSF block is refused without a state block:
authn-bridge: ssf: needs a state block: a queue a restart empties loses revocations
data.the-lists#The lists:
Both are issued as go-authn/revocation’s protocol says, so that they can travel through anything (a mirror, plain HTTP, a file) and still be checked by whoever reads them:
KRL CRL format OpenSSH PROTOCOL.krl, written by go-authn/krl: what sshd’s RevokedKeys and ssh-keygen -Q read DER, RFC 5280 signed a detached SSHSIG by the SSH CA key, namespace krl@go-authn.github.io by the CA that signs the certificates current until its expires@go-authn.github.io extension (which sshd ignores) its nextUpdate ordered by its krl_version, then its generation date its CRL Number, then thisUpdate Each list says it stops being current an hour after it is issued. A list is kept and served unchanged until it is half way to that, or until something is revoked; the next request then gets a new issue. An issue is never dated before the one it replaces, even if the clock steps back, since a reader refuses an earlier issue of the same version as a rollback. The CRL Number rises at every issue.
The KRL from a test provider with nothing revoked:
$ curl -s -D - -o var/bridge.krl http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/krl HTTP/1.1 200 OK Cache-Control: max-age=60 Content-Type: application/octet-stream Etag: "db5b4e920d2da3911da51a8f70db8c4f" Date: Sun, 11 Oct 2026 09:48:14 GMT Content-Length: 130 $ ssh-keygen -Q -l -f var/bridge.krl # KRL version 0 # Generated at 20261011T114814 # Comment: go-authn/bridge http://127.0.0.1:28473 The ETag is the content’s. A reader polls with If-None-Match, and gets 304 while the issue it holds is still the one served; since the content changes at least every half hour, a polling reader never keeps a copy past its expiry:
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -H 'If-None-Match: "db5b4e920d2da3911da51a8f70db8c4f"' -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/krl 304 The signature is fetched with If-Match on the list’s ETag. A list issued again in between answers 412, rather than a signature that does not match it:
$ curl -s -o var/bridge.krl.sig -H 'If-Match: "db5b4e920d2da3911da51a8f70db8c4f"' -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/krl.sig 200 $ curl -s -o /dev/null -H 'If-Match: "stale"' -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/krl.sig 412 ssh-keygen checks the signature, and refuses it in any other namespace:
$ ssh-keygen -Y verify -f allowed -I bridge -n krl@go-authn.github.io -s bridge.krl.sig < bridge.krl Good "krl@go-authn.github.io" signature for bridge with ED25519 key SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q where allowed is the line bridge namespaces="krl@go-authn.github.io" .
The CRL, issued fifteen seconds later:
$ openssl crl -inform DER -in var/bridge.crl -noout -text Certificate Revocation List (CRL): Version 2 (0x1) Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA256 Issuer: CN=go-authn bridge NFS client CA Last Update: Oct 11 09:48:29 2026 GMT Next Update: Oct 11 10:48:29 2026 GMT CRL extensions: X509v3 Authority Key Identifier: 2A:90:7A:50:FF:65:52:BA:70:4E:E1:F8:70:EE:7A:FC:B1:8B:FE:4E X509v3 CRL Number: 1791712109993 No Revoked Certificates. Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA256 Signature Value: 30:44:02:20:37:90:14:6f:c1:f2:ea:98:29:04:61:88:a8:17: 88:e3:f6:84:9d:46:a7:fc:2b:ac:81:26:47:9d:ac:84:23:38: 02:20:0a:a6:93:cb:7d:2d:81:e4:59:d4:0d:a0:fd:f4:6e:75: c9:0d:53:e7:92:49:ac:a1:31:a8:90:09:91:d1:87:b6 A certificate stays in its list until it expires: an expired certificate is refused everywhere without being listed.
data.who-reads-them#Who reads them: A plain sshd, or nginx and other TLS servers: authn-revokd fetches the lists, keeps only those that verify, writes them where the servers read them, and fails closed for sshd when a list lapses. go-fileshare fetches and verifies them itself, and refuses the provider’s certificates while it holds no current list.

data: Every credential here starts with the same login at the person’s institution. What differs is who the credential is for, and how it is taken back. The certificates are on their own page.
data.application-passwords#Application passwo:
NTLMv2 and SigV4 prove a secret the server must already hold, so no token will do for SMB or S3. A client with app_passwords = true lets a token with the app_password scope set one, generated and shown once: authn-bridge app-password --issuer ... --client files (--remove deletes it).
app_passwords { driver = "sqlite" # sqlite, postgres or mysql dsn_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/apppw.dsn" store = ["nt_hash"] # the default, SMB only; add "password" for S3 lifetime = "2160h" # the default, 90 days # table = "app_passwords" # the default } The table is created if missing: login, password, nt_hash, expires, idp. Only what the protocols need is stored: the NT hash for SMB, the password itself only when store asks for it. go-fileshare reads it with a users "sql" block; name the columns in its query, never *.
Disabling a person removes their password; disabling an institution removes its people’s. A removed password stops working in go-fileshare when it next reads its directory.
data.openpubkey-and-opkssh#OpenPubkey and opk:
opkssh turns an ID token into SSH logins with no CA at all, and the token it makes (a PK Token) outlives the ID token inside it. The provider returns the nonce verbatim in the code flow and in the device flow, signs RS256, and keeps a retired key published for as long as retired_signing_key_files names it, so that a PK Token signed before a rotation still verifies:
retired_signing_key_files = ["/var/lib/authn-bridge/oidc-2026-03.key"] Give opkssh a client of its own with id_token_claims = true: it matches people on the PK Token’s claims, and its ID token travels to every server it logs into.
data.the-access-token#The access token:
For the resource servers in the client’s audience, as RFC 9068 describes: signed with signing_key_file (RS256) or access_token_key_file (ES256), typ: at+jwt, valid token_lifetime (an hour by default). It carries what a resource server needs to decide without asking anybody: preferred_username, groups, idp (the entity ID of the IdP that vouched), scope, client_id, and session_end when the IdP said when its session ends. The groups can be left out, per client: below.
A client whose audience names several resource servers can ask for a token addressed to one of them, with RFC 8707’s resource: see several resource servers.
data.the-id-token#The ID token:
For the client, and about the login, not the person: RS256, aud the client ID, sub, auth_time, at_hash, the nonce when the request had one, and acr when the IdP said which authentication context it used. Lifetime id_token_lifetime, five minutes by default.
Nothing about the person is in it. The claims the scopes release are at /userinfo, as OIDC Core 5.4 says when an access token is issued, and one always is. A client whose ID token is itself the credential, such as opkssh, sets id_token_claims = true to have them copied in. An ID token is only issued for a request with the openid scope.
scope releases profile name, given_name, family_name, preferred_username email email (never email_verified) eduperson eduperson_principal_name, eduperson_scoped_affiliation, eduperson_entitlement and entitlements, eduperson_assurance, eduperson_orcid, schac_home_organization, voperson_id (the SAML subject-id, lower-cased) groups groups
data.what-it-leaves-out#What it leaves out, a:
No auth_time and no acr, although RFC 9068 allows both. They stay in the ID token, where OIDC Core puts them. Nothing reads them from an access token: not this provider, which looks a token up by its jti, and not go-fileshare. An access token, however, is also pasted as an SSH keyboard-interactive answer (ssh-oidc’s mccli, checked by motley-cue at /userinfo), and OpenSSH reads 1023 characters of one; an IdP’s acr alone, urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:PasswordProtectedTransport, is about 90 of them. Before v0.22.0 the access token carried both.
The length of an ES256 access token (access_token_key_file) for a long eppn and three AARC entitlements, measured by authn-bridge’s TestES256AccessTokens with an issuer of a real length, against the shibmd:Scope lengths of RENATER’s metadata (743 scopes):
scope length characters 13 median 885 22 95th percentile 945 29 99th percentile 992 44 the longest 1092: over Before v0.22.0 the same token was 1014 / 1074 / 1121 / 1221 characters: over from the 95th percentile on. What still does not fit is the longest scopes and, above all, many groups: every entitlement adds its whole URN, and nothing bounds how many an IdP sends. An RS256 access token, signed with a 3072-bit key, is about 1150 characters before any group, so a token meant for SSH is signed ES256. Past 1023 characters, mccli asks motley-cue for a one-time password instead, which motley-cue allows by default; a token pasted into plain ssh has to fit.
No groups, for a client that asks (v0.23.0). Every group adds its whole URN, and nothing bounds how many an IdP sends, so no key and no signature algorithm makes a token that carries groups fit for certain. A client with access_token_groups = false gets access tokens without the person’s groups:
client "oidc-agent" { device = true audience = ["ssh"] access_token_groups = false } It is meant for ssh-oidc: oidc-agent gets the token, mccli pastes it as the keyboard-interactive answer, and motley-cue checks it at /userinfo and reads the groups there. Measured by authn-bridge’s TestAccessTokenWithoutGroups, an ES256 token for somebody in 50 groups, with the longest RENATER scope (44) and an issuer of a real length, is 732 characters.
Against a test federation, a person in three groups logs in through that client, with the device grant:
$ authn-bridge token --issuer http://127.0.0.1:28473 --client oidc-agent --scope "openid eduperson groups" --cache var/tokens.json > at To log in, open http://127.0.0.1:28473/device and enter the code DHBT-DBZD (or open http://127.0.0.1:28473/device?user_code=DHBT-DBZD) $ tr -d '\n' < at | wc -c 625 The token names the person and their IdP, and no group:
$ cut -d. -f2 at | tr "_-" "/+" | jq -R "@base64d | fromjson" { "aud": "ssh", "client_id": "oidc-agent", "exp": 1791741018, "iat": 1791737418, "idp": "https://idp.univ-example.example/idp/shibboleth", "iss": "http://127.0.0.1:28473", "jti": "0zVsbDeAwcubhCCFXtj9Dh0u-93sDBza5sti7EmcSL8", "preferred_username": "alice@univ-example.example", "scope": "openid eduperson groups", "sub": "KEQ1dJYNUw8TtXF5HNbuy3EYZ3rmFMKiqaVY8RH7eLE" } /userinfo still serves them, as groups (scope groups) and as eduperson_entitlement (scope eduperson):
$ { printf 'Authorization: Bearer '; cat at; } > auth.hdr $ curl -s -H @auth.hdr http://127.0.0.1:28473/userinfo | jq . { "eduperson_entitlement": [ "urn:geant:univ-example.example:group:physique#idp.univ-example.example", "urn:geant:univ-example.example:group:physique:calcul#idp.univ-example.example", "urn:geant:univ-example.example:group:hpc-users#idp.univ-example.example" ], "eduperson_principal_name": "alice@univ-example.example", "entitlements": [ "urn:geant:univ-example.example:group:physique#idp.univ-example.example", "urn:geant:univ-example.example:group:physique:calcul#idp.univ-example.example", "urn:geant:univ-example.example:group:hpc-users#idp.univ-example.example" ], "groups": [ "urn:geant:univ-example.example:group:hpc-users#idp.univ-example.example", "urn:geant:univ-example.example:group:physique#idp.univ-example.example", "urn:geant:univ-example.example:group:physique:calcul#idp.univ-example.example" ], "sub": "KEQ1dJYNUw8TtXF5HNbuy3EYZ3rmFMKiqaVY8RH7eLE" } The default stays true. go-fileshare, like any resource server that decides from the token alone, needs the groups in it: leave them out only for a client whose tokens go to a server that reads /userinfo.
Refused with certificates. SSH and X.509 certificates take the person’s groups from the access token, so a client with access_token_groups = false and ssh_certificates or x509_certificates would issue certificates that carry none, and a server that authorizes by group would refuse the person with nothing anywhere saying why. check, like the server at startup, refuses the pair:
client "oidc-agent" { device = true audience = ["ssh"] access_token_groups = false ssh_certificates = true } $ authn-bridge check --config etc/bridge.hcl authn-bridge: client "oidc-agent": access_token_groups = false with ssh_certificates or x509_certificates: the certificates take the groups from the access token, and would carry none -- use one client for the certificates and another for tokens pasted into ssh $ echo $? 1 Give the certificates one client, and the tokens pasted into ssh another.
A token holding one of the provider’s own scopes (ssh, nfs, app_password, wireguard, wireguard_peers) is addressed to the provider alone: its aud is the issuer, and those endpoints refuse any other. A token a resource server received cannot be replayed here:
$ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/certificate -d x -D - -o - HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8 Www-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token" X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff Date: Sun, 11 Oct 2026 09:48:07 GMT Content-Length: 23 the token is not valid An access token already handed out is a signed statement a resource server checks on its own. What RevokePerson ends is everything that comes back here with it; the resource server learns from Shared Signals.
data.what-the-provider-publishes#What the pro: $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:28473/.well-known/openid-configuration | jq . { "authorization_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/authorize", "authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported": true, "claims_parameter_supported": false, "claims_supported": [ "sub", "iss", "aud", "exp", "iat", "auth_time", "nonce", "acr", "name", "given_name", "family_name", "preferred_username", "email", "groups", "eduperson_principal_name", "eduperson_scoped_affiliation", "eduperson_entitlement", "entitlements", "eduperson_assurance", "eduperson_orcid", "schac_home_organization", "voperson_id" ], "code_challenge_methods_supported": [ "S256" ], "device_authorization_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/device_authorization", "grant_types_supported": [ "authorization_code", "refresh_token", "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code" ], "id_token_signing_alg_values_supported": [ "RS256" ], "issuer": "http://127.0.0.1:28473", "jwks_uri": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/jwks", "request_parameter_supported": false, "request_uri_parameter_supported": false, "response_modes_supported": [ "query" ], "response_types_supported": [ "code" ], "scopes_supported": [ "openid", "profile", "email", "eduperson", "groups" ], "subject_types_supported": [ "public", "pairwise" ], "token_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/token", "token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": [ "client_secret_basic", "client_secret_post", "none" ], "userinfo_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/userinfo" } The authorization code flow, with PKCE S256 required for every client. A request with no code_challenge_method is refused rather than read as S256, since RFC 7636 makes plain the default. A confidential client configured pkce = "or_nonce" may send an OpenID nonce instead.
data.wireguard-keys#WireGuard keys:
WireGuard authenticates a peer by its public key and nothing else: no certificate, no expiry, no revocation. So the provider keeps the answer to whose is this key, and may it still connect? The device’s VPN client registers the public key, for a lease; the private key never leaves the device; a gateway reads the live keys as a list signed for it alone.
certificates_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/certificates.json" # keys are recorded beside the certificates wireguard { lifetime = "24h" # the default: how long a key is listed; registering again renews it max_keys = 10 # the default: devices per person } client "vpn" { # what people log in with device = true wireguard_keys = true } client "vpn-gw" { # the gateway's own client secret_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/vpn-gw.secret" wireguard_peers = ["vpn"] # the clients whose keys it reads ssf_receiver = true # optional: told at once when somebody is disabled } POST /wireguard/key {"public_key": "...", "device": "laptop"}, with a token of the wireguard scope; answers the lease’s end DELETE /wireguard/key {"public_key": "..."}: the owner takes a key back GET /wireguard/peers for the gateway’s own client_credentials token, scope wireguard_peers: a signed JWT of type wireguard-peers+jwt, addressed to that gateway, valid five minutes A key somebody else holds, a key that was taken back, and one key too many are refused with 409. A gateway client must be confidential, and must name clients that have wireguard_keys. The format of the list, and the gateway’s side, are go-authn/wireguard’s.
data.without-a-browser-the-device-grant#Witho:
A WebDAV client, a script, a terminal has no browser to send to a university. A client with device = true asks for a code (RFC 8628), and the person logs in on any other device:
client "rclone" { device = true audience = ["fileshare"] refresh_lifetime = "720h" # refresh tokens, off unless set name = "rclone (WebDAV)" } authn-bridge token --issuer https://login.example.org --client rclone prints an access token, logging in the first time and refreshing after that; it is golang.org/x/oauth2’s device client, not one written here.
user codes eight letters from BCDFGHJKLMNPQRSTVWXZ (no vowels, no digits), valid ten minutes; ten wrong codes per host in that time (an IPv4 address, an IPv6 /64), and ten times as many for the /24 or /48 around it polling every five seconds; polling faster earns slow_down waiting devices at most 20,000; past that the oldest is pushed out rather than everybody refused refresh tokens rotated at every use, inside a family whose end is fixed at the login by refresh_lifetime; a retired one used again revokes the family and the access tokens it bought

data:
OpenSSH has no way to distribute a KRL, and nothing in a KRL says it is stale. sshd reads a file that stopped updating months ago as the current list. authn-revokd closes both gaps for the lists authn-bridge publishes: it fetches each list, keeps it only if it verifies, writes it where sshd or a TLS server reads it, and, when a list lapses, writes one that revokes the CA itself. Pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0, one binary. These pages describe v0.6.4.
$ go install github.com/go-authn/revocation/cmd/authn-revokd@v0.6.4 $ authn-revokd -version authn-revokd v0.6.4 $ authn-revokd -help Usage of authn-revokd: -config string the configuration file (default "/etc/authn-revokd/revokd.hcl") -once sync once and exit: 1 when a list is not current, or could not be fetched -version print the version and exit -help exits 0; before v0.6.2 it exited 2.
Before v0.6.0 the command was revokd, and read /etc/revokd.hcl by default. Nothing reads that file any more; when it is there and the new default is not, the error names both paths.
data.what-it-does-in-one-run#What it does, in:
Against a test authn-bridge on loopback, with a KRL source and a CRL source:
$ authn-revokd -config revokd.hcl -once bridge-ssh: version 0, issued 2026-10-11T09:50:24Z, expires 2026-10-11T10:50:24Z bridge-x509: version 1791712224691, issued 2026-10-11T09:50:24Z, expires 2026-10-11T10:50:24Z output sshd: wrote /tmp/authn/revokd/out/sshd.krl output tls: wrote /tmp/authn/revokd/out/bridge.crl $ ssh-keygen -Q -l -f out/sshd.krl # KRL version 0 # Generated at 20261011T115024 # Comment: authn-revokd sshd A second run with nothing new prints nothing and exits 0: an output is rewritten only when its content changes.
data.what-it-does-not-do#What it does not do: A revocation reaches a server no faster than authn-revokd polls (refresh), plus the issuer’s delay in issuing again. While the issuer is down, its certificates are refused from the list’s expiry on. Whoever holds a CA’s key can sign any list, as they can sign any certificate.
data.where-to-go-next#Where to go next: Installing it the daemon, or -once on a timer; wiring sshd and nginx The configuration sources, outputs, the mirror, and what is refused How a list is verified signature, dates, and never older than the list held, across restarts When a list lapses the KRL that revokes the CA itself
data.why-the-transport-does-not-matter#Why th:
Every list authenticates itself: a KRL by a detached SSHSIG signature by the CA’s own key, a CRL by its CA’s signature. Every list says when it stops being current. So a list may come over HTTPS, plain HTTP inside a cluster, a mirror, or a file. The transport decides how fast a change arrives, never whether a forged or stale list is taken.
KRL CRL authentic SSHSIG by the SSH CA key, namespace krl@go-authn.github.io signed by its CA current expires@go-authn.github.io, which sshd ignores nextUpdate never backwards krl_version, then generation date CRL Number, then thisUpdate fail closed authn-revokd writes a KRL that revokes the CA key OpenSSL refuses an expired CRL by itself

data:
One file, /etc/authn-revokd/revokd.hcl by default (-config names another). It is read once, at start.
state_dir = "/var/lib/authn-revokd/state" # the verified copies: what orders the next list refresh = "1m" source "univ-a-ssh" { url = "https://login.univ-a.example/ssh/krl" # and .../ssh/krl.sig beside it ssh_ca = "/etc/authn-revokd/ca/univ-a-ssh.pub" # what the list must be signed by } source "univ-b-ssh" { url = "http://mirror.cluster.local:8080/univ-b-ssh" # a mirror: plain http is fine ssh_ca = "/etc/authn-revokd/ca/univ-b-ssh.pub" } source "univ-a-x509" { url = "https://login.univ-a.example/x509/crl" x509_ca = "/etc/authn-revokd/ca/univ-a-x509.pem" } output "sshd" { # sshd_config: RevokedKeys /var/lib/authn-revokd/sshd.krl path = "/var/lib/authn-revokd/sshd.krl" sources = ["univ-a-ssh", "univ-b-ssh"] # merged into one file } output "tls" { # nginx: ssl_crl /var/lib/authn-revokd/univ-a.crl path = "/var/lib/authn-revokd/univ-a.crl" sources = ["univ-a-x509"] format = "pem" } # listen = "127.0.0.1:8080" # serve the verified lists: a mirror
data.one-krl-for-several-cas#One KRL for seve:
RevokedKeys takes a single file before OpenSSH 10.3, so the KRL sources of an output are merged, and each list keeps its full effect on its own CA, and none on another:
Kept: its serials and key IDs, its sections that name no CA (scoped to its own), and its own CA key, which revokes all its certificates. Left out, and logged: another CA’s section, and another CA’s key. Plain user keys are left out when the output has more than one source, unless the source has revoke_keys = true. A KRL cannot scope a key to one CA: sshd checks a certificate’s own key against the file whoever signed it, so a key one CA names would lock its holder out under every CA of the file. An output with one source keeps them. Each list is first merged alone. One that cannot be merged fails closed for its own CA only; the merged file expires with the first of its current inputs, so a reader that checks expiry sees authn-revokd stop.
data.the-keys#The keys:
key default state_dir required, absolute; created 0700 if missing refresh 1m how often every source is fetched, a second or more; each wait varies by a tenth either way, so a fleet does not stay in step listen host:port: serve the verified lists, a mirror; ignored with -once source "": one list. The name is letters, digits, ., _ and -, not starting with a dot, at most 64 characters: it names a file in the state directory and a path of the mirror.
key url https://, http:// or file://; a KRL’s signature is fetched from the same URL with .sig appended ssh_ca the SSH CA’s public key, one authorized_keys line: a KRL source. A certificate is refused here x509_ca the CA’s PEM certificate: a CRL source max_age also refuse a list issued longer ago than this, besides its own expiry; refused on a source that feeds a CRL output revoke_keys let this source’s list revoke plain keys in an output shared with other sources; KRL sources only output "": one file a server reads.
key path absolute; written beside itself and renamed over sources KRL sources, merged into one file; or exactly one CRL source format der (the default) or pem; CRL outputs only on_change a command and its arguments, run after the file changes, and again at every sync until it succeeds
data.the-mirror#The mirror:
With listen, authn-revokd serves what it holds, from memory, never from the files a write may be half way through:
GET / the list, with an ETag; If-None-Match answers 304 GET /.sig a KRL’s signature; If-Match on another ETag answers 412 GET /healthz 200 ok, or 503 naming each source with no current list and each output that failed $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:28474/healthz ok $ curl -s -D - -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:28474/bridge-ssh HTTP/1.1 200 OK Cache-Control: max-age=30 Content-Type: application/octet-stream Etag: "83278365ecb0f44b05170bb12f151756" Date: Sun, 11 Oct 2026 09:51:05 GMT Content-Length: 130 $ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -H 'If-Match: "stale"' http://127.0.0.1:28474/bridge-ssh.sig 412 A CRL source has no .sig (404). Mirrors chain: a mirror’s source can be another mirror, since every list verifies by itself. A slow upstream never blocks the mirror’s answers.
data.what-is-refused-at-start#What is refused:
Each of these exits 2 before anything is fetched:
authn-revokd: v/relative-state.hcl: state_dir "state": an absolute path authn-revokd: v/refresh.hcl: refresh "500ms": a duration of a second or more authn-revokd: v/both-ca.hcl: source "bridge-ssh": ssh_ca and x509_ca together: one source is one list authn-revokd: v/sig-name.hcl: source "bridge-ssh.sig": a name that ends in .sig, or healthz, is a path the mirror already serves authn-revokd: v/mixed.hcl: output "sshd" mixes KRL and CRL sources authn-revokd: v/krl-format.hcl: output "sshd": format is for CRL outputs; a KRL is what sshd reads authn-revokd: v/revoke-keys-crl.hcl: source "bridge-x509": revoke_keys is for a KRL source (ssh_ca): a CRL revokes its own CA's certificates only So does a configuration that is not there:
$ authn-revokd -config nowhere.hcl -once authn-revokd: nowhere.hcl: no such file or directory Before v0.6.2 it was the HCL parser’s message: nowhere.hcl: : Failed to read file; The configuration file "nowhere.hcl" could not be read.
A CRL output also takes one source (a TLS server reads one CRL per issuer), and a CRL source with max_age is refused, because nothing could enforce it:
authn-revokd: v/crl-maxage.hcl: output "tls": source "bridge-x509" has a max_age, which a CRL output cannot enforce: the TLS server judges a CRL by its nextUpdate alone. Remove max_age, or ask the CA for a closer nextUpdate A TLS server that loaded a CRL keeps it in memory until its nextUpdate, whatever authn-revokd writes.
The state directory is held to sshd’s StrictModes rule. Whoever can replace or remove its files decides which list comes next, and an emptied state lets a replayed older list in. So it may not be a symbolic link, writable by group or others, or owned by anybody but authn-revokd’s user or root. These exit 1:
authn-revokd: state_dir /tmp/authn/revokd/state-wide is writable by its group or by others (mode -rwxrwxrwx): whoever can write there decides which list comes next authn-revokd: state_dir /tmp/authn/revokd/state-link is a symbolic link (L---------): whoever owns it decides where the state is; name the directory itself

data:
The repository ships three units and an account in packaging/: authn-revokd.service (the daemon), authn-revokd-once.service with authn-revokd-once.timer (the alternative), and sysusers.d/authn-revokd.conf.
path what owner, mode /usr/local/bin/authn-revokd the binary root, 0755 /usr/lib/sysusers.d/authn-revokd.conf the authn-revokd system account root, 0644 /etc/systemd/system/authn-revokd.service the daemon root, 0644 /etc/authn-revokd/revokd.hcl the configuration, the default -config root, 0644 /etc/authn-revokd/ca/ the CA keys and certificates the lists must be signed by root, 0755; the files in it 0644 /var/lib/authn-revokd/ StateDirectory=, the only writable place authn-revokd, 0755 /var/lib/authn-revokd/state/ state_dir: the verified copies authn-revokd, 0700 /var/lib/authn-revokd/sshd.krl an output: what sshd reads authn-revokd, 0644 Write the outputs to /var/lib/authn-revokd, and point the servers there. An output is written beside its final name and renamed over it, so its directory must be writable. Making /etc/ssh writable would let the authn-revokd account replace sshd_config. Outputs are 0644, chmod-ed explicitly despite UMask=0077, so that sshd and a TLS server running as its own user can read them; the state stays 0700.
data.a-tls-servers-crl#A TLS server’s CRL: ssl_client_certificate /etc/authn-revokd/ca/univ-a-x509.pem; ssl_verify_client on; ssl_crl /var/lib/authn-revokd/univ-a.crl; # format = "pem" A TLS server reads its CRL when it loads its configuration, so it must be reloaded when the file changes. An on_change command runs as the authn-revokd account, which cannot systemctl reload nginx: let systemd watch the file instead, as root, with a path unit (PathChanged= on the output) that starts a oneshot running systemctl reload nginx.
data.enable-it-before-wiring-sshd#Enable it B:
sshd refuses every certificate when RevokedKeys names a file that does not exist
