So start authn-revokd first, and wait until the output is there: ssh-keygen -Q -l -f /var/lib/authn-revokd/sshd.krl prints its comment, authn-revokd sshd while every source is current.
systemctl enable --now authn-revokd journalctl -u authn-revokd -n 20 # ": version N, issued ..., expires ..." # "output sshd: wrote /var/lib/authn-revokd/sshd.krl" Then, in /etc/ssh/sshd_config:
TrustedUserCAKeys /etc/ssh/ca/univ-a-ssh.pub RevokedKeys /var/lib/authn-revokd/sshd.krl and sshd -t && systemctl reload ssh. sshd reads RevokedKeys at every authentication, so it needs no reload when authn-revokd rewrites the file: the atomic rename is enough.
data.or--once-on-a-timer#Or: -once, on a time:
authn-revokd -once syncs once and exits, 1 when a list is not current or could not be fetched (what -once reports). The outputs are written either way, and failed closed for sshd once a list lapses.
# authn-revokd-once.service [Unit] Conflicts=authn-revokd.service [Service] Type=oneshot ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/authn-revokd -config /etc/authn-revokd/revokd.hcl -once TimeoutStartSec=5min # authn-revokd-once.timer [Unit] Conflicts=authn-revokd.service [Timer] OnBootSec=30s OnUnitActiveSec=1min AccuracySec=5s RandomizedDelaySec=10s [Install] WantedBy=timers.target The one-shot has the daemon’s account and hardening. TimeoutStartSec=5min keeps a sync that hangs on a source from outliving the next tick, and RandomizedDelaySec=10s keeps a fleet started together from polling its issuer in step.
install -m 0644 authn-revokd-once.service authn-revokd-once.timer /etc/systemd/system/ systemctl daemon-reload systemctl disable --now authn-revokd systemctl enable --now authn-revokd-once.timer Never enable both: the units conflict, so starting one stops the other. The daemon remains the better choice. It fails a lapsed list closed at its next refresh, where the timer waits for its next tick, and only the daemon serves as a mirror: listen is ignored with -once. A timer that stops firing is a daemon that stopped, so monitor systemctl status authn-revokd-once.
data.the-binary-the-account-the-unit#The bina:
A release carries authn-revokd-- for Linux, macOS and Windows on amd64 and arm64, with SHA256SUMS and build provenance (verifying a download). Or go install github.com/go-authn/revocation/cmd/authn-revokd@v0.6.4.
The account and the unit come from the packaging/ directory of the release tag, the same version as the binary: copy that directory beside the binary, from a checkout of the tag or, for v0.6.4, from https://github.com/go-authn/revocation/tree/v0.6.4/packaging.
install -m 0755 authn-revokd-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/authn-revokd install -m 0644 packaging/sysusers.d/authn-revokd.conf /usr/lib/sysusers.d/authn-revokd.conf systemd-sysusers /usr/lib/sysusers.d/authn-revokd.conf install -m 0644 packaging/systemd/authn-revokd.service /etc/systemd/system/ systemctl daemon-reload The account is static, not DynamicUser=. authn-revokd refuses a state directory owned by anyone but its own uid or root, and the state must keep ordering the next list across restarts and upgrades. With a dynamic user the files would sit under /var/lib/private, 0700 root, and a TLS server running as its own user could not read the CRL.
data.the-daemon#The daemon:
[Service] Type=exec ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/authn-revokd -config /etc/authn-revokd/revokd.hcl ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID Restart=always and around it: User=authn-revokd, no capability at all, NoNewPrivileges=, ProtectSystem=strict with StateDirectory=authn-revokd (0755) the one writable place, PrivateUsers=, PrivateTmp=, PrivateDevices=, PrivateIPC=, AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX only, @system-service system calls minus @privileged @resources.
Restart=always, because sshd ignores the expiry in the KRL. The file is failed closed by this process when a list lapses. While it is stopped, sshd keeps reading the last file it wrote, and a revocation issued meanwhile never arrives. Monitor the unit, or /healthz when the mirror is on.
systemctl reload syncs now. It sends SIGHUP, and the agent fetches every source at once instead of at the next refresh:
hangup: syncing now It does not re-read the configuration, which is read once, at start: after changing revokd.hcl, systemctl restart authn-revokd. (Before v0.6.0 an uncaught SIGHUP killed the process, and systemd counts that as a clean exit.)
data.uninstalling#Uninstalling: Remove RevokedKeys and ssl_crl from the servers’ configuration first, and reload them: sshd refuses every certificate once the file is gone.
data.upgrading-and-going-back#Upgrading, and: Install the new binary beside the old, swap, restart. The state carries over: the verified copies keep ordering the next lists, so neither an upgrade nor a rollback to an older binary lets an older list in.

data:
A revocation check that lets everything through when the list cannot be had is the one an attacker who can block the list defeats. So when authn-revokd holds no current list from a source, what that source’s list protects is refused, until a current list arrives again.
output while a source has no current list a KRL, for sshd authn-revokd writes a KRL that revokes the source’s CA key a CRL, for a TLS server the expired CRL is left in place; OpenSSL refuses an expired CRL by itself
data.each-ca-for-itself#Each CA for itself: In an output that merges several sources, only the lapsed source’s CA is revoked. The others keep their lists. A list that cannot be merged (past the serial ranges go-authn/krl keeps) fails closed for its own CA only, and /healthz names it. Only if the lists merge alone but not together is every CA of the output revoked, and the comment says so (FAIL CLOSED, the output could not be rendered). Keeping the old file instead would let a later lapse go unseen.
data.for-a-tls-server-the-crl-itself#For a TL: A CRL already says when it stops being current, and OpenSSL refuses one past its nextUpdate (“CRL has expired”). So authn-revokd leaves the last verified CRL in place, and the TLS server fails closed by itself. That is also why max_age is refused on a source that feeds a CRL output: a server that loaded the CRL keeps it until its nextUpdate, whatever authn-revokd writes.
data.for-sshd-revoking-the-ca-itself#For sshd:
sshd has no notion of a list’s expiry: it would go on reading the last file written for ever. But it checks the CA key of every certificate against RevokedKeys. So, in place of the list it cannot vouch for, authn-revokd puts the CA’s own key into the output, and every certificate that CA signed is refused, and nothing else.
Here the issuer is stopped, and the KRL source has max_age = "30s", so the copy held lapses within a minute instead of an hour. The CRL source has no max_age, and its copy is still current:
$ authn-revokd -config revokd-maxage.hcl -once bridge-ssh: revocation: Get "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/krl": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:28473: connect: connection refused bridge-x509: revocation: Get "http://127.0.0.1:28473/x509/crl": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:28473: connect: connection refused output sshd: wrote /tmp/authn/revokd/out/sshd.krl authn-revokd: not current: bridge-ssh; not fetched: bridge-x509 (the list held is current until 2026-10-11T10:50:24Z) $ ssh-keygen -Q -l -f out/sshd.krl # KRL version 0 # Generated at 19700101T010000 # Comment: authn-revokd sshd: FAIL CLOSED, every certificate refused from bridge-ssh hash: SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q # ssh-ed25519 $ ssh-keygen -Q -f out/sshd.krl ca-ssh.pub ca-ssh.pub (go-authn/bridge SSH CA): REVOKED bridge-ssh is not current, and its output is failed closed; bridge-x509 is only not fetched, and its CRL is left as it was (what -once reports). SHA256:Fpa/... is the bridge’s SSH CA. A certificate it signed is now revoked as far as anything reading the file is concerned. The commands above ran in the revokd directory, where out/ is; this one runs beside it, in the directory that holds the test certificates, as on sshcert-authorize’s page, so the same file is ../revokd/out/sshd.krl:
$ ssh-keygen -Q -f ../revokd/out/sshd.krl alice-cert.pub alice-cert.pub (alice): REVOKED The comment says FAIL CLOSED and names the source, so a person reading ssh-keygen -Q -l sees why. The file’s date is 1970 when every source has lapsed. The output is written as soon as a sync notices, which for the daemon is its next refresh and for the timer its next tick. When a current list arrives again, the next sync writes it in place of the CA’s key, and the CA’s certificates are accepted again.
The same happens before the first list: a source never fetched has nothing current, and its CA is revoked from the first write. A new installation refuses the CA’s certificates until its first list verifies, rather than accepting them unchecked.
data.readers-that-check-the-expiry-themselves:
The merged KRL carries an expiry, the first of its current inputs’. A reader that checks it, such as go-fileshare’s ssh_krl_file or sshcert-authorize --krl, sees authn-revokd stop as it would see the issuer stop.
This only works while authn-revokd runs
The file is failed closed by authn-revokd. While it is stopped, sshd keeps reading the last file written, current or not. Hence Restart=always on the daemon, and monitoring the unit, or the timer, or /healthz.

data: A list that does not verify is never written, served or used. The last good copy stays. A fetch that fails, for any reason, never replaces it with an empty answer, which would revoke nothing.
data.across-restarts-too#Across restarts too:
The list held is kept in state_dir, one file per source holding the list and its signature together, written by a single rename with the directory synced. At start each copy is verified again (expired or not, it orders what comes next), and a copy that no longer verifies is not trusted, not even to order the next one, and is said so in the log.
Here a source is pointed, after a restart, at a list an earlier bridge process served nineteen seconds before, still signed and still unexpired:
$ authn-revokd -config revokd.hcl -once bridge-ssh: version 0, issued 2026-10-11T09:50:24Z, expires 2026-10-11T10:50:24Z bridge-x509: version 1791712224691, issued 2026-10-11T09:50:24Z, expires 2026-10-11T10:50:24Z $ authn-revokd -config revokd-old.hcl -once bridge-ssh: file:///tmp/authn/revokd/old/bridge.krl: revocation: the list is older than the one held: version 0 issued at 2026-10-11T09:50:05Z, the copy held at 2026-10-11T09:50:24Z authn-revokd: not fetched: bridge-ssh (the list held is current until 2026-10-11T10:50:24Z) $ ssh-keygen -Q -l -f out/sshd.krl # KRL version 0 # Generated at 20261011T115024 # Comment: authn-revokd sshd The first run wrote no output: the files already held those lists. The older list is refused and the output keeps the newer one. The process that refused it had never seen the newer list: it read it back from state_dir.
Since the state is what makes a rollback detectable, the directory is held to sshd’s StrictModes rule (the configuration). A crash between two writes cannot leave a pair that fails to verify, which would take the rollback guard with it: the list and its signature are one file.
data.never-older-than-the-list-held#Never old: A list’s position is its version (the KRL’s krl_version, the CRL Number), then its issue time (the KRL’s generation date, the CRL’s thisUpdate). A list may replace the one held only when it has a higher version, or the same version issued later: the same revocations, issued again with a new expiry. Anything else is a rollback: a replayed or restored older list, still signed and unexpired, that would un-revoke what the newer one revoked.
data.the-dates#The dates:
A list is current when:
now is before its expiry (the KRL’s extension, the CRL’s nextUpdate); it was not issued more than five minutes in the future: an issuer whose clock is ahead by more than that writes lists whose age cannot be known; with max_age, it was issued no longer ago than that. A list that is not current is refused when fetched. A 304 Not Modified is no news: the copy held may have expired since, and it is judged again at every sync.
data.the-signature#The signature:
A KRL is fetched with its signature, .sig: an armored SSHSIG over the whole file, by the SSH CA key configured as ssh_ca, in the namespace krl@go-authn.github.io. The namespace keeps the signature from being taken for anything else. A signer hashes with SHA-512; SHA-256 is accepted too. An RSA signature in the SHA-1 form, which PROTOCOL.sshsig forbids, is refused.
The KRL itself must parse as sshd parses it, and must not carry OpenSSH’s own signature section, which OpenSSH never verifies.
A list signed by any other key is refused:
$ authn-revokd -config revokd-other.hcl -once bridge-ssh: revocation: the KRL's signature does not verify by SHA256:xm8VDcZUh44N+RQSiPbroPInzkMhN/KCWI/TC+9HPNQ: public key does not match bridge-x509: version 1791712224691, issued 2026-10-11T09:50:24Z, expires 2026-10-11T10:50:24Z output sshd: wrote /tmp/authn/revokd/out/other.krl output tls: wrote /tmp/authn/revokd/out/other.crl authn-revokd: not current: bridge-ssh Here ssh_ca named a key that did not sign bridge’s list, and the error names that key. A signature that does not verify may also be a list issued again between the two requests, so both are fetched once more before it is reported. This was the first fetch of that source, so there was no good copy to keep, and the output is the fail-closed list at once. (Before v0.6.2 the same failure carried “the list changed between it and its signature” in front of the message above, as if the list had been issued again.)
The signature is fetched with If-Match:
data.what--once-reports#What -once reports:
-once exits 1 when a source has no current list, when its last fetch failed, or when an output could not be written, and its last line says which of the first two it is:
last line the source its outputs not current: holds no current list: never fetched, expired, or past max_age failed closed for sshd not fetched: (the list held is current until ) its fetch failed, but the copy held is still current written from that copy, unchanged, until T Here the issuer is stopped while both lists held are still current:
$ authn-revokd -config revokd.hcl -once bridge-ssh: revocation: Get "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/krl": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:28473: connect: connection refused bridge-x509: revocation: Get "http://127.0.0.1:28473/x509/crl": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:28473: connect: connection refused authn-revokd: not fetched: bridge-ssh (the list held is current until 2026-10-11T10:50:24Z), bridge-x509 (the list held is current until 2026-10-11T10:50:24Z) That run left sshd.krl as it was. Once a list held lapses, the same source is reported not current, and both kinds can share the line, as on when a list lapses. Before v0.6.2 both cases were reported not current, which said a list had lapsed when only its fetch had failed; the exit status was 1 then too.
The mirror’s /healthz judges by the copy held instead, and answered ok while the issuer was down and the copies still current.

data:
A site’s people are already in a database, a file or another directory. The things that want to authenticate them speak LDAP. authnd is the front: it binds and searches over go-authn/directory’s sources, so what a database holds can be read by anything that knows how to ask a directory. Pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0, one binary. These pages describe v0.11.1, whose entries follow the standard schemas and pass the schema it serves at cn=Subschema, with go-authn/ldap v0.8.0 and go-authn/directory v0.14.0 under it; what is verified and what is not is on the status page.
Upgrading from v0.10.x
publish_nt_hash = true now needs a samba block, or authnd does not start. A person without uidNumber, gidNumber and homeDirectory is no longer a posixAccount, and a group without a gidNumber no longer a posixGroup, so a consumer filtering on those classes sees fewer entries: see the entries. A users "ldap" block reads more of the directory behind it by default: see people. authnd check with the new binary says all three before the restart.
authnd --config /etc/authnd # serve authnd check /etc/authnd # say what would be served, without listening
data.the-smallest-configuration#The smallest:
listen = "127.0.0.1:3893" # the default base_dn = "dc=example,dc=org" # required reader "cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org" { password_file = "/etc/authnd/reader.pw" } user "alice" { password_file = "/etc/authnd/passwords/alice.pw" } group "staff" { members = ["alice"] } People are published as uid=,ou=people,, groups as cn=,ou=groups,. What each entry is follows from what its source gave: a person is an account, or an inetOrgPerson when there is an sn, and a posixAccount only with uidNumber, gidNumber and homeDirectory; every person is a uidObject. A group is a posixGroup (with memberUid) when it has a gidNumber, otherwise a groupOfNames (with member DNs), or an organizationalRole when it is also empty. sshPublicKey is added when the person has keys, and sambaNTPassword when publish_nt_hash says so and a SID can be given. Every entry passes the schema served at cn=Subschema before it is published: see the entries and the schema. Up to v0.10.2 every person was a posixAccount and every group a posixGroup, whatever they had.
--config (-c) takes a file or a directory and may be repeated; a directory is every .hcl file in it, read in name order and merged into one configuration. A configuration with no base_dn, or with nobody in it, does not start.
data.where-to-go-next#Where to go next:
Installing it the release binary, the authnd account, the systemd unit, upgrades Where the people come from user and group blocks, a SQL database, another LDAP directory The entries and the schema what each person and group is published as, cn=Subschema, attributes, what is dropped or withheld check read the configuration back before restarting TLS ldaps:// or StartTLS, and publish_nt_hash Changing a password ldappasswd, ldapmodify, and why the old password is always asked for A Kerberos realm the keytab, and who can be issued a ticket A second factor a one-time code on the end of the password A token at the bind OIDC over SASL OAUTHBEARER Running it signals, restarts, what it logs, how to tell it is up About the transcripts
Every startup line, the root DSE and the --version lines were printed by the v0.11.1 release binary (authnd-darwin-arm64, go version -m: mod github.com/go-authn/authnd v0.11.1, vcs.modified=false), and so was every other command shown in the same transcript as a startup line. v0.11.1 changes nothing but that line. Every check table, the entries read back with ldapsearch, cn=Subschema and the samba refusals were printed by the v0.11.0 release binary (mod github.com/go-authn/authnd v0.11.0, vcs.modified=false). So were the configuration refusals on these pages, which v0.11.0 printed byte for byte as v0.10.0 had. The other binds, kinits, password changes and token exchanges were printed by the v0.10.0 release binary and were not run again, since neither v0.11.0’s nor v0.11.1’s release notes change any of them. All of them were asked by the OpenLDAP and Heimdal clients that ship with macOS, on 127.0.0.1 on unprivileged ports, in a scratch directory under /tmp. That is why the configurations behind them name files by relative paths such as etc/authnd/passwords/alice.pw, and why the password files have names like alice.pwin. The /etc/authnd paths in the examples are what an installed server uses.
data.who-may-bind-and-who-may-read#Who may bi:
An LDAP server is asked to prove people, so its refusals are the design. These are answers from the v0.10.0 release binary to OpenLDAP’s own client:
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin dn:uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org $ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y wrong.pwin ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49) $ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -w '' ldap_bind: Server is unwilling to perform (53) additional info: an unauthenticated bind proves nothing, and this server does not accept one $ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -b dc=example,dc=org '(uid=alice)' Insufficient access (50) Additional information: only a reader may search request answer why empty name, empty password (RFC 4513 §5.1.1, anonymous) success it says “I am nobody”, which is true, and a client sends it before it has discovered anything a name and an empty password (§5.1.2, unauthenticated) unwillingToPerform it names somebody and proves nothing; §5.1.2 asks for exactly this code. invalidCredentials would tell a person their password was wrong a wrong password, or a name nobody here has invalidCredentials the two are not told apart a search by anybody but a reader insufficientAccessRights binding proves who you are; reading everybody is a separate thing to be allowed add, delete, modifyDN unwillingToPerform no handler is wired for them; the one write is a person’s own password A reader is a service account with a bind DN and password or password_file; a reader with neither is refused at startup (a reader that proves nothing is anonymous search with extra steps). Without any reader, nothing may search, and check says so.
The root DSE is answered to an anonymous client, as discovery needs:
$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -s base -b '' '+' '*' dn: objectClass: top objectClass: OpenLDAProotDSE supportedLDAPVersion: 3 namingContexts: dc=example,dc=org supportedExtension: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.3 supportedExtension: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.1 supportedControl: 1.2.840.113556.1.4.319 supportedControl: 1.3.6.1.1.13.1 supportedControl: 1.3.6.1.1.13.2 supportedFeatures: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.1 supportedFeatures: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.3 subschemaSubentry: cn=Subschema vendorName: go-authn/authnd vendorVersion: v0.11.1 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.1 is the RFC 3062 password modify operation. subschemaSubentry names the schema, which is answered to an anonymous client as well. supportedSASLMechanisms: OAUTHBEARER appears only with an oidc block.

data: authnd check /etc/authnd authnd check --config a.hcl --config b.hcl check reads the configuration exactly as the server does, opens everything the server opens before it listens — the files, the database, the directory behind this one, the identity provider’s discovery document, the TLS certificate and key, the keytab — and prints what would be published and to whom, without listening. It prints where every credential comes from and never what is in it. It exits 0 and ends with this configuration can be served, or exits 1 with the one sentence that stops the server.
data.a-configuration-that-can-be-served#A con:
Two user blocks, a reader, and a SQLite database, in a directory of two files (authnd.hcl and people.hcl):
$ authnd check etc/authnd ldap://127.0.0.1:3893, base dc=example,dc=org USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH alice the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid bob the configuration file an NT hash account, uidObject uid dora a sqlite database a password account, uidObject uid eli a sqlite database an NT hash account, uidObject uid GROUP MEMBERS PUBLISHED AS engineers dora and eli groupOfNames staff alice, bob and dora groupOfNames alice has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject bob has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject dora has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject eli has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject group engineers has no gidNumber: not a posixGroup, published as a groupOfNames (member DNs, no memberUid) group staff has no gidNumber: not a posixGroup, published as a groupOfNames (member DNs, no memberUid) a bind carries a password bob and eli cannot bind with a password: their sources hold only what an SMB server needs (an NT hash), which a bind cannot be checked against cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org may search; every other bound client may not sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it) this configuration can be served
data.reading-it#Reading it:
The first line is the scheme, the address and the base: ldap://, ldaps://, or ldap+starttls:// — see TLS.
column FROM the source that owns the name: the configuration file, a sqlite database (or postgres, mysql), or the url of a directory behind this one CAN PROVE a password (held, so it can be compared and keys derived from it), a password check (another directory answers yes or no), an NT hash, N keys, a one-time-code secret, or nothing PUBLISHED AS the entry’s object classes, without top, as the shapes give them — or NOT PUBLISHED (see below) for an entry that fails the schema WITH the attributes the entry carries, read off the entry a search returns: uid; cn wherever a class allows it; what the sources gave, less what was dropped; sshPublicKey when there are keys; sambaSID and sambaNTPassword when publish_nt_hash is on and the person has an NT key and a SID The group table has a PUBLISHED AS column too: posixGroup, groupOfNames or organizationalRole. Up to v0.10.2, PUBLISHED AS was the list of attributes, uid and cn for nearly everybody, and there was no WITH column.
The lines after the tables say what a person needs to know before relying on the configuration. First, about the entries:
who is not a posixAccount, and which of uidNumber, gidNumber and homeDirectory they lack; which groups have no gidNumber, and what they are published as instead; every attribute dropped because no class of its entry allows it, and which classes would; every entry not published, with each problem the schema check found; who has an NT key and no sambaSID, and so no sambaNTPassword. Then, about binds and searches:
what a bind carries: a password, or, with an mfa block, a password with a 6-digit code after it; with an oidc block, where tokens come from and over what; who cannot bind with a password at all: people known only by an NT hash — see people; who may search: the readers, or no reader is declared: nothing may search, and binds are not affected; whether sambaNTPassword is published, and over what — see publish_nt_hash; with a kerberos block, the realm and who can and who cannot be issued a ticket, with the reason; with an mfa block, who has no second factor, and so cannot bind with a password; with an oidc block beside it the line adds that a token whose amr names two kinds still can; a group that names somebody no source has. That last one is published as it stands — a front for one system legitimately carries names another one owns — but it is said, because the other reading is a typo. In a posixGroup the stranger is a memberUid; in a groupOfNames it is a member DN that names no entry here, member: uid=zoe,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org here, which go-authn/directory’s ldapdir from v0.14.0 maps to nobody. Here the database’s team_members table has a row for zoe, who is nobody here:
GROUP MEMBERS PUBLISHED AS engineers dora, eli and zoe groupOfNames staff alice, bob and dora groupOfNames [...] engineers names zoe, who has no entry here: the group is published as it stands, and nothing here can prove them (A group block naming a stranger is refused outright; see people.)
data.run-it-as-the-service-account#Run it as: sudo -u authnd authnd check /etc/authnd so that a file only root can read fails here, not at the restart. Run it with the new binary before an upgrade; see install.
data.the-certificate-the-keytab-and-the-one-t:
A certificate that does not load and a keytab without krbtgt/REALM are refused by check, in the words the server would use:
$ authnd check cases/badcert authnd: the certificate: open tls/missing.pem: no such file or directory $ authnd check cases/nokrbtgt authnd: kdc: the keytab has no krbtgt key for this realm: matching key not found in keytab. Looking for "krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG" realm: EXAMPLE.ORG kvno: 0 etype: 18 What check cannot know without listening is whether the ports are free. A second server on the same Kerberos address passes check and is refused at start:
$ authnd --config cases/realm2 authnd: kerberos udp 127.0.0.1:18388: listen udp 127.0.0.1:18388: bind: address already in use
data.what-it-refuses#What it refuses:
Each of these stops check and the server alike, with exit status 1. They are on the pages where they belong; a few, as printed:
$ authnd check cases/nobody.hcl authnd: there is nobody here: name a user, or a users block reading a database or a directory $ authnd check cases/nthash-clear.hcl authnd: publish_nt_hash needs cert_file and key_file: an NT hash IS the credential, and 0.0.0.0:3893 is not loopback, so it would cross a network in the clear $ authnd check cases/krb-mfa.hcl authnd: kerberos and mfa together: the mfa block asks every bind for a password AND a code, and a kinit carries only the password -- this KDC has no second-factor pre-authentication, so a realm here would accept one factor where the mfa block demands two. Remove one of the blocks $ authnd check empty authnd: empty has no .hcl files in it $ authnd authnd: no configuration: give a .hcl file or a directory of them

data:
Every entry authnd publishes passes the schema it serves. From v0.11.0 each person and group is a standard-schema entry, built from what its source gave, and checked with go-authn/ldap’s schema.Validate against the schema a client can read at cn=Subschema before it is ever returned by a search. A client that reads the schema and believes it — an LDAP browser, a synchronisation tool, a directory replicating this one — is shown what it was told. Up to v0.10.2 every person was top, person, posixAccount with none of the attributes those classes require, and sambaNTPassword sat on an entry with no class that allows it.
A consumer filtering on posixAccount or posixGroup sees fewer entries
A person without uidNumber, gidNumber and homeDirectory is no longer a posixAccount, and a group without a gidNumber is no longer a posixGroup. A program that searches (objectClass=posixAccount) or (objectClass=posixGroup) no longer finds them. That includes go-authn/directory’s ldapdir up to v0.13.0, and so go-fileshare until it requires directory v0.14.0, whose defaults also read account, uidObject and groupOfNames (directory). Give people and groups those attributes, or point the consumer at (objectClass=uidObject), which every person carries.
data.a-configuration-and-what-it-publishes#A:
The SQL block above, with a reader, over a SQLite database of five people and four groups, as the v0.11.0 release binary checks it:
listen = "127.0.0.1:3893" base_dn = "dc=example,dc=org" reader "cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org" { password_file = "etc/authnd/reader.pw" } users "sql" { driver = "sqlite" dsn_file = "etc/authnd/people.dsn" users = "select login, secret, null, ssh_keys from staff" groups = "select team, member from teams" users_attributes = "select login, sn, uid as uidNumber, gid as gidNumber, home as homeDirectory, mail from person_attrs" groups_attributes = "select team, gid as gidNumber, description from team_attrs" } $ authnd check etc/authnd ldap://127.0.0.1:3893, base dc=example,dc=org USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH dora a sqlite database a password and 1 key person, organizationalPerson, inetOrgPerson, posixAccount, ldapPublicKey, uidObject uid, cn, sn, uidNumber, gidNumber, homeDirectory, mail and sshPublicKey eli a sqlite database a password account, posixAccount, uidObject uid, cn, uidNumber, gidNumber and homeDirectory fay a sqlite database a password person, organizationalPerson, inetOrgPerson, uidObject uid, cn, sn and mail gus a sqlite database a password account, uidObject uid hal a sqlite database a password account, uidObject uid GROUP MEMBERS PUBLISHED AS alumni nobody organizationalRole engineers dora and eli posixGroup nobody-yet nobody posixGroup readers fay and gus groupOfNames fay has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as person, organizationalPerson, inetOrgPerson, uidObject gus has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject hal has no homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject hal is published without uidNumber: no class of the entry allows it; posixAccount would hal is published without gidNumber: no class of the entry allows it; posixAccount and posixGroup would hal is published without mail: no class of the entry allows it; inetOrgPerson would group alumni has no gidNumber and nobody in it: not a posixGroup, published as an organizationalRole (a groupOfNames needs a member) group readers has no gidNumber: not a posixGroup, published as a groupOfNames (member DNs, no memberUid) a bind carries a password cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org may search; every other bound client may not sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it) this configuration can be served PUBLISHED AS is each entry’s object classes, without top, and WITH its attributes, read off the entries a search returns. hal has a uidNumber, a gidNumber and a mail and no homeDirectory or sn: hal is an account, which allows none of the three, so they are dropped and the rest is published. The server says the same at startup (and stopping when it was stopped):
$ authnd --config etc/authnd ldap on 127.0.0.1:3893, serving 5 people from a sqlite database uid=hal,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org is published without uidNumber: no class of the entry allows it; posixAccount would uid=hal,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org is published without gidNumber: no class of the entry allows it; posixAccount and posixGroup would uid=hal,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org is published without mail: no class of the entry allows it; inetOrgPerson would stopping Read back by OpenLDAP’s ldapsearch, with the reader’s password in a file:
$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -o ldif-wrap=no -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b ou=people,dc=example,dc=org '(|(uid=dora)(uid=eli)(uid=gus)(uid=hal))' dn: uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org objectClass: top objectClass: person objectClass: organizationalPerson objectClass: inetOrgPerson objectClass: posixAccount objectClass: ldapPublicKey objectClass: uidObject uid: dora cn: dora sn: Explorer uidNumber: 1000 gidNumber: 1000 homeDirectory: /home/dora mail: dora@example.org sshPublicKey: ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIKTfVR7FqXWE/0VEcjrUhK+Fz/MLqlwGPIxalr6onRMn dora@laptop dn: uid=eli,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org objectClass: top objectClass: account objectClass: posixAccount objectClass: uidObject uid: eli cn: eli uidNumber: 1001 gidNumber: 1001 homeDirectory: /home/eli dn: uid=gus,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org objectClass: top objectClass: account objectClass: uidObject uid: gus dn: uid=hal,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org objectClass: top objectClass: account objectClass: uidObject uid: hal $ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org '(objectClass=*)' dn: cn=alumni,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org objectClass: top objectClass: organizationalRole cn: alumni description: people who were here dn: cn=engineers,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org objectClass: top objectClass: posixGroup cn: engineers gidNumber: 2000 memberUid: dora memberUid: eli dn: cn=nobody-yet,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org objectClass: top objectClass: posixGroup cn: nobody-yet gidNumber: 2001 dn: cn=readers,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org objectClass: top objectClass: groupOfNames cn: readers description: people who read member: uid=fay,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org member: uid=gus,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org alumni is named only in groups_attributes, so it exists with nobody in it; without a gidNumber it is an organizationalRole. nobody-yet has a gidNumber and nobody, so it is a posixGroup without memberUid.
Which class finds whom:
$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b dc=example,dc=org '(objectClass=uidObject)' 1.1 dn: uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org dn: uid=eli,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org dn: uid=fay,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org dn: uid=gus,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org dn: uid=hal,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org $ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b dc=example,dc=org '(objectClass=posixAccount)' 1.1 dn: uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org dn: uid=eli,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
data.adding-attributes#Adding attributes: What a source says about somebody that proves nothing — a uidNumber, a home directory, a mail address — is an attribute, published as given. They are go-authn/directory’s attributes, from v0.13.0, and they are kept apart from credentials: a name that holds a secret, or one the server derives itself, is refused before anything is read.
data.from-another-ldap-directory#From another: A users "ldap" block copies the attributes it is told to, from each person’s entry and each group’s: attributes = ["mail", "uidNumber", "homeDirectory"] and group_attributes = ["gidNumber"]. See people.
data.in-a-sql-database#In a SQL database:
Two optional queries of a users "sql" block read attributes by column alias. The first column is the person’s or the group’s name; every other column is an attribute named by its alias:
users "sql" { driver = "sqlite" dsn_file = "/etc/authnd/people.dsn" users = "select login, secret, null, ssh_keys from staff" groups = "select team, member from teams" users_attributes = "select login, sn, uid as uidNumber, gid as gidNumber, home as homeDirectory, mail from person_attrs" groups_attributes = "select team, gid as gidNumber, description from team_attrs" } The positional users and groups queries are unchanged, and a sixth positional column is still refused: attributes come by name, in their own query. A column whose alias is not an attribute description (an unaliased expression such as count(*)), or names a credential, is refused with its column number before a row is read. NULL and '' are absent. A name may come back on several rows, and the values of all of them are kept, so a join to a table of addresses gives a person several. A group named only in groups_attributes exists, with nobody in it: that is how a person’s own primary group is written. The case of an alias is the database’s
PostgreSQL folds an unquoted alias to lower case: as uidNumber comes back as uidnumber. Attribute names are case-insensitive, so it is the same attribute and the entry is the same entry to every LDAP client, but the spelling authnd prints is the database’s. Quote the alias where the spelling matters: gid as "gidNumber". SQLite keeps an alias as written.
data.in-a-user-or-group-block#In a user or gr:
user "dora" { password_file = "/etc/authnd/passwords/dora.pw" authorized_keys = ["ssh-ed25519 AAAA… dora@laptop"] attributes = { sn = "Explorer" # inetOrgPerson uidNumber = "1000" # the three: posixAccount gidNumber = "1000" homeDirectory = "/home/dora" mail = ["dora@example.org", "d.explorer@example.org"] } } group "engineers" { members = ["dora", "eli"] attributes = { gidNumber = "2000" } # a posixGroup; without it, a groupOfNames } A value is a string or a list of strings; null leaves the attribute out. A number is refused, because an LDAP value is a string and authnd does not choose how a number is spelled:
$ authnd check cases/number.hcl authnd: user "alice": attributes: uidNumber is the number 1000: write it as a string, "1000" -- an LDAP value is a string, and this does not choose how a number is spelled $ authnd check cases/secret.hcl authnd: user "alice": attributes: directory: not an attribute this package carries: "userPassword" holds a secret, and attributes are published: a credential has its own option or none Refused the same way, whatever their case: any name holding a secret (userPassword, sambaNTPassword, unicodePwd, krbPrincipalKey and the rest of go-authn/directory’s list, or any name containing password, passwd, pwd, secret, credential, hash or privatekey); sshPublicKey, which has authorized_keys; uid, cn and objectClass, which the server derives; member, memberUid and the other membership attributes, which members answers; the operational attributes a server maintains; and a name in numeric form (2.5.4.35 is userPassword).
data.the-schema-it-serves#The schema it serve:
The root DSE names it (subschemaSubentry: cn=Subschema, on the root DSE), and a base search of cn=Subschema returns it (RFC 4512 §4.2): the standard definitions go-authn/ldap embeds — RFC 4512, 4517, 4519, 4523, 4524, 2798, 2307, 3672 and 3045, and openssh-lpk — plus Samba’s sambaSamAccount, sambaSID and sambaNTPassword when there is a samba block. The definitions are published only when asked for by name or with +. Trimmed where marked:
$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -o ldif-wrap=no -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -s base -b cn=Subschema '+' '*' dn: cn=Subschema objectClass: top objectClass: subentry objectClass: subschema cn: Subschema subtreeSpecification: {} ldapSyntaxes: ( 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.3 DESC 'Attribute Type Description' ) [...] matchingRules: ( 2.5.13.15 NAME 'integerOrderingMatch' SYNTAX 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.27 ) [...] attributeTypes: ( 1.3.6.1.1.1.1.0 NAME 'uidNumber' DESC 'An integer uniquely identifying a user in an administrative domain' EQUALITY integerMatch ORDERING integerOrderingMatch SYNTAX 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.27 SINGLE-VALUE ) attributeTypes: ( 1.3.6.1.1.1.1.1 NAME 'gidNumber' DESC 'An integer uniquely identifying a group in an administrative domain' EQUALITY integerMatch ORDERING integerOrderingMatch SYNTAX 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.27 SINGLE-VALUE ) [...] objectClasses: ( 2.5.6.9 NAME 'groupOfNames' SUP top STRUCTURAL MUST ( member $ cn ) MAY ( businessCategory $ seeAlso $ owner $ ou $ o $ description ) ) [...] objectClasses: ( 1.3.6.1.1.3.1 NAME 'uidObject' SUP top AUXILIARY MUST uid ) objectClasses: ( 0.9.2342.19200300.100.4.5 NAME 'account' SUP top STRUCTURAL MUST uid MAY ( description $ seeAlso $ l $ o $ ou $ host ) ) [...] objectClasses: ( 1.3.6.1.1.1.2.0 NAME 'posixAccount' DESC 'Abstraction of an account with POSIX attributes' SUP top AUXILIARY MUST ( cn $ uid $ uidNumber $ gidNumber $ homeDirectory ) MAY ( userPassword $ loginShell $ gecos $ description ) ) [...] objectClasses: ( 1.3.6.1.1.1.2.2 NAME 'posixGroup' DESC 'Abstraction of a group of accounts' SUP top STRUCTURAL MUST ( cn $ gidNumber ) MAY ( userPassword $ memberUid $ description ) ) [...] The whole entry was 327 lines: 49 syntaxes, 40 matching rules, 36 matching rule uses, 143 attribute types and 52 object classes. Unlike a search under the base, the subschema entry, like the root DSE, is answered to an anonymous client: the same query without -D and -y returned it.
Filters use the schema’s matching rules, so (uidNumber>=1000) compares integers. uidNumber and gidNumber have ORDERING integerOrderingMatch, which RFC 2307 does not give them; slapd and draft-howard-rfc2307bis-02 do, and so does go-authn/ldap (its one departure). As strings, 1000 sorts before 999:
$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b dc=example,dc=org '(uidNumber>=1000)' uidNumber dn: uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org uidNumber: 1000 dn: uid=eli,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org uidNumber: 1001 $ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b dc=example,dc=org '(uidNumber>=999)' uidNumber dn: uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org uidNumber: 1000 dn: uid=eli,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org uidNumber: 1001 hal is not there: hal’s uidNumber was dropped. A range on an attribute with no ORDERING rule, such as uid, is Undefined and matches nothing.
data.the-shapes#The shapes:
Every superclass is listed, as RFC 4512 §3.3 asks.
a person with… objectClass cn no sn top, account (RFC 4524 §3.1) only when another class allows it sn top, person, organizationalPerson, inetOrgPerson (RFC 4519, RFC 2798) yes … and uidNumber, gidNumber, homeDirectory, all three + posixAccount (RFC 2307) yes … and SSH keys + ldapPublicKey (openssh-lpk), with sshPublicKey … and a published NT hash with a sambaSID + sambaSamAccount (Samba), with sambaSID and sambaNTPassword: see the samba block allowed … always + uidObject (RFC 4519 §3.14), so (objectClass=uidObject) finds everybody a group with… objectClass members a gidNumber top, posixGroup (RFC 2307) memberUid, names no gidNumber, somebody in it top, groupOfNames (RFC 4519 §3.5) member, the DNs this server publishes no gidNumber, nobody in it top, organizationalRole (RFC 4519 §3.10) none a gidNumber, nobody in it top, posixGroup none: an attribute has at least one value uid is the person’s name, and so is cn wherever a class allows it. An account alone does not allow cn (its MAY is description, seeAlso, l, o, ou and host), so a person without sn and without the POSIX trio carries uid and no cn.
Why these choices, from authnd’s own reasons:
posixGroup follows RFC 2307, not draft-howard-rfc2307bis-02. The draft makes posixGroup AUXILIARY and expired unpublished; an AUXILIARY posixGroup would need a structural class beside it, groupOfNames, whose member an empty group cannot give. organizationalRole for an empty group without a gidNumber. groupOfNames and groupOfUniqueNames both require a member, and the ways of inventing one are false: member: "" names the root DSE, and the group’s own DN makes it a member of itself. organizationalRole is the one standard structural class whose only MUST is cn, and it takes description, ou and seeAlso as groupOfNames does. Auxiliary classes without DIT content rules. RFC 4512 §2.4.3 forbids auxiliary classes on an entry whose structural class has no DIT content rule. Every directory server in use allows them, and so does Validate.
data.what-is-dropped-and-what-is-withheld#Wha:
given the entry why uidNumber, gidNumber, no homeDirectory, no sn account, uidObject, without the two no class of the entry allows it; posixAccount would mail, no sn account, uidObject, without it no class of the entry allows it; inetOrgPerson would a type the schema does not define the rest the schema served here does not define it mail on a group without a gidNumber groupOfNames, without it two homeDirectory values with the POSIX trio withheld: SINGLE-VALUE, nothing to drop a gidNumber that is not an integer withheld: not of its syntax Only what a source gave is dropped, and which attribute is not allowed is Validate’s answer, not a second reading of the schema. The entry is validated again after dropping. An entry that still fails is withheld: it is absent from every search, the startup log names it, and check lists it with every problem Validate found. An attribute authnd derives itself (uid, cn, objectClass, sshPublicKey, sambaSID, sambaNTPassword) that the schema refused would be a defect in authnd, and withholds the entry rather than publish it without.
alice’s gidNumber is a word here:
listen = "127.0.0.1:3893" base_dn = "dc=example,dc=org" reader "cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org" { password_file = "etc/authnd/reader.pw" } user "alice" { password_file = "etc/authnd/alice.pw" attributes = { uidNumber = "1000" gidNumber = "staff" homeDirectory = "/home/alice" } } user "bob" { password_file = "etc/authnd/bob.pw" } $ authnd check cases/withheld.hcl ldap://127.0.0.1:3893, base dc=example,dc=org USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH alice the configuration file a password NOT PUBLISHED (see below) uid, cn, gidNumber, homeDirectory and uidNumber bob the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid bob has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject alice is NOT published: as account, posixAccount, uidObject it fails the schema: - the value "staff" of gidNumber is not of its syntax 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.27 a bind carries a password cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org may search; every other bound client may not sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it) this configuration can be served Served, alice can still bind and is in no search, and the server says why at startup:
$ authnd --config cases/withheld.hcl ldap on 127.0.0.1:3893, serving 2 people from the configuration file uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org is NOT published: it fails the schema: the value "staff" of gidNumber is not of its syntax 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.27 $ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin dn:uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org $ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b dc=example,dc=org '(uid=alice)' What is withheld is the entry a search returns, not the identity.

data: The repository carries the two files a systemd host needs: packaging/sysusers.d/authnd.conf (the account) and packaging/systemd/authnd.service (the unit). This page explains both and the steps around them. go-pkgx’s versioned services are meant to do this for you later; they do not exist yet.
data.building-only-what-you-want#Building onl: The server is always there; two build tags leave out where people can come from. -tags nosql drops the three database drivers (PostgreSQL through pgx, MySQL/MariaDB, SQLite through modernc.org/sqlite) and the users "sql" block; -tags noldap drops the LDAP client and the users "ldap" block. A configuration naming a block the binary was built without is told so — this binary was built without SQL support (-tags nosql) — rather than that the block does not exist. The release binaries are built without tags.
data.the-account#The account:
#Type Name ID Description Home Shell u authnd - "authnd LDAP directory and Kerberos KDC" /var/lib/authnd - A static account from sysusers.d, not DynamicUser=. The files authnd reads — password files, a DSN, a keytab, a TLS key — are secrets given to the authnd group ahead of time, and a password change writes back into them. A dynamic uid does not exist until the service starts, and a file it wrote would belong to a number that later means somebody else.
The two files come from the packaging/ directory of the release tag, the same version as the binary: copy that directory beside the binary, from a checkout of the tag or, for v0.11.1, from https://github.com/go-authn/authnd/tree/v0.11.1/packaging.
sudo install -m 0755 "authnd-linux-$arch" /usr/local/bin/authnd sudo install -m 0644 packaging/sysusers.d/authnd.conf /usr/lib/sysusers.d/authnd.conf sudo systemd-sysusers /usr/lib/sysusers.d/authnd.conf sudo install -m 0644 packaging/systemd/authnd.service /etc/systemd/system/authnd.service sudo systemd-analyze verify /etc/systemd/system/authnd.service sudo systemctl daemon-reload
data.the-configuration-directory#The configur:
sudo install -d -o root -g authnd -m 0750 /etc/authnd Every file inside it root:authnd, mode 0640. Secrets go in files named by *_file keys rather than inline: a file has permissions, and a configuration someone pastes does not. With ProtectSystem=strict the service cannot write under /etc, which is right for the configuration and wrong for the passwords people change themselves — give those a directory of their own:
sudo install -d -o authnd -g authnd -m 0700 /etc/authnd/passwords sudo systemctl edit authnd [Service] ReadWritePaths=/etc/authnd/passwords Why that directory and not the file is explained in changing a password.
key default base_dn — (required) the root of the tree, e.g. dc=example,dc=org; a value with no = is refused listen 127.0.0.1:3893 one address. Loopback by default: a directory that appears on every interface the moment it starts is a decision somebody should make on purpose. A site that needs LDAP and LDAPS runs two instances reader "" none a service account that may search; see who may read cert_file, key_file, starttls, publish_nt_hash, samba off TLS user, group, users — the people; at least one user or users block kerberos none a realm mfa none a second factor oidc none a token at the bind A relative path in the configuration is resolved against the directory the process runs in, not the configuration file’s; the unit runs from /, so write paths absolute.
Before every start:
sudo -u authnd authnd check /etc/authnd sudo systemctl enable --now authnd journalctl -u authnd check is described on its own page; running it as authnd also proves the account can read every file.
data.the-release-binary#The release binary:
Each tag publishes authnd-- for linux, darwin and windows on amd64 and arm64 (.exe on windows), built with CGO_ENABLED=0, a SHA256SUMS manifest, and a build provenance attestation for every binary.
version=v0.11.1 arch=amd64 # or arm64 base=https://github.com/go-authn/authnd/releases/download/$version curl -fsSLO "$base/authnd-linux-$arch" curl -fsSLO "$base/SHA256SUMS" sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing # the bytes the release published gh attestation verify "authnd-linux-$arch" --repo go-authn/authnd # built by the release workflow, at that tag Stop if either check fails. The release workflow refuses to publish a binary that does not report exactly the tag it is published under, so the version is something to compare:
$ authnd --version authnd version v0.11.1
data.upgrade-roll-back-remove#Upgrade, roll b:
Check the configuration with the new binary before it replaces the old one, and keep the old one. The new binary is installed beside the old one first: that makes it executable, and puts it where the authnd account can run it.
sudo install -m 0755 "authnd-linux-$arch" /usr/local/bin/authnd.new sudo -u authnd /usr/local/bin/authnd.new check /etc/authnd sudo cp /usr/local/bin/authnd /usr/local/bin/authnd.previous sudo mv /usr/local/bin/authnd.new /usr/local/bin/authnd sudo systemctl restart authnd authnd --version Compare packaging/ at the new tag with what is installed (v0.11.1’s is v0.10.2’s, unchanged). Rolling back is the same install from authnd.previous, and a restart.
From v0.10.x to v0.11.0 the check above is the step that matters: a configuration with publish_nt_hash = true and no samba block is refused there rather than at the restart, and the lines after its tables say who is no longer a posixAccount and which groups are no longer posixGroups (the entries).
To remove it:
sudo systemctl disable --now authnd sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/authnd.service sudo rm -r /etc/systemd/system/authnd.service.d # if a drop-in was added sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo rm /usr/local/bin/authnd /usr/local/bin/authnd.previous /usr/lib/sysusers.d/authnd.conf /etc/authnd, /var/lib/authnd and the authnd account are left in place: the first two hold people’s credentials, and a uid that is reused can be given somebody else’s files. Remove them deliberately.
data.what-the-unit-grants-and-why#What the un:
[Service] Type=exec ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/authnd --config /etc/authnd Restart=on-failure RestartSec=5s User=authnd Group=authnd UMask=0077 AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE NoNewPrivileges=yes StateDirectory=authnd StateDirectoryMode=0700 ProtectSystem=strict The rest of the unit is the usual hardening (ProtectHome, PrivateTmp, PrivateDevices, ProtectProc=invisible, the kernel and cgroup protections, MemoryDenyWriteExecute, SystemCallFilter=@system-service, RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX). Three things it leaves out are deliberate:
ExecReload= authnd has no reload. It reads its configuration, certificate and keytab once; see running it PrivateUsers= inside a user namespace CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE no longer applies to the host’s network, and the bind to 389 is refused ProcSubset=pid it hides /proc/sys, where Go reads net/core/somaxconn, and every listener’s backlog falls to Go’s fallback of 128 IPAddressAllow=/IPAddressDeny= are not set either: which networks may ask a directory is the site’s to say, in a drop-in:
sudo systemctl edit authnd [Service] IPAddressDeny=any IPAddressAllow=localhost 10.0.0.0/8 The one capability is for the privileged ports: LDAP 389, LDAPS 636, and Kerberos 88 over UDP and TCP. A PostgreSQL or MariaDB on the same machine is reached through its socket, which a read-only file system allows. The state directory, /var/lib/authnd, is there for a SQLite database; authnd keeps no state of its own — the second-factor lockout counts live in memory and are reset at every restart.

data:
kerberos { realm = "EXAMPLE.ORG" # required, upper case keytab = "/etc/authnd/krb5.keytab" # required; must hold krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG listen = "127.0.0.1:88" # the default; UDP and TCP both lifetime = "10h" # the default, MIT's } A kerberos block makes authnd a KDC as well as a directory, through go-authn/kdc: the same people are issued tickets instead of only being looked up. It answers on UDP and TCP at the same address, requires encrypted-timestamp pre-authentication, and issues aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 tickets only. lifetime is a Go duration ("10h", "90m"). The directory and the realm are equals: if either stops, the process stops, because a server that kept answering LDAP after its KDC died would look healthy to everything that does not speak Kerberos.
Refused at startup:
$ authnd check cases/realm-lower.hcl authnd: kerberos: realm "example.org" is not upper case: clients uppercase the realm they derive from a domain, and would then ask for a realm this server does not answer for and likewise a realm with no name, no keytab, an address that does not parse, a lifetime Go cannot read, and a kerberos block beside an mfa block (below).
data.a-password-changed-over-ldap#A password:
The KDC reads the same people the directory serves, so a password changed over LDAP reaches the realm at once — the old one stops working for kinit the moment it stops working for a bind:
$ ldappasswd -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -t alice.pwin -T alice.new $ kinit --password-file=alice.pwin alice@EXAMPLE.ORG kinit: Password incorrect $ kinit --password-file=alice.new alice@EXAMPLE.ORG $
data.kinit-against-it#kinit against it:
A krb5.conf that names this KDC. ⛔ For MIT Kerberos the braces go on their own lines: its parser silently ignores a realm written on one line.
[libdefaults] default_realm = EXAMPLE.ORG dns_lookup_kdc = false [realms] EXAMPLE.ORG = { kdc = 127.0.0.1:18388 } The same configuration served, and asked by macOS’s Heimdal kinit (--password-file reads the password from a file):
$ authnd --config realm ldap on 127.0.0.1:3893, serving 4 people from the configuration file, then a sqlite database realm EXAMPLE.ORG on 127.0.0.1:18388 (udp and tcp) $ kinit --password-file=alice.pwin alice@EXAMPLE.ORG $ klist Credentials cache: FILE:ccache Principal: alice@EXAMPLE.ORG Issued Expires Principal Oct 18 16:10:19 2026 Oct 19 02:10:19 2026 krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG $ kinit --password-file=wrong.pwin alice@EXAMPLE.ORG kinit: Password incorrect $ kinit --password-file=bob.pwin bob@EXAMPLE.ORG kinit: krb5_get_init_creds: Error from KDC: this realm holds no Kerberos key for that principal $ kinit --password-file=dora.pwin zed@EXAMPLE.ORG kinit: krb5_get_init_creds: Error from KDC: no such principal in this realm The ticket lasts the default ten hours. bob typed the password their NT hash was computed from, and is still refused: the realm has no key for them. The KDC writes what it refused, with the Kerberos error code, to its output:
kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication required (code 25) kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication required (code 25) kerberos: the timestamp does not decrypt (client etype 18, our key type 18): error decrypting: integrity verification failed kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication does not decrypt (code 24) kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: this realm holds no Kerberos key for that principal (code 9) kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: no such principal in this realm (code 6) Pre-authentication required is the normal first round of a kinit: the client asks without pre-authentication and is told it is required, then asks again with it. alice’s successful kinit leaves only that line.
The realm says which names exist; the directory does not
An LDAP bind for a name nobody has is answered invalidCredentials, the same as a wrong password. The KDC answers no such principal in this realm (KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN, code 6), as Kerberos KDCs do. With a kerberos block on an address others can reach, the list of names is therefore as guessable as it is from any KDC; listen defaults to loopback.
data.not-beside-an-mfa-block#Not beside an mf: $ authnd check cases/krb-mfa.hcl authnd: kerberos and mfa together: the mfa block asks every bind for a password AND a code, and a kinit carries only the password -- this KDC has no second-factor pre-authentication, so a realm here would accept one factor where the mfa block demands two. Remove one of the blocks RFC 4120’s encrypted-timestamp pre-authentication is keyed by the password alone. A second factor needs OTP pre-authentication (RFC 6560) inside FAST (RFC 6113), which this KDC does not implement. A realm here would hand out tickets on one factor to the people the mfa block says need two, and a ticket opens everything a bind does — so the choice is made closed: one or the other.
data.ports#Ports: 88 is privileged. Under the packaged unit, CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE covers it; a server run as an ordinary user wants a high port, as above, and a krb5.conf that names it.
data.the-keytab#The keytab:
The keytab holds the key authnd signs its own tickets with — krbtgt/REALM@REALM — and one key per service it issues tickets to. It is the same file those services read. The krbtgt password is never typed again, so make it random. With MIT’s ktutil (package krb5-user on Debian and Ubuntu; this recipe is the one docs/install.md gives, and was not run for these pages):
printf 'addent -password -p krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG -k 1 -e aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96
%s
wkt /tmp/krb5.keytab
quit
' \ "$(head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64)" | ktutil sudo install -o root -g authnd -m 0640 /tmp/krb5.keytab /etc/authnd/krb5.keytab rm /tmp/krb5.keytab Add a service’s key the same way (-p nfs/files.example.org@EXAMPLE.ORG), and give that service the same key in its own keytab. On macOS, Heimdal’s ktutil -k add -r -p -V 1 -e aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 writes a random key without a password at all. Either way, read the keytab back before starting (klist -k with MIT, ktutil -k list with Heimdal):
$ ktutil -k etc/authnd/krb5.keytab list etc/authnd/krb5.keytab: Vno Type Principal Aliases 1 aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG A keytab without krbtgt/REALM is refused by check and at start; see check. The keytab is read once, at start: replacing it takes a restart.
data.who-can-be-issued-a-ticket#Who can be is:
A KDC must decrypt the client’s pre-authentication with that person’s long-term key, so it needs the person’s password, not only a way to check one. check says who can and who cannot, with the reason:
$ authnd check realm ldap://127.0.0.1:3893, base dc=example,dc=org USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH alice the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid bob the configuration file an NT hash account, uidObject uid dora a sqlite database a password account, uidObject uid eli a sqlite database an NT hash account, uidObject uid GROUP MEMBERS PUBLISHED AS staff alice and bob groupOfNames alice has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject bob has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject dora has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject eli has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject group staff has no gidNumber: not a posixGroup, published as a groupOfNames (member DNs, no memberUid) realm EXAMPLE.ORG on 127.0.0.1:18388 (udp and tcp), keytab etc/authnd/krb5.keytab can be issued a ticket: alice and dora CANNOT, whatever they type: bob and eli a KDC must decrypt the pre-authentication with the person's key bob and eli: an NT hash is only the RC4-HMAC key (RFC 4757), and this realm issues aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 alone, whose key is derived from the password itself a bind carries a password bob and eli cannot bind with a password: their sources hold only what an SMB server needs (an NT hash), which a bind cannot be checked against no reader is declared: nothing may search, and binds are not affected sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it) this configuration can be served the source has a ticket a password (password, password_file, a SQL password column) yes only an NT hash no: it is the RC4-HMAC key, and this realm issues AES only only a password check (a users "ldap" directory behind this one) no: a source that only verifies a password cannot produce any key For a directory behind this one, the last line of the realm part reads alice, bob, dora and eli: the source only verifies a password, so it cannot produce any key. That is structural rather than a matter of configuration, and finding it in check beats finding it from somebody whose kinit says their correct password is wrong.

data:
LDAP’s simple bind carries a name and a password and nothing else — no place for a code, no round trip to ask for one, and a client that speaks LDAP will not learn one. So the code goes on the end of the password, which is what appliances that do this do, and what people already know how to type:
password: hunter2314159 ^^^^^^^ ^^^^^^ password the six digits on their phone mfa { factors = 2 distinct_kinds = true # two things they KNOW are not two factors # digits = 6, period = 30 (seconds) and window = 1 are the defaults } user "tess" { password_file = "/etc/authnd/passwords/tess.pw" totp_secret = "JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXPJBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP" # ⛔ this IS the second factor } key default factors 2 1 is refused (a password and nothing else: remove the block, or ask for 2); above 2 is refused, since a bind carries a password and a code and no third thing distinct_kinds false the factors must be of different kinds — what “two-factor” is normally taken to mean digits 6 6 to 10 (RFC 4226) period 30 seconds one code lasts window 1 steps either side of now that are accepted, for clocks that differ. Each step is a step of somebody else’s guessing time: set it on purpose readers false whether readers carry a code too. A service account has no phone; one that does gets a totp_secret in its reader block The secret can equally come from a database column (the fifth) or an LDAP attribute (totp_attribute); see people. A totp_secret in a user or reader block under 128 bits (RFC 4226 R6) stops the server, naming the person, rather than failing every one of their logins later:
$ authnd check cases/shorttotp.hcl authnd: user "alice": totp_secret is 80 bits, and RFC 4226 requires at least 128: enrol again with a longer secret
data.not-with-a-realm#Not with a realm: A kerberos block and an mfa block in one configuration are refused: a kinit proves the password and nothing else, and this KDC has no second-factor pre-authentication. See the realm.
data.tokens-under-the-same-policy#Tokens, und: A token at the bind, with an oidc block, is counted by what its issuer says it checked — the amr claim. A token with no amr is one factor, and this policy refuses it.
data.what-follows-from-the-one-field#What fol: The split is by length. The last digits characters are the code. A password ending in digits is fine — that is why tess’s password alone was read as a wrong password followed by a code. A field no longer than a code is refused rather than guessed at, because a short password cannot be told apart from one. Both halves are always checked. Returning early on a wrong password would say, in the time taken, which half was wrong. A code is used once. It is valid for a whole step, so a server that accepts one twice accepts a replay; every step up to the last accepted one is refused, not merely the same one. Guessing is limited per name, with go-authn/totp’s defaults: after five wrong codes in a row a person is refused for fifteen minutes, the right code included, and after a hundred they are locked out until authnd restarts. The counts are kept in memory, per process. Only a code behind the right password is counted: otherwise anybody who knew a name could freeze its owner with five binds. Behind a wrong password the code is still computed, against nothing that remembers — the first line of the output above, not looked at. A reader is counted under its DN as the configuration spells it, so CN=Reader gets no fresh budget of its own. Nobody enrolled is not a wrong code. A person with no secret has answered nothing rather than answered wrongly, and the server’s output says nobody enrolled an authenticator for this person.
data.what-the-binds-look-like#What the binds:
The same configuration served, tess’s code computed from their secret at the moment of the bind:
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=tess,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y tess.only ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49) $ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=tess,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y tess.both dn:uid=tess,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org $ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=tess,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y tess.both ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49) $ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=tess,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y tess.badcode ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49) $ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.code ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49) $ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin dn:cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org tess.only is tess’s password with no code; tess.both the same password and the current code, sent twice; tess.badcode that password and 000000; alice.code alice’s password and six digits. The client is told one thing — invalid credentials — whichever half was wrong: which one is a fact about the account, and telling somebody who has proved nothing narrows their next guess. The server’s own output says which:
tess was refused: mfa: 2 factor(s) needed, 0 answered: your password (knowledge): directory: wrong password; your authenticator app (possession): not looked at, since the password in front of it was wrong tess was refused: mfa: 2 factor(s) needed, 1 answered: your authenticator app (possession): totp: that code has already been used tess was refused: mfa: 2 factor(s) needed, 1 answered: your authenticator app (possession): totp: that code is not right alice was refused: mfa: 2 factor(s) needed, 1 answered: your authenticator app (possession): not available your authenticator app: mfa: this factor cannot be asked here: totp: nobody enrolled an authenticator for this person
data.who-cannot-bind-under-it#Who cannot bind: $ authnd check mfa ldap://127.0.0.1:3893, base dc=example,dc=org USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH alice the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid tess the configuration file a password and a one-time-code secret account, uidObject uid alice has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject tess has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject a bind carries a password with a 6-digit code after it, of two different kinds alice has no second factor here, and cannot bind while one is required cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org may search; every other bound client may not sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it) this configuration can be served That is the question to ask before turning the block on.

data.it-reads-everything-once#It reads everyt:
The configuration files, every source behind them, the TLS certificate and the keytab are read at start. There is no reload, and the packaged unit has no ExecReload=. After changing any of them:
sudo -u authnd authnd check /etc/authnd sudo systemctl restart authnd The one thing applied while it runs is a password a person changes through authnd, which re-reads the user blocks and nothing else.
data.signals#Signals:
signal what happens SIGTERM, SIGINT it prints stopping, closes the listeners and every established connection, stops the realm, closes the sources, and exits 0 once the server has really finished SIGHUP it is caught and logged, and authnd stays up without reloading anything $ authnd --config etc/authnd ldap on 127.0.0.1:3893, serving 4 people from the configuration file, then a sqlite database hangup: authnd does not reload; restart it to apply a changed configuration, certificate or keytab alice's password change was refused: the old password did not verify: directory: wrong password alice changed their own password stopping That is one run: a kill -HUP, two attempts to change a password (the first refused, the second accepted), then a kill -TERM. The process was still there after the SIGHUP.
A SIGHUP used to kill authnd — Go’s default for a signal nobody handles — and systemd counts death by SIGHUP as a clean exit, so Restart=on-failure did not start it again: one kill -HUP or one logrotate postrotate took a directory down for good. It is caught now so that the habit is harmless, and the line says what to do instead.
Closing established connections, not only the listener, is deliberate: a server that stopped accepting and left its open connections answering would look stopped and not be, which is the restart that does not take.
data.telling-that-it-is-up#Telling that it is:
There is no health endpoint and no metrics. What there is:
the process and its exit status — under systemd, systemctl is-active authnd. If the LDAP listener or the realm stops of its own accord, the whole process ends with that error, so a live process is one whose two halves both answer; the root DSE, which answers an anonymous client and says which version it is talking to: $ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -s base -b '' '+' '*' dn: objectClass: top objectClass: OpenLDAProotDSE supportedLDAPVersion: 3 namingContexts: dc=example,dc=org supportedExtension: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.3 supportedExtension: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.1 supportedControl: 1.2.840.113556.1.4.319 supportedControl: 1.3.6.1.1.13.1 supportedControl: 1.3.6.1.1.13.2 supportedFeatures: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.1 supportedFeatures: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.3 subschemaSubentry: cn=Subschema vendorName: go-authn/authnd vendorVersion: v0.11.1 On a StartTLS listener that query needs -ZZ. A probe that proves more — that a source still answers — is a bind as a person or a reader kept for the purpose; with a users "ldap" block, that bind reaches the directory behind this one.
data.what-it-writes#What it writes:
Everything goes to standard output, which under systemd is the journal (journalctl -u authnd):
at start, where it listens and whom it serves — ldap on …, ldaps on … or ldap+starttls on …, then realm EXAMPLE.ORG on … (udp and tcp) with a kerberos block; every refused bind under an mfa block, every refused token, every refused or completed password change, with the reason — which the client is never told; see the second factor and tokens; every request the KDC refuses, prefixed kerberos:, with the Kerberos error code; see the realm; the LDAP library’s own log, in slog text form, at level info. A plain wrong password on a simple bind, with no mfa block, is answered invalidCredentials and not logged by authnd itself.
data.what-lives-where-and-what-a-restart-lose: configuration, passwords, DSN, certificate, keytab the files the configuration names; nothing is copied a SQLite database wherever its DSN says; /var/lib/authnd under the unit second-factor counts and lockouts memory only: a restart forgets them, including a person locked out after a hundred wrong codes used one-time codes memory only
data.when-it-does-not-start#When it does not:
A refusal is one line on standard error, prefixed authnd:, and exit status 1; under the unit, Restart=on-failure then tries again every five seconds and the line is in the journal each time. Everything check refuses is refused here too, and the one thing only the server finds is an address it cannot listen on — see check. The LDAP listener, the certificate and the realm are all opened before the first line is printed, so a server that cannot start prints only the refusal. Here a second instance meets the first one’s Kerberos port:
$ authnd --config cases/realm2 authnd: kerberos udp 127.0.0.1:18388: listen udp 127.0.0.1:18388: bind: address already in use The ldap on … line, and realm … on … after it, mean both halves are listening.

data:
A person may change their own password, and nobody else’s, through the RFC 3062 password modify operation (what ldappasswd sends) or an RFC 4511 modify. In both, the current password must be sent with the new one, whatever the connection bound with. A session bound with an OAUTHBEARER token — short-lived, and possibly one factor — could otherwise turn it into a permanent password that also works for kinit.
This is OpenLDAP’s ppolicy behaviour with pwdSafeModify set, with the result codes its ppolicy.c returns. RFC 3062 §3 allows it: “If oldPasswd is not present, the server MAY use other policy to determine whether or not to change the password.”
data.where-the-new-password-is-written#Where:
Back into the file that declares the person, and nowhere else:
a user block with password_file has that file rewritten, keeping its owner and group where the process may, and its mode narrowed to at most 0600 — never widened; a user block with password inline has the configuration file rewritten with the new value, keeping its comments, order and mode; a user block with only an nt_hash is not given a password: that would change what can prove them, which is a change to the configuration. Every write goes to a temporary file in the same directory, then a rename — so a full disk or a crash leaves the old password, not an empty file. That needs write access to the directory. Under the packaged unit, ProtectSystem=strict takes it away, and a change is refused like this:
$ ldapmodify -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -f safe.ldif ldap_modify: Other (e.g., implementation specific) error (80) additional info: the password could not be written modifying entry "uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org" with the reason in the server’s output:
changing the password for alice: etc/authnd/passwords/alice.pw: open etc/authnd/passwords/.hcldir-863420940: permission denied So keep the passwords in a directory of their own, writable by the service, and the configuration read-only to it — the ReadWritePaths= drop-in. A person whose password is written inline would need /etc/authnd itself writable, which would also let the service rewrite its own configuration.
After a successful write, the configuration files are read again for the user blocks only: an unrelated edit waiting on disk does not take effect halfway because somebody changed a password. Everything else still waits for a restart.
