The files are still read whole, though, so if one of them no longer loads, the password is written and the client is told the password was written but this server did not reload it — the running server keeps the old one until it is restarted.
data.who-can-change-what#Who can change what:
request answer no old password, or a bare replace: userPassword insufficientAccessRights an old password that is not the current one unwillingToPerform somebody else’s entry insufficientAccessRights, a password may be changed only by the person it belongs to an anonymous connection insufficientAccessRights, an anonymous connection has not said who it is somebody with no password at all — they can only have bound with a token unwillingToPerform: a bearer token is not a password, and does not set the first one. An administrator sets it in the configuration somebody served from a users block unwillingToPerform: authnd reads those sources and does not write them the file cannot be written other (80), the password could not be written; the reason is in the server’s output The second-to-last, from the release binary, for dora, who comes from a SQLite database:
$ ldappasswd -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y dora.pwin -t dora.pwin -T dora.new Result: Server is unwilling to perform (53) Additional info: dora is served from a sqlite database, which this server reads and does not write The person is matched by identity, not by DN: the session’s own name must be exactly the target’s, byte for byte, so a session bound as uid=Backup cannot change backup’s password even though the two DNs compare equal. That and the refusal of names that differ only by case are two controls that do not depend on each other.
data.with-ldapmodify#With ldapmodify:
The change is a delete of the old value followed by an add of the new one, in one request. RFC 4511 §4.6 applies a modify’s changes in order and atomically, so the delete — and the whole request with it — fails unless the value deleted is the one held:
dn: uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org changetype: modify delete: userPassword userPassword: alice-test-pw - add: userPassword userPassword: alice-new-pw - A bare replace proves nothing, and anything but userPassword is not something this server changes:
$ ldapmodify -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -f replace.ldif ldap_modify: Insufficient access (50) additional info: a password change must send the old password with the new one modifying entry "uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org" $ ldapmodify -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -f other.ldif ldap_modify: Server is unwilling to perform (53) additional info: this server changes userPassword and nothing else, not cn modifying entry "uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org" A modify that asks for a password and something else is refused whole: a modify is atomic, and honouring half of it would report success for something nobody asked for.
data.with-ldappasswd#With ldappasswd:
-t is a file holding the old password, -T one holding the new; -A and -S prompt for them instead.
$ ldappasswd -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -T alice.new Result: Insufficient access (50) Additional info: a password change must send the old password with the new one $ ldappasswd -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -t wrong.pwin -T alice.new Result: Server is unwilling to perform (53) Additional info: the old password sent is not the current one $ ldappasswd -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -t alice.pwin -T alice.new $ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49) $ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.new dn:uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org The old password stops working at once, for a bind and — with a realm — for kinit. The server says so in its output:
alice's password change was refused: the old password did not verify: directory: wrong password alice changed their own password authnd does not generate a password: a request without a new one is refused with unwillingToPerform (this server does not generate passwords: send the one you want). A password it invented would have to be sent back over the connection, and the one place it is certain to end up is a terminal’s scrollback.

data: A user block is the whole directory for a small site, or the service accounts a big one keeps out of its database. A site whose people are already in a database or in LDAP should not copy them into a second place that goes stale, so a users block reads them where they are. The users block is go-authn/directory’s hcldir, the same one go-fileshare reads: one directory is described the same way to both.
data.in-a-sql-database#In a SQL database:
users "sql" { driver = "postgres" # or mysql (mariadb), or sqlite dsn_file = "/etc/authnd/pg.dsn" # required: a DSN may hold a password users = "select login, secret, nt_hash from staff" # required groups = "select team, member from team_members" # optional } The queries are yours, because a site’s people are already in that site’s shape. The users query’s columns are read by position: a name, then any of a password, an NT hash, SSH keys (one per line) and a one-time-code secret, in that order — up to five columns. A NULL is a credential that person does not have. A password column is compared as it is stored: authnd has no setting for a hashed column. The groups query returns a group name and a member, one row per membership.
Two more queries, optional, read attributes by column alias rather than by position: users_attributes (a name, then one column per attribute) and groups_attributes (a group, then the same). An unquoted alias is lower-cased by PostgreSQL. See the entries.
driver accepts postgres (or postgresql, pgx), mysql (or mariadb) and sqlite (or sqlite3). The database is reached at startup, before anything listens, so one that is not answering stops the server where somebody is watching:
$ authnd check cases/nodb authnd: users "sql": the postgres database is not answering: failed to connect to `user=authnd database=authnd`: 127.0.0.1:1 (127.0.0.1): dial error: dial tcp 127.0.0.1:1: connect: connection refused 127.0.0.1:1 (127.0.0.1): dial error: dial tcp 127.0.0.1:1: connect: connection refused PostgreSQL on the same machine through its socket and peer authentication needs no password in the DSN: host=/run/postgresql dbname=authnd user=authnd. SQLite in the state directory: file:/var/lib/authnd/people.db.
A key that belongs to the other kind of block is refused rather than ignored:
$ authnd check cases/sqlwrongkey.hcl authnd: users "sql" has base_dn in it, which belongs to an ldap block
data.in-another-ldap-directory#In another LDA:
users "ldap" { url = "ldaps://ldap.example.org" base_dn = "ou=people,dc=example,dc=org" bind_dn = "cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org" bind_password_file = "/etc/authnd/upstream.pw" } url and base_dn are required. Where the people and groups are, and which attributes name them:
key default user_filter (|(objectClass=posixAccount)(objectClass=account)(objectClass=uidObject)) user_attribute uid group_base_dn base_dn group_filter (|(objectClass=posixGroup)(objectClass=groupOfNames)) group_attribute cn group_member_attribute none: memberUid (names) and member (DNs); set, it is the one attribute read totp_attribute none: there is no standard attribute, and a guess would read nothing while looking like it had looked attributes, group_attributes none: the attributes to copy from each person’s entry and each group’s, such as ["mail", "uidNumber", "homeDirectory"] and ["gidNumber"] (the entries) start_tls false A member DN counts only when it is the DN of an entry the people search returned: a DN outside them, or naming nobody, maps to nobody, and the name is never read out of the DN. sambaNTPassword and sshPublicKey are read under those names.
From v0.11.0 the defaults read more of an institution’s directory
The block is go-authn/directory’s, and directory v0.14.0, which authnd v0.11.0 embeds, widened its defaults: up to v0.10.2, user_filter was (objectClass=posixAccount), group_filter (objectClass=posixGroup) and group_member_attribute memberUid. A directory holding account or uidObject entries that are not posixAccounts — service accounts, hosts named by uid, people imported from elsewhere — now gives them to authnd, and each can be checked by a bind; its groupOfNames groups become groups here. To keep exactly the old set, write the old values:
users "ldap" { # ... user_filter = "(objectClass=posixAccount)" group_filter = "(objectClass=posixGroup)" group_member_attribute = "memberUid" } Two things are refused before anything is opened:
$ authnd check cases/ldap-clear.hcl authnd: users "ldap" would send every password to "ldap.example.org" in the clear: use ldaps://, or start_tls = true (RFC 4513 §5.1.3) $ authnd check cases/ldap-cred.hcl authnd: users "ldap" has credentials in its url, and a url is printed: use bind_dn with bind_password_file ldap:// to a loopback address and ldapi:// are accepted: nobody is on the way.
A directory behind this one checks passwords by binding to it; it does not hand them over. Here one authnd fronts another, under a different base; the one behind is the check example, served on 3893:
listen = "127.0.0.1:3894" base_dn = "dc=example,dc=net" users "ldap" { url = "ldap://127.0.0.1:3893" base_dn = "ou=people,dc=example,dc=org" group_base_dn = "ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org" bind_dn = "cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org" bind_password_file = "etc/authnd/reader.pw" } user "svc-backup" { password_file = "etc/authnd/svc-backup.pw" } $ authnd check front2 ldap://127.0.0.1:3894, base dc=example,dc=net USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH alice ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 a password check account, uidObject uid bob ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 a password check account, uidObject uid dora ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 a password check account, uidObject uid eli ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 a password check account, uidObject uid svc-backup the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid GROUP MEMBERS PUBLISHED AS engineers dora and eli groupOfNames staff alice, bob and dora groupOfNames alice has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject bob has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject dora has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject eli has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject svc-backup has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject group engineers has no gidNumber: not a posixGroup, published as a groupOfNames (member DNs, no memberUid) group staff has no gidNumber: not a posixGroup, published as a groupOfNames (member DNs, no memberUid) a bind carries a password no reader is declared: nothing may search, and binds are not affected sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it) this configuration can be served Every person the directory behind publishes is an account and every group a groupOfNames, since none has POSIX attributes: the defaults read them, and the groups’ member DNs map to the people imported. With the defaults up to v0.10.2, (objectClass=posixAccount) would have matched none of them.
A password check is enough for a bind, and is never enough for a Kerberos ticket or for SMB.
data.order-and-the-one-exception#Order, and t:
Sources are asked in the order they are written, and the first one that knows a name owns it. The user blocks always come first, so a service account written down locally is not overridden by somebody with the same name in the database. Group membership is the union of every source: a group that a group block and a database’s groups query both name has the members of both.
Two names that differ only by case are refused
A uid is compared ignoring case (RFC 4519 §2.39), and so is every DN, so Dora in the file and dora in a database are one name to LDAP and two people to anything that compares bytes — a password change by one would land on the other. Such a configuration does not start:
$ authnd check cases/case.hcl authnd: "Dora" (from the configuration file) and "dora" (from a sqlite database) differ only by case, and an LDAP name does not tell them apart: a uid is compared ignoring case. Rename one of them
data.read-once#Read once: Every source is read once, at startup. A person added to the database, or a membership changed in the directory behind this one, is served after a restart, not before. That includes a password column in a database: it is read with the rest of the row. A directory behind this one is different only in that a bind is checked by binding to it, so a password changed there is the one that works. The other exception is a password a person changes through authnd itself, which is applied at once. There is no reload; see running it.
data.written-in-the-configuration#Written in:
user "alice" { password_file = "/etc/authnd/passwords/alice.pw" } user "carol" { nt_hash = "…" # MD4(UTF16LE(password)), 32 hex authorized_keys = ["ssh-ed25519 AAAA… carol@laptop"] # published as sshPublicKey } group "staff" { members = ["alice", "carol"] } field what it is password the password, inline password_file the same, read from a file (surrounding white space removed) nt_hash MD4(UTF16LE(password)), 32 hex characters — for a site that holds that and not the password totp_secret a base32 one-time-code secret, at least 128 bits; see a second factor authorized_keys authorized_keys lines, published as sshPublicKey authorized_keys_file the same, from a file attributes from v0.11.0, what describes the person and proves nothing — sn, uidNumber, gidNumber, homeDirectory, mail… — as a map of strings or lists of strings; a group block takes it too. They decide what the entry is published as: see the entries Refused at startup, naming the person:
password and password_file together — say which one; password and nt_hash together — the hash is derived from the password, so two of them can disagree; authorized_keys and authorized_keys_file together; an nt_hash that is not 32 hex characters, an authorized_keys line that does not parse, a totp_secret under 128 bits; the same user or group twice, and a group with no members. A group member that no source knows is refused too, which is what catches a typo before it silently grants nothing:
$ authnd check cases/typo.hcl authnd: group "staff" has "alise" in it, who is not in the configuration file An nt_hash alone cannot bind
A person written with only nt_hash is published, can be handed to an SMB server through sambaNTPassword, and cannot bind to authnd itself: an LDAP simple bind sends the password, and an NT hash is not a way to check one here. bob below has only an NT hash, and the hash is that of the password sent:
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=bob,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y bob.pwin ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49) check says so, after the tables:
bob and eli cannot bind with a password: their sources hold only what an SMB server needs (an NT hash), which a bind cannot be checked against Why it is refused, by design. An NT hash is MD4(UTF16LE(password)), unsalted and fast (MS-NLMP §3.3.1, NTOWFv1). Accepting it to check LDAP binds would widen what a leaked hash opens, from SMB to every application that binds through authnd. Kerberos refuses these people for a related reason: the NT hash is the RC4-HMAC key (RFC 4757 §2), and the realm issues AES only. This is a deliberate decision, not a missing feature, and there is no option to change it.
What to do instead. When migrating from a directory that holds only NT hashes (Samba, an exported AD), give each person a real password or a password check in their source: a password reset, or a users "ldap" source whose upstream directory checks the password itself. Do not keep the NT hash as the only credential.

data: listen = "0.0.0.0:636" cert_file = "/etc/authnd/cert.pem" # the chain, leaf first key_file = "/etc/authnd/key.pem" cert_file and key_file together turn TLS on; one without the other is refused (one without the other serves nothing). TLS 1.2 is the minimum. authnd has no ACME client: the two files are written by something else — go-authn/servercert, certbot, a site’s own CA — and authnd is restarted after each renewal, because the certificate is read once, when the listener opens.
data.ldaps#ldaps://:
The server, a CA-signed certificate for 127.0.0.1, and the chain verified by a client that is not this program:
$ authnd --config ldaps ldaps on 127.0.0.1:3636, serving 3 people from the configuration file uid=carol,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org is published without sambaNTPassword: no sambaSID and no uidNumber to derive one from $ openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:3636 -CAfile tls/ca.pem -verify_return_error -verify_ip 127.0.0.1 &1 | grep -E 'Verify return|Protocol|subject=|issuer=' subject=CN=localhost issuer=CN=docs test CA Protocol: TLSv1.3 Verify return code: 0 (ok) Protocol : TLSv1.3 Verify return code: 0 (ok)
data.publish_nt_hash#publish_nt_hash:
sambaNTPassword is what lets a Samba or another SMB server authenticate people through this directory, and it is not a password hash in the sense a login form means: whoever holds MD4(UTF16LE(password)) authenticates as that person over NTLMv2 without ever learning the password. So it is published only when asked for, and, from v0.11.0, with the domain the people’s SIDs belong to:
publish_nt_hash = true samba { domain_sid = "S-1-5-21-1004336348-1177238915-682003330" # `net getlocalsid` on the SMB server } Asking for it is refused unless the listener has TLS, or is loopback (127.0.0.0/8, ::1, localhost) and so on no network at all:
$ authnd check cases/nthash-clear.hcl authnd: publish_nt_hash needs cert_file and key_file: an NT hash IS the credential, and 0.0.0.0:3893 is not loopback, so it would cross a network in the clear
data.starttls-which-refuses-until-it-is-asked:
StartTLS is requested by the client, so merely offering it promises nothing: a client that never asks would bind in the clear. A listener with starttls = true therefore refuses every bind and every search until the connection has been upgraded, with confidentialityRequired:
$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3389 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b ou=people,dc=example,dc=org '(uid=bob)' ldap_bind: Confidentiality required (13) additional info: this listener requires TLS, and nothing asked for it $ LDAPTLS_REQCERT=never ldapsearch -ZZ -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3389 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b ou=people,dc=example,dc=org '(uid=bob)' dn: uid=bob,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org objectClass: top objectClass: account objectClass: sambaSamAccount objectClass: uidObject uid: bob cn: bob sambaSID: S-1-5-21-1004336348-1177238915-682003330-1104 sambaNTPassword: 8846F7EAEE8FB117AD06BDD830B7586C (-ZZ is “StartTLS, and fail if it fails”. LDAPTLS_REQCERT=never is there because the ldapsearch macOS ships trusts the system store and could not be told to trust this test CA; the chain was checked separately with openssl s_client -starttls ldap -CAfile tls/ca.pem -verify_return_error, which answered Verify return code: 0 (ok).)
That refusal is what makes cert_file a guarantee rather than an offer — and it is what publish_nt_hash relies on. It includes the anonymous bind ldapsearch -x sends before reading the root DSE, so on a StartTLS listener that discovery query, too, needs -ZZ.
data.the-samba-block#The samba block:
sambaNTPassword belongs to Samba’s sambaSamAccount, whose MUST is uid and sambaSID, and no other class allows it. Every entry authnd publishes passes the schema it serves, so the attribute is published only on a sambaSamAccount, and that needs a SID:
key domain_sid required: the SMB server’s domain SID, S-1-5-21-…, as net getlocalsid prints it algorithmic_rid_base optional, 1000 by default, Samba’s. An odd number, or one below 1000, is refused: Samba would silently use another one A person’s sambaSID is their own sambaSID attribute when a source gives one (attributes). Otherwise it is domain_sid-RID, with RID = 2 × uidNumber + algorithmic_rid_base: Samba’s algorithmic mapping (smb.conf(5), algorithmic rid base). A person with an NT key and neither is published without sambaNTPassword, and check and the startup log say who. The Samba definitions are added to the schema served at cn=Subschema only when the block is there; they were written from Samba’s published OIDs, names and syntaxes, not copied from its GPL-3.0 samba.schema.
Breaking for v0.10.x configurations: publish_nt_hash without a samba block does not start
v0.10.x served publish_nt_hash = true alone. From v0.11.0 that configuration is refused at startup and by check, with what to add:
$ authnd check cases/nthash.hcl authnd: publish_nt_hash needs a samba block: sambaNTPassword belongs to Samba's sambaSamAccount, whose MUST is uid and sambaSID, and a SID needs the domain's. Add samba { domain_sid = "S-1-5-21-..." # the SMB server's: `net getlocalsid` prints it } and each person's sambaSID is their own sambaSID attribute, or domain_sid-(2 x uidNumber + 1000), Samba's algorithmic mapping; `authnd check` lists who has neither Run check with the new binary before upgrading. Refusing is deliberate: the v0.10.x entry cannot pass the schema, and the two quiet alternatives — dropping the attribute, which takes SMB away from everybody, or dropping the entry, which takes the person away — would both happen with nothing on the console.
A samba block without publish_nt_hash is refused too, since it would publish nothing:
$ authnd check cases/samba-alone.hcl authnd: a samba block without publish_nt_hash publishes nothing: it is the domain of the sambaSID that sambaNTPassword needs. Remove it, or set publish_nt_hash = true
data.tokens-need-it-too#Tokens need it too: An oidc block refuses a token over a connection that is not encrypted, unless allow_plaintext = true says that TLS is terminated in front of this process.
data.two-ways-one-listener-each#Two ways, one:
starttls the listener check says ldaps:// not set the TLS handshake happens before a byte of LDAP is spoken ldaps://… StartTLS starttls = true plaintext, upgraded when the client asks (RFC 4511 §4.14) ldap+starttls://… It is one or the other and has to be: a listener cannot both require a handshake and wait to see whether one is asked for. Which one a site wants is about its clients: ldaps:// on 636 is what most of them are configured for, and StartTLS is what a client pointed at 389 with “use TLS” ticked will ask for. A site that needs both runs two instances, each with its own --config. starttls = true without a certificate is refused:
$ authnd check cases/starttls-nocert.hcl authnd: starttls needs cert_file and key_file: there is nothing to upgrade a connection WITH
data.what-check-says#What check says:
Three people on an ldaps:// listener: alice has a password and the POSIX trio, so their SID is derived (2 × 1000 + 1000); bob has only an NT hash and a sambaSID of their own; carol has a password and neither.
listen = "127.0.0.1:3636" base_dn = "dc=example,dc=org" cert_file = "tls/cert.pem" key_file = "tls/key.pem" publish_nt_hash = true samba { domain_sid = "S-1-5-21-1004336348-1177238915-682003330" } reader "cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org" { password_file = "etc/authnd/reader.pw" } user "alice" { password_file = "etc/authnd/alice.pw" attributes = { uidNumber = "1000", gidNumber = "1000", homeDirectory = "/home/alice" } } user "bob" { nt_hash = "8846F7EAEE8FB117AD06BDD830B7586C" attributes = { sambaSID = "S-1-5-21-1004336348-1177238915-682003330-1104" } } user "carol" { password = "carol-pw" } $ authnd check ldaps ldaps://127.0.0.1:3636, base dc=example,dc=org USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH alice the configuration file a password account, posixAccount, sambaSamAccount, uidObject uid, cn, gidNumber, homeDirectory, uidNumber, sambaSID and sambaNTPassword bob the configuration file an NT hash account, sambaSamAccount, uidObject uid, cn, sambaSID and sambaNTPassword carol the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid bob has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, sambaSamAccount, uidObject carol has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject carol is published without sambaNTPassword: no sambaSID and no uidNumber to derive one from a bind carries a password bob cannot bind with a password: the source holds only what an SMB server needs (an NT hash), which a bind cannot be checked against cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org may search; every other bound client may not sambaNTPassword is published over TLS: it IS the credential, and whoever reads it authenticates as that person over NTLMv2 in sambaSamAccount, with sambaSIDs in S-1-5-21-1004336348-1177238915-682003330 (a person's own sambaSID, or RID 2 x uidNumber + 1000) this configuration can be served and, for the StartTLS listener, sambaNTPassword is published over TLS, once StartTLS has been asked for. alice has no NT hash written down; theirs is derived from the password they have. bob’s hash is published for an SMB server to use, and check says, too, that bob cannot bind to authnd itself. carol’s entry is published without the attribute, and an SMB server cannot serve carol until a source gives them a uidNumber or a sambaSID.
What a reader is given, over the StartTLS listener of the same people:
$ LDAPTLS_REQCERT=never ldapsearch -ZZ -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3389 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b ou=people,dc=example,dc=org '(uid=alice)' dn: uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org objectClass: top objectClass: account objectClass: posixAccount objectClass: sambaSamAccount objectClass: uidObject uid: alice cn: alice gidNumber: 1000 homeDirectory: /home/alice uidNumber: 1000 sambaSID: S-1-5-21-1004336348-1177238915-682003330-3000 sambaNTPassword: D061EF15E9494B458016FA760CECDD63 Only a reader can search, so only a reader ever sees the attribute. Who may read it is therefore the same question as who holds a reader’s password.
NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and nothing else will do
A file server asking authnd about somebody can serve them over SMB only if the source held enough for that: a password, or the hash. A person who comes from a directory that only checks passwords — a password check in check — can never be given a sambaNTPassword, whatever authnd does in between. Without publish_nt_hash, nobody can: check then says sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session.

data:
go-authn/oidc verifies a token into an identity. The obvious way to carry one to an LDAP server is the password field, and it works once and then stops: the password field is where the mfa block takes the code off the end, and a token cannot be both.
So the token goes where the protocol has a place for it. A SASL bind’s credentials are an octet string of the mechanism’s own shape, and RFC 7628’s OAUTHBEARER shape is a GS2 header followed by key/value pairs, one of which is auth=Bearer :
n,,^Aauth=Bearer eyJ…^A^A The password field is left alone. On one listener, at the same time, a person can type a password with a code on the end and another can send a token.
oidc { issuer = "https://login.example.org/realms/staff" # the "iss" a token must carry, and where discovery starts audience = "ldap" # this server's client id at the provider # username_claim = "preferred_username" which claim names the person here # jwks_url = "…" skips discovery, for a provider that does not publish it # allow_plaintext = true only when TLS is terminated in front of this process } issuer and audience are required. Without username_claim, the name is preferred_username, then email when email_verified is true, then sub. With the block, the root DSE advertises the mechanism:
$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -s base -b '' supportedSASLMechanisms dn: supportedSASLMechanisms: OAUTHBEARER Without it, every SASL bind is answered authMethodNotSupported — not this way, which sends a client somewhere different from wrong password.
data.discovery-happens-at-startup#Discovery h:
The provider’s discovery document and keys are read when the server starts, and by check. A provider that cannot be reached stops the server where somebody is watching, rather than refusing every bind later:
$ authnd check cases/oidc.hcl authnd: oidc "https://127.0.0.1:1/realms/staff": oidc: reading https://127.0.0.1:1/realms/staff/.well-known/openid-configuration: Get "https://127.0.0.1:1/realms/staff/.well-known/openid-configuration": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:1: connect: connection refused An issuer that is not https is refused, except on loopback:
$ authnd check cases/oidc-http.hcl authnd: oidc "http://login.example.org/realms/staff": oidc: http://login.example.org/realms/staff is not https: the key set decides every signature, and over cleartext so does anybody on the way
data.how-many-factors-is-a-token#How many fac:
Whatever the issuer says it checked, and nothing more. A token carries RFC 8176’s amr, the methods the provider used. That is the only evidence there is, so it is what the mfa policy counts, by kind:
amr method kind pwd, pin, kba, mca knowledge otp, hwk, swk, sms, tel, sc, pop, user, wia, mfa possession fpt, face, iris, retina, vbm, geo inherence anything else unknown, which never satisfies distinct_kinds no amr at all one factor, possession — the token itself Two methods of one kind are one factor. The alternative would be this server inventing a second factor nobody performed; and a server that believes the issuer about who this is has no separate ground for disbelieving it about how it checked.
With an mfa block, check says it:
$ authnd check sasl ldaps://127.0.0.1:3636, base dc=example,dc=org USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH alice the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid tess the configuration file a password and a one-time-code secret account, uidObject uid alice has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject tess has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject a bind carries a password with a 6-digit code after it, of two different kinds or a token from http://127.0.0.1:18481, over SASL OAUTHBEARER over TLS a token counts for the factors its amr claim names, so one with no amr is refused by this policy alice has no second factor here, so a password cannot satisfy this policy; a token whose amr names two kinds still can no reader is declared: nothing may search, and binds are not affected sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it) this configuration can be served alice has no totp_secret, so a password with a code can never be enough for them; a token whose amr names two kinds can, as the first bind below shows.
data.what-it-refuses#What it refuses:
A token in the clear. A bearer token needs no other half: whoever reads it off the wire is that person until it expires. allow_plaintext = true exists for a deployment that terminates TLS in front of this process, and check then says a token may cross this socket in the clear. A request to be somebody else. The GS2 header may name an authzid. A token for alice carrying a request to act as tess is refused, not quietly treated as either. A token for somebody no source here publishes. The client is told only invalid_token; which names exist is not something to hand out one guess at a time. The reason is in the server’s output. Channel binding. A GS2 header with p= — the client insists on channel binding — is refused: this server does not do it, and accepting the header while binding nothing would let the client believe the channel was checked. A mechanism this server does not speak, with authMethodNotSupported. A refusal of the token itself is RFC 7628 §3.2.3’s: a JSON error carrying openid-configuration, returned as saslBindInProgress so the client can send the ^A that ends the exchange. A token that verifies but does not satisfy the mfa policy is answered plainly invalidCredentials, as the second and third binds above show.
A token does not set a password
A person who has only ever signed in with a token cannot use that session to give themselves a first password, and a person who has one must still send it to change it. See changing a password.
data.what-the-binds-look-like#What the binds:
The issuer here is a small test provider on loopback, and oidctool a test client written for these pages: it signs a token for the name given, with the amr given, sends it in an OAUTHBEARER bind (with an authzid when a fifth argument names one), and prints the bind’s result code and the server’s SASL credentials. Against the configuration above, over ldaps://:
$ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls bind result 0, serverSaslCreds $ ./oidctool alice '' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls bind result 49 $ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","kba"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls bind result 49 $ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls tess bind result 14, serverSaslCreds {"status":"insufficient_scope","openid-configuration":"http://127.0.0.1:18481/.well-known/openid-configuration"} $ ./oidctool zed '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls bind result 14, serverSaslCreds {"status":"invalid_token","openid-configuration":"http://127.0.0.1:18481/.well-known/openid-configuration"} 0 is success, 49 invalidCredentials, 14 saslBindInProgress. A ["pwd","kba"] token names two methods of one kind, so it counts once. And to the same configuration without cert_file and key_file, on a plaintext listener:
$ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3893 clear bind result 13 13 is confidentialityRequired: a token is not taken over a connection that is not encrypted.
What the server wrote for the four binds over ldaps:// that were refused:
alice was refused: mfa: the policy needs 2 factor(s) and 1 were offered alice was refused: mfa: the policy needs 2 factor(s) and 1 were offered alice was refused: the token is for "alice" and asks to act as "tess"; this server does not delegate zed was refused: the token verified, and no source here publishes anybody by that name and for the plaintext one:
a token was refused: OAUTHBEARER was offered over a connection that is not encrypted, and allow_plaintext is not set A successful OAUTHBEARER bind leaves the connection bound as uid=,ou=people,, spelled as every other entry is.

Programs such as authnd and authn-bridge are built from modules that are published, versioned and tested on their own. Each answers one question, and a program imports the ones whose questions it asks.
All of them are pure Go and build with CGO_ENABLED=0.
module the question it answers these pages describe import path mfa did enough factors answer, of enough kinds, and which ones? v0.5.0 github.com/go-authn/mfa totp is this six-digit code right, and has it been used before? v0.4.2 github.com/go-authn/totp fido how is a security key spoken to, over 64-byte reports? v0.6.2 github.com/go-authn/fido keyfactor did the registered key answer, and did a person touch it? v0.4.2 github.com/go-authn/keyfactor directory who is somebody, and what can prove them? v0.14.0 github.com/go-authn/directory ldap what are the bytes of an LDAP server? v0.8.0 github.com/go-authn/ldap krb5 is this Kerberos ticket good for this service? v0.3.1 github.com/go-authn/krb5 kdc how does a realm issue tickets from a directory? v0.4.3 github.com/go-authn/kdc oidc who does this bearer token say is asking, and should it be believed? v0.4.1 github.com/go-authn/oidc saml what did a federation’s identity provider say about this person? v0.4.1 github.com/go-authn/saml krl is this SSH certificate or key revoked, as sshd would answer? v0.6.1 github.com/go-authn/krl servercert where does a daemon’s TLS server certificate come from? v0.5.2 github.com/go-authn/servercert wireguard may this WireGuard key connect, and whose is it? v0.1.1 github.com/go-authn/wireguard scim who has the identity provider just created, changed or deleted? v0.1.0 github.com/go-authn/scim
data.every-page-has-the-same-parts#Every page: The question; the go get line for the version described; a minimal example that compiles against that version; what the module refuses, from its code; and what it is checked against — the implementation that is not this one, named in its CI or its tests. Where a README and the code disagree, the page follows the code.
data.how-they-group#How they group:
Factors — whether a person is present. mfa decides how much proof is enough and knows about no device. totp is one factor: a code from a phone. fido speaks CTAP to a security key and knows about no policy; keyfactor is the one piece that imports both, and turns a key into a factor.
The directory, and its protocol. directory is the model: a person, and which credentials a source holds for them — a password, an NT hash, a verifier, SSH keys, a one-time-code secret — and, apart from them, the attributes that describe them and prove nothing. ldap is the LDAP wire protocol, as a server, and the directory schema an entry can be checked against; what it answers is the handler’s business.
Kerberos, in two halves. krb5 accepts tickets: a keytab, an AP-REQ in, an AP-REP out. kdc issues them, from a directory that holds passwords.
Federation and tokens. saml is a SAML 2.0 service provider in front of a federation such as RENATER or eduGAIN. oidc verifies the OpenID Connect tokens a provider signs — the resource-server half, with no login flow. scim is the other direction: the SCIM 2.0 endpoint an identity provider calls to create, update and delete the people and groups of your application.
Revocation and certificates. krl reads, writes and checks OpenSSH key revocation lists. servercert gives a daemon its TLS certificate, from files or from ACME.
wireguard carries the signed list of WireGuard public keys people have registered with a provider, which a gateway turns into peers.
data.why-they-are-separate-modules#Why they a:
A service that only accepts tickets never links a KDC. An NFS server verifies the tickets a client presents; it has a keytab and nothing else to do with a realm. If accepting and issuing were one module, every such server would carry a ticket-issuing code path it never runs, and the directory module a KDC reads people from, which it never uses.
This is measured, not intended. In a scratch module that imports only github.com/go-authn/krb5@v0.3.1:
$ GOWORK=off go list -deps . | grep go-authn github.com/go-authn/krb5 $ GOWORK=off go list -m all | grep go-authn github.com/go-authn/krb5 v0.3.1 The same command for a module that imports github.com/go-authn/kdc@v0.4.3 lists github.com/go-authn/directory and github.com/go-authn/kdc: issuing needs the people, accepting does not.
The same rule holds elsewhere. mfa imports nothing outside the standard library, and fido does not import mfa: a program that only wants to make a key blink does not carry a policy package. totp depends on mfa only, and oidc has no dependency at all. directory keeps its LDAP, SQL and HCL sources in subpackages: the core package imports nothing outside the standard library, and sqldir takes an *sql.DB, so the database driver is the program’s choice.

Who is somebody, and what can prove them? One model over a list held in memory, a SQL database, an LDAP server, or user and group blocks in a configuration file — and the point of it is the second half of the question.
go get github.com/go-authn/directory@v0.14.0
data.attributes#Attributes:
From v0.13.0 an Identity can carry attributes: what a source says about somebody that proves nothing — a uidNumber, a home directory, a mail address. They are kept apart from credentials on purpose: a credential decides who may log in, an attribute is published to everybody allowed to search. A server such as authnd turns them into the attributes of an LDAP entry, and its schema decides what the entry is.
package main import ( "errors" "fmt" "github.com/go-authn/directory" ) func main() { a, err := directory.NewAttributes( directory.Attribute{Name: "uidNumber", Values: []string{"1000"}}, directory.Attribute{Name: "mail", Values: []string{"dora@example.org"}}, directory.Attribute{Name: "MAIL", Values: []string{"d.explorer@example.org", "dora@example.org"}}, ) fmt.Println(err) dora := directory.NewIdentity("dora", directory.WithPassword("hunter2"), directory.WithAttributes(a)) fmt.Println(dora.Attributes().Names(), dora.Attributes().Get("UIDNUMBER"), dora.Attributes().Get("mail")) // What is published cannot hold a secret, nor what a server derives or answers itself. for _, name := range []string{"userPassword", "sambaNTPassword", "radiusHash", "cn", "memberUid", "2.5.4.35"} { _, err := directory.NewAttributes(directory.Attribute{Name: name, Values: []string{"x"}}) fmt.Println(errors.Is(err, directory.ErrAttributeName), err) } } [uidNumber mail] [1000] [dora@example.org d.explorer@example.org] true directory: not an attribute this package carries: "userPassword" holds a secret, and attributes are published: a credential has its own option or none true directory: not an attribute this package carries: "sambaNTPassword" holds a secret, and attributes are published: a credential has its own option or none true directory: not an attribute this package carries: "radiusHash" looks like it holds a secret (its name contains "hash"), and attributes are published: a credential has its own option or none true directory: not an attribute this package carries: "cn" is derived by the server from the name it publishes the entry under true directory: not an attribute this package carries: "memberUid" is membership, which Members answers: a second answer would disagree with it true directory: not an attribute this package carries: "2.5.4.35" is an OID: name it by its descriptor, so that what is refused by name stays refused Names are RFC 4512 attribute descriptions, compared ignoring case and the order of options, so mail and MAIL are one attribute, spelled the first way it was given; an exact repeat of a value is kept once. Values are strings and are not interpreted: "1000" is a uidNumber because a server’s schema says so. An empty value, or none, is refused.
refused why 56 named secrets — userPassword, authPassword, userPKCS12, sambaNTPassword, sambaLMPassword, unicodePwd, krbPrincipalKey, krb5Key, ipaNTHash, ipatokenOTPkey, oathSecret, olcRootPW, … read off RFC 4519, RFC 3112, RFC 2798 and the Samba, Active Directory, MIT and Heimdal Kerberos, FreeIPA, 389-ds and OpenLDAP schemas any name containing password, passwd, pwd, secret, credential, hash or privatekey a list only knows the schemas somebody read; the one standard name this would catch, secretary (RFC 4524), is allowed sshPublicKey it has its own path, WithPublicKeys, so that Can(PublicKeys) stays true uid, userid, cn, commonName, objectClass a server derives them from the name it publishes the entry under member, uniqueMember, memberUid, memberOf membership is what Members answers, and a second answer would disagree createTimestamp, modifyTimestamp, creatorsName, modifiersName, structuralObjectClass, governingStructureRule, subschemaSubentry, entryDN, entryUUID a server maintains them; a configuration could only forge them a name in numeric form refusals are by name, and 2.5.4.35 is userPassword ReservedAttributes() returns the whole list, 75 names with their reasons; CheckAttributeName applies the rule alone, so a configuration can be refused before anything is read.
Where they come from:
hcldir: attributes = { … } in user and group blocks, a string or a list of strings per name; a number is refused with the fix in the message (write it as a string, “1000”), and null leaves the attribute out. sqldir: two optional queries, users_attributes and groups_attributes (Queries.PeopleAttributes, GroupAttributes), read by column alias: the first column is the name, every other column an attribute named by its alias. A column whose alias is not an attribute description, or names a credential, is refused with its column number before a row is read. NULL and '' are absent, and several rows for one name add values. A group named only there exists, with nobody in it. ⛔ PostgreSQL lower-cases an unquoted alias (as uidNumber comes back uidnumber): the same attribute, spelled the database’s way. Quote it, as "uidNumber", where the spelling matters. ldapdir: Config.Attributes and GroupAttributes (attributes and group_attributes in a users "ldap" block) name what to copy from each person’s entry and each group’s, matched by RFC 4512 equivalence and kept in the configured spelling. Besides the list above, it refuses the totp_attribute and the group’s naming and member attributes. A subtype the directory returns besides (description;lang-fr for description) is not copied: ask for it by name. A group’s attributes come from Set.GroupAttributes, through the optional GroupAttributer: the first source to give an attribute owns it, so a gidNumber in a local file overrides the directory’s while a description only the directory has comes through, and a broken source is an error even when another answered. A person’s attributes come with the person, from the source that owns the name.
data.example#Example:
package main import ( "errors" "fmt" "github.com/go-authn/directory" ) func main() { local := &directory.Static{ Name: "the configuration file", People: []*directory.Identity{ directory.NewIdentity("dora", directory.WithPassword("hunter2")), directory.NewIdentity("eli", directory.WithVerifier(func(pw string) error { return directory.ErrWrongPassword // a bind against somebody else's LDAP, say })), directory.NewIdentity("svc-backup", directory.WithPublicKeys("ssh-ed25519 AAAA...elided... backup")), }, Groups: map[string][]string{"staff": {"dora", "eli"}, "nobody": {}}, } people := directory.NewSet(local) // more sources after it: sqldir, ldapdir... ids, _ := people.Identities() for _, id := range ids { fmt.Println(id.Name(), "password:", id.Can(directory.Password), "verifier:", id.Can(directory.Verifier), "keys:", id.Can(directory.PublicKeys), "from", id.Where()) } // NTLMv2 needs MD4(UTF16LE(password)): dora's can be derived, eli's cannot. for _, id := range ids[:2] { _, err := id.NTKey() fmt.Println(id.Name(), "SMB:", err == nil, errors.Is(err, directory.ErrNoCredential)) } // An empty group is an empty answer; a group nobody has is an error. fmt.Println(people.Members("nobody")) fmt.Println(people.Members("admins")) // @group is expanded; an empty group, or one nobody has, is refused. fmt.Println(directory.Expand([]string{"@staff", "svc-backup"}, people)) fmt.Println(directory.Expand([]string{"@nobody"}, local)) _, err := directory.Expand([]string{"@nobody"}, people) fmt.Println(err, errors.Is(err, directory.ErrEmptyGroup), errors.Is(err, directory.ErrNoSuchGroup)) _, err = directory.Expand([]string{"@admins"}, people) fmt.Println(err, errors.Is(err, directory.ErrEmptyGroup), errors.Is(err, directory.ErrNoSuchGroup)) } dora password: true verifier: true keys: false from the configuration file eli password: false verifier: true keys: false from the configuration file svc-backup password: false verifier: false keys: true from the configuration file dora SMB: true false eli SMB: false true [] [] directory: no such group: "admins", in the configuration file [dora eli svc-backup] [] directory: the group has no members: "nobody": nobody would be allowed directory: the group has no members: "nobody": nobody would be allowed true false directory: no such group: "admins", in the configuration file false true A held password also answers Can(Verifier): it can be compared.
An empty group is a group: Members answers it, Expand refuses it
From v0.12.0, Set.Members returns an empty list and no error for a group a source has with nobody in it, so a server that lists groups can publish it. Expand still refuses it, with ErrEmptyGroup, which is not ErrNoSuchGroup: a group nobody has is a typo or a deleted group, an empty one is a group to fill. A caller that tolerates a group granting nothing tests for both. In v0.11.x, Set.Members returned ErrNoSuchGroup for an empty group, and Expand of @nobody through the Set printed [] directory: no such group: "nobody".
data.ldapdir-defaults#ldapdir’s defaults:
setting (users "ldap" / ldapdir.Config) default from v0.14.0 up to v0.13.0 user_filter / UserFilter (|(objectClass=posixAccount)(objectClass=account)(objectClass=uidObject)), ldapdir.DefaultUserFilter (objectClass=posixAccount) user_attribute / UserAttribute uid the same group_base_dn / GroupBaseDN base_dn the same group_filter / GroupFilter (|(objectClass=posixGroup)(objectClass=groupOfNames)), ldapdir.DefaultGroupFilter (objectClass=posixGroup) group_attribute / GroupAttribute cn the same group_member_attribute / MemberAttribute none: memberUid (names) and member (DNs); set, it is the one attribute read memberUid The three classes are the standard ones that carry a uid: posixAccount (RFC 2307), account (RFC 4524 §3.1) and uidObject (RFC 4519 §3.14). go-authn/authnd from v0.11.0 publishes a person without the POSIX attributes as an account or an inetOrgPerson, puts uidObject on every person, and publishes a group without a gidNumber as a groupOfNames. Under the old defaults such people and groups were not read at all.
v0.14.0 widens what an institution’s directory gives
A directory holding account or uidObject entries that are not posixAccounts — service accounts, hosts named by uid, people imported from elsewhere — now gives them to every program that kept the default, and each of them can then be checked against the directory by a bind. Its groupOfNames groups become groups, and an @group rule naming one now grants what it says. A plain inetOrgPerson with none of the three classes is still not read. To keep exactly the old set:
users "ldap" { # ... user_filter = "(objectClass=posixAccount)" group_filter = "(objectClass=posixGroup)" group_member_attribute = "memberUid" } A member DN adds no person. It maps to somebody only when it is, by distinguishedNameMatch (RFC 4517 §4.2.15), the DN of an entry the people search returned. A DN outside those entries, or naming nobody, maps to nobody, and so does uid=alice,ou=elsewhere,… when alice was imported from ou=people. Up to v0.13.0 a DN in the member attribute was reduced to the value of its first RDN, whoever’s it was, so uid=alice,ou=elsewhere,…, cn=alice,… and uid=zed,… became members named alice, alice and zed.
ldaptest, the test directory, now applies base and filter to every search, gives each person an objectClass (Person.ObjectClasses, by default top, account, posixAccount) and has groupOfNames groups (GroupsOfNames), so a test of a client’s filters can fail.
data.the-sources#The sources:
package reads imports directory a Static list, and a Set of sources in order the standard library only directory/sqldir any *sql.DB, with your queries no driver: the program picks one directory/ldapdir an LDAP server go-ldap/ldap/v3 directory/hcldir a users block naming a database or an LDAP server, and user/group blocks holding people x/crypto/ssh, hashicorp/hcl/v2, zclconf/go-cty directory/ldaptest an LDAP server to test against glauth/ldap In a Set, the first source that knows a name owns it, so a service account written down locally need not be put in LDAP. Group membership is the union of every source. Sources are read when a server starts; a password check may reach the source every time, because a bind cannot be cached without holding the secret.
hcldir does not decode HCL: the caller decodes the block and hands it over. It imports HCL only to write, for SetPassword. The build tags nosql and noldap leave a kind out of hcldir entirely.
data.what-it-is-checked-against#What it is ch: OpenLDAP’s ldapsearch reads ldaptest’s directory — the entries, the sambaNTPassword of the one person who has it, the group — and is refused with Invalid credentials (49) for a wrong password. The CI’s Linux lanes install ldap-utils; where ldapsearch is absent the test skips, as nothing in this module’s CI turns that skip into a failure. ldapdir against glauth/ldap, an independent LDAP server, not a fake; the fixture allows the unauthenticated bind, so the test fails if ldapdir stops refusing it first. sqldir against a real SQLite database through a real driver. The attributes queries were also run once by hand against PostgreSQL 18.6 through pgx, not in CI: an unquoted alias came back lower-cased and was found anyway, a quoted one kept its case, and an alias naming userPassword was refused. ldapdir’s filters against ldaptest, which from v0.14.0 applies them: the default user filter leaves out a plain inetOrgPerson (TestTheDefaultUserFilter), and the group filter adds no identity (TestTheGroupFilterAddsNoIdentity). MD4 against RFC 1320’s test vectors. The coverage lane fails below 85% (its stated standard is 100%), and the nosql and noldap builds are checked in CI.
data.what-it-refuses-and-why#What it refuses,:
A group with nobody in it, and a group no source has, when Expand turns @group into people — errors, not empty lists: a configuration that grants nothing to nobody reads exactly like one that works. The first is ErrEmptyGroup, the second ErrNoSuchGroup, and errors.Is tells them apart. Set.Members answers an empty group with an empty list; a group no source has is ErrNoSuchGroup there too. A source that is broken is reported apart from one that lacks the group, and wins over an empty answer. An LDAP directory reached in the clear. A simple bind carries the password itself (RFC 4513), so ldapdir.New and a users "ldap" block refuse ldap:// to another machine unless StartTLS is set. ldaps://, ldapi:// and ldap:// to a loopback address are accepted. There is no switch to turn this off. An empty password at an LDAP bind. In LDAP it is an unauthenticated bind, which most directories answer with success; ldapdir answers ErrWrongPassword without dialling. Any other failed bind taken for a wrong password. Only LDAP result 49, invalidCredentials, is ErrWrongPassword. A connection dropped during the bind, a directory answering busy (51) or unavailable (52), is returned as ldapdir: the directory did not answer the bind: …, wrapping the LDAP error. The password is refused either way; what changes is that a server’s log no longer says wrong password to somebody who typed it right. Before v0.11.2 every failed bind was ErrWrongPassword. Credentials in an LDAP URL — a URL is printed; BindDN and BindPassword are fields. An NT hash that is not 16 bytes (ParseNTHash), rather than padding it into a hash that fails every login as a wrong password. Derive or KerberosKey for an identity without the password. A verifier’s yes is not a key. An attribute that is a secret, or that a server answers itself — the list above — wherever it is configured: in a block, as a SQL alias, or in ldapdir’s list to copy. The NT hash and the TOTP secret are credentials, not hashes of one
Whoever holds sambaNTPassword authenticates as that person exactly as if they held the password; whoever holds a TOTP secret produces every future code. WithVerifier’s error goes to the server, never to the client.
data.what-proves-somebody-is-not-one-thing#Wh:
It is a fact about protocols. NTLMv2 (SMB) is a challenge-response: the client never sends the password, so the server must hold the password or MD4(UTF16LE(password)) — the NT hash — and an LDAP bind cannot authenticate an SMB session. A KDC must decrypt with the person’s key, so only a source holding the password can back a realm. SSH needs a public key. A second factor needs the secret behind the six digits.
So an Identity says which Credentials its source gave — Password, NTHash, Verifier (a hash comparison or a bind), PublicKeys, TOTPSecret — and Identity.Can lets a server say you can use WebDAV and not SMB before somebody meets a refusal at a mount. Each protocol has its own method:
answers from Verify(password) anything handed the password the source’s verifier first (it may be an LDAP bind), else the held password, compared in constant time on SHA-256 digests so not even the length leaks NTKey() NTLMv2 the published hash, or derived from the password; ErrNoCredential with neither Derive(f), KerberosKey(f) a KDC, AWS SigV4 — anything that must possess the secret the password only; the derivation is the caller’s function Keys() SSH authorized_keys lines TOTPSecret() totp a column, or an LDAP attribute the caller names

data:
How is a security key spoken to? The FIDO client-to-authenticator protocol — the CTAPHID framing, the channel handshake, and the CTAP2 commands that register a credential, ask for a signature and exchange a PIN for a token — in pure Go, on any operating system.
go get github.com/go-authn/fido@v0.6.2 Nothing here is platform-specific. A Transport moves 64-byte reports to and from one authenticator and says what the device is called; where those reports come from — IOKit on macOS, hidraw on Linux, WebHID in a browser — is somebody else’s package. Everything above it is here:
Open(ctx, t) the INIT handshake on the broadcast channel; returns a *Key with its own channel. The Key owns t: Close closes it, and so does a failed Open Key.Ping, Key.Wink a round trip, and a blink — the cheapest way to ask which of these keys is this one? Key.GetInfo versions, extensions, AAGUID, options, PIN protocols Key.MakeCredential, Key.GetAssertion register, and sign; ParseAuthData reads the authenticator data, and AuthData.PublicKey turns a P-256 COSE key into an *ecdsa.PublicKey Key.PINRetries, Key.KeyAgreement, Key.PINToken authenticatorClientPIN, both PIN/UV auth protocols Split, NewReassembler, ParseInit, Key.CBOR the framing, exported for whoever drives a key some other way AuthData.PublicKey is a conversion, not a verification: which algorithms count and what to do with a sign counter that went backwards belongs to the caller. keyfactor is one such caller.
data.example#Example:
The framing alone, with no key: a message cut into reports, and put back together.
package main import ( "bytes" "fmt" "github.com/go-authn/fido" ) func main() { // A 200-byte ping, cut into the 64-byte reports a key reads... payload := bytes.Repeat([]byte{0xA5}, 200) reports, err := fido.Split(0x01020304, fido.CmdPing, payload) if err != nil { panic(err) } fmt.Println(len(reports), "reports of", len(reports[0]), "bytes") // ...and put back together, as a reply would be. r := fido.NewReassembler(0x01020304) for _, rep := range reports { msg, done, err := r.Feed(rep) if err != nil { panic(err) } if done { fmt.Println(bytes.Equal(msg.Data, payload), msg.Cmd == fido.CmdPing) } } // A report for another channel is an error, not something to drop. other, _ := fido.Split(0x0A0B0C0D, fido.CmdPing, []byte("hi")) _, _, err = fido.NewReassembler(0x01020304).Feed(other[0]) fmt.Println(err) // The framing's real limit, not the length field's. fmt.Println(fido.MaxMessage) } 4 reports of 64 bytes true true fido: the report belongs to another channel 7609 With a key, fido.Open(ctx, transport) does the handshake and the *Key it returns carries every later command.
data.what-it-is-checked-against#What it is ch:
The CI has no security key, so the tests use a fake transport that reassembles what it is sent — a key that refuses, stalls, keeps saying it is busy, or shares its channel with another program — with coverage held at 100%. Two fixtures come from outside this code:
testdata/yubikey-fido-5.7.4-getinfo.hex, the GetInfo reply captured from a YubiKey FIDO 5.7.4, decoded by ctap2_test.go; testdata/webauthn-reference-authdata.b64, a sample from the tests of go-webauthn/webauthn, which checks the authenticator-data parser and AuthData.PublicKey. The status-code table follows libfido2’s err.h. The module’s README records a registration and an assertion run against a real YubiKey, with the signature verified against the public key it handed out; that run is not part of CI.
data.what-it-refuses-and-why#What it refuses,:
A key is not trusted to answer what it was asked. A reply that carries a different command from the one sent is refused (CTAP 2.1 §11.2.9 gives each response its own command, and libfido2 checks it too). An INIT reply whose nonce is not the one sent is refused: it is another program’s handshake on the same key. A PIN token that is not its protocol’s length — 16 or 32 bytes under protocol one, exactly 32 under protocol two — is refused.
A keepalive is not an answer. A key waiting for a finger sends CTAPHID_KEEPALIVE about every hundred milliseconds; it is skipped, and the only bound on how long a touch may take is the context.
A message longer than the framing can carry. Two length bytes would allow 65535, but 57 bytes in the initialisation packet plus 128 continuations of 59 is 7609 (MaxMessage); past that a sequence number would reach 0x80 and a key would read it as a new message. Split returns ErrTooLong.
Reports that do not add up: one for another channel (ErrWrongChannel — two programs on one key), continuations out of order (ErrOutOfOrder), a report shorter than a packet (ErrShortPacket), an INIT reply shorter than its 17 bytes (ErrTruncated).
A command the key did not say it supports. Wink is not sent to a key without CapWink, nor GetInfo to one without CapCBOR: the key would answer CTAPHID_ERROR, and the caller would have to tell that refusal from a fault.
An empty PIN, and anything but P-256 in AuthData.PublicKey — refused by name rather than half-decoded.
A wrong PIN costs a retry
CTAP gives an authenticator a counter of PIN retries, eight at most, and each wrong PIN spends one. Three wrong PINs in a row block the PIN until the key is unplugged and plugged back in. A counter that reaches zero blocks it for good: only a reset lifts that, and a reset erases every credential on the key. Ask Key.PINRetries before prompting anybody: it says how many retries are left, and whether the key is waiting to be unplugged.
When a key refuses a PIN, the error says which of the two it is. CTAP2_ERR_PIN_AUTH_BLOCKED (0x34), which unplugging lifts, reads too many wrong PINs in a row; unplug the key and plug it in again (0x34); CTAP2_ERR_PIN_BLOCKED (0x32), which only a reset lifts, reads the PIN is blocked: no tries are left, and only a reset, which erases the credentials, unblocks it (0x32). Before v0.6.2 the two sentences were swapped: a key that only had to be unplugged was called locked, and somebody told that might reset it and lose every credential on it.
