How does a realm issue tickets from a directory? AS-REQ and TGS-REQ, over UDP and TCP, with encrypted-timestamp pre-authentication required, for the people a directory knows and the services a keytab holds. It runs under authnd.
go get github.com/go-authn/kdc@v0.4.3 At v0.4.3 its go.mod requires at least go-authn/directory v0.12.0 and gokrb5 v8.4.4: minimums, so a program that requires directory v0.14.0, the version these pages describe, builds with v0.14.0, as authnd v0.11.0 does. The accepting half is krb5, and a service that only verifies tickets needs this module not at all.
Not implemented: cross-realm referrals, PKINIT, FAST, renewable or postdated tickets, and any kadmin protocol. Keys come from the directory and from a keytab, and change where they live.
data.example#Example:
A realm in memory, on loopback:
package main import ( "crypto/rand" "fmt" "log" "net" "time" "github.com/go-authn/directory" "github.com/go-authn/kdc" "github.com/jcmturner/gokrb5/v8/iana/etypeID" "github.com/jcmturner/gokrb5/v8/keytab" ) func main() { // People: a source that holds PASSWORDS. A verifier cannot back a realm. people := &directory.Static{Name: "the configuration file", People: []*directory.Identity{ directory.NewIdentity("alice", directory.WithPassword("correct horse battery staple")), }} // Services: the realm's own krbtgt key, and one per service. kt := keytab.New() for _, p := range []string{"krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG", "nfs/files.example.org"} { if err := kt.AddEntry(p, "EXAMPLE.ORG", rand.Text(), time.Now(), 1, etypeID.AES256_CTS_HMAC_SHA1_96); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } // A keytab without krbtgt/REALM is refused before anything listens. _, err := kdc.New(kdc.Config{Realm: "OTHER.ORG", People: people, Services: kt}) fmt.Println(err) srv, err := kdc.New(kdc.Config{ Realm: "EXAMPLE.ORG", People: people, Services: kt, Logf: log.Printf, // why each request was refused; never a key }) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } pc, err := net.ListenPacket("udp", "127.0.0.1:18088") if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } ln, err := net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:18088") if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } go srv.ServeTCP(ln) fmt.Println("EXAMPLE.ORG answers on", pc.LocalAddr()) log.Fatal(srv.ServeUDP(pc)) } With a krb5.conf naming kdc = tcp/127.0.0.1:18088 for EXAMPLE.ORG, the Heimdal kinit that macOS ships (1.5.1) gets a ticket-granting ticket, with KRB5_CONFIG=krb5.conf and KRB5CCNAME=FILE:cc:
$ kinit --password-file=STDIN alice@EXAMPLE.ORG < alice.pw $ klist Credentials cache: FILE:cc Principal: alice@EXAMPLE.ORG Issued Expires Principal Oct 10 21:54:46 2026 Oct 11 07:54:46 2026 krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG $ kinit --password-file=STDIN alice@EXAMPLE.ORG < bad.pw kinit: Password incorrect $ kinit --password-file=STDIN bob@EXAMPLE.ORG < alice.pw kinit: krb5_get_init_creds: Error from KDC: no such principal in this realm $ kgetcred nfs/files.example.org@EXAMPLE.ORG $ klist Credentials cache: FILE:cc Principal: alice@EXAMPLE.ORG Issued Expires Principal Oct 10 21:54:46 2026 Oct 11 07:54:46 2026 krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG Oct 10 21:54:47 2026 Oct 11 07:54:46 2026 nfs/files.example.org@EXAMPLE.ORG The ten hours are Config.Lifetime’s default, and the service ticket ends with the ticket-granting ticket it was bought with. The KDC said why it refused each request, in its own log:
kdc: the keytab has no krbtgt key for this realm: matching key not found in keytab. Looking for "krbtgt/OTHER.ORG" realm: OTHER.ORG kvno: 0 etype: 18 EXAMPLE.ORG answers on 127.0.0.1:18088 2026/10/10 21:54:46 refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication required (code 25) 2026/10/10 21:54:46 refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication required (code 25) 2026/10/10 21:54:46 the timestamp does not decrypt (client etype 18, our key type 18): error decrypting: integrity verification failed 2026/10/10 21:54:46 refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication does not decrypt (code 24) 2026/10/10 21:54:47 refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: no such principal in this realm (code 6) The first refusal of each exchange is the protocol working: the KRB-ERROR that demands pre-authentication carries an ETYPE-INFO2 hint naming the etype and the salt, and the client tries again with a timestamp.
Before v0.4.2, a till of 19700101000000Z got a ticket that had already expired
RFC 4120 §5.4.1: a till of 19700101000000Z asks for the maximum end time the KDC’s policy permits. Heimdal’s kgetcred sends exactly that. v0.4.1 tested only for Go’s zero time, so it took the Unix epoch for a real end and issued a service ticket that klist showed as >>>Expired<<<; MIT’s kvno, the CI’s judge, sends a real till and never met the case. v0.4.2 issues the longest ticket allowed, as above, and answers a till that has already passed with KDC_ERR_NEVER_VALID instead of a ticket expired on arrival (go-authn/kdc#19).
data.only-a-source-holding-the-password-can-b: A KDC must decrypt the client’s pre-authentication with that person’s long-term key, so a directory.Verifier — a bind against somebody else’s LDAP, a hash comparison — cannot serve, however well it answers is this the right password. A person whose source holds no password is answered KDC_ERR_NULL_KEY (null key), never the code a wrong password gets, so it reads as a configuration to fix rather than a password to retype.
data.what-it-is-checked-against#What it is ch: MIT’s own kinit and kvno, through pkgx, against a realm built in Go — no MIT KDC is involved, only the client is borrowed. TestMITClientGetsATGTAndAServiceTicket gets a TGT and a service ticket and checks the key version kvno reports. The Linux test lane, the race detector and the coverage lane set KDC_REQUIRE_JUDGE=1, and a further step fails unless the log says were served by this realm. The tests also pin the refusals a real client never triggers: a timestamp under the wrong key, one from an hour ago, a three-byte cipher, a service asked for straight from an AS-REQ, a forged service ticket at the TGS, and a realm backed by a verifier. The coverage lane’s floor is 80%.
data.what-it-refuses-and-why#What it refuses,:
At configuration (New): no realm (ErrNoRealm), no directory (ErrNoPeople), no keytab (ErrNoServices), or a keytab without krbtgt/REALM@REALM (ErrNoTGTKey) — rather than starting and failing at the first kinit, where the error reaches a person who cannot fix it.
At the AS: a request without pre-authentication is answered with the demand for it, and the person’s key is not derived until there is a timestamp to check, so a spoofed UDP packet naming a real principal costs no key derivation. A wrong password, a timestamp under another etype and one from an hour ago are all answered KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED, the code a wrong password gets; the error text names the reason, and so does Logf. A service asking for a TGT of its own is refused: services authenticate from a keytab.
One encryption type. Tickets and keys are aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 (etype 18) only. A request whose etype list lacks 18 is answered KDC_ERR_ETYPE_NOSUPP before anybody is looked up. With Logf set, the log records both etypes, so an operator can tell a mismatched cipher from a mistyped password.
At the TGS (RFC 4120 §3.3.2), a ticket is issued only when:
the ticket presented is a TGT of this realm, decrypted under the krbtgt/REALM key the KDC names — not under the key of whatever service the ticket claims (KRB_AP_ERR_NOT_US); the authenticator decrypts under its session key, within MaxSkew; its checksum is over this request’s body, as the bytes arrived, keyed with the session key (KRB_AP_ERR_INAPP_CKSUM when missing or unkeyed, KRB_AP_ERR_MODIFIED when wrong); the TGT is not past its end (KRB_AP_ERR_TKT_EXPIRED), not before its start and not flagged invalid (KRB_AP_ERR_TKT_NYV), with no skew allowed: this KDC’s clock wrote those times; the client is of this realm and still in the directory (KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN). Lifetimes. Config.Lifetime caps a ticket, ten hours when zero; a client asking for less gets less, and a ticket bought with a TGT ends no later than that TGT, so asking for krbtgt again cannot stretch a credential.
What an unauthenticated peer can hold: a TCP message, its length included, must arrive within 30 seconds; at most 256 TCP connections are served at once, and at most 64 datagrams are answered at once — one more is dropped, and the client resends or falls back to TCP.

data:
Did the key that was registered answer, and did a person touch it? keyfactor is the one piece between fido, which speaks CTAP and knows about no policy, and mfa, which decides how much proof is enough and knows about no device. Neither imports the other; this imports both.
go get github.com/go-authn/keyfactor@v0.4.2 At v0.4.2 its go.mod requires at least go-authn/fido v0.6.2 and go-authn/mfa v0.5.0, the versions these pages describe.
The platform supplies an Opener — how a key is found on this system — and keeps only that. Everything else is the same wherever CTAP is: the assertion, the checks, the refusal to spend somebody’s last PIN attempt.
data.example#Example: package main import ( "context" "crypto/ecdsa" "errors" "fmt" "github.com/go-authn/fido" "github.com/go-authn/keyfactor" "github.com/go-authn/mfa" ) func main() { // The platform supplies the Opener: how a key is found on this system. // This one finds nothing, and says so the way a policy understands. open := func(context.Context) (fido.Transport, error) { return nil, keyfactor.Unavailable(errors.New("no security key is plugged in")) } // From the registration: the credential ID and its public key, which // fido.AuthData.PublicKey returns from the attestation. var pub *ecdsa.PublicKey // nil here, to show the refusal f := keyfactor.New(open, keyfactor.Options{ RPID: "example.test", CredentialID: []byte{0x01, 0x02}, PublicKey: pub, }) fmt.Println(f.Name(), f.Kind()) _, err := mfa.Verify(context.Background(), mfa.Policy{Count: 1}, f) fmt.Println(err) } your security key possession mfa: 1 factor(s) needed, 0 answered: your security key (possession): keyfactor: no public key for the credential; without one any device that answers would pass, so pass the one from the registration The refusal comes before the Opener is called. With the registration’s public key, the same factor opens the key, asks it for an assertion over a fresh random challenge, and checks the answer.
data.what-it-is-checked-against#What it is ch: The tests fake the authenticator, not the transport, built from go-authn/fido’s own exported framing: a CTAPHID handshake, a CTAP2 assertion, and a ClientPIN exchange. The PIN half plays the authenticator’s side of protocol two independently — its own ECDH, HKDF and AES-CBC, written from the specification (fakepin_test.go) — so a derivation that differed by a byte would fail the exchange. forged_test.go is the device that holds no credential. Coverage is held at 100%, and the tests run on eight architectures.
data.what-it-refuses-and-why#What it refuses,:
A device answering is not the key answering. A programmable USB board speaks CTAP as well as a security key does, so the answer is checked against the registration:
refused message before anything is opened: no Opener, no RPID, no PublicKey, or a key not on P-256 keyfactor: no opener; …, … needs a relying party id …, … no public key for the credential; …, … is not on P-256 … a relying-party hash that is not SHA-256 of RPID … answered for another relying party a credential other than CredentialID, when the device names one … answered with a credential other than the one asked for a signature over the authenticator data and the challenge that PublicKey did not make … answered with a signature the credential's key did not make no UP flag … answered without anyone touching it no UV flag when a PIN was given … was asked to establish who holds it and did not The last PIN attempt is not spent on a guess. PINRetries is asked first; a key that will take no more PINs until it is unplugged is refused, and so is one with one attempt or fewer left. Under CTAP, three wrong PINs in a row block a key’s PIN until it is unplugged, and a retry counter that reaches zero blocks it for good: only a reset lifts that, erasing every credential on it.
When the key itself refuses a PIN, the error is fido’s, and from fido v0.6.2 it names the right one of the two: too many wrong PINs in a row; unplug the key and plug it in again (0x34) when unplugging lifts the block, and the PIN is blocked: no tries are left, and only a reset, which erases the credentials, unblocks it (0x32) when only a reset does. Before fido v0.6.2 the two sentences were swapped.
A PIN is not a second factor. The kind stays mfa.Possession: a PIN entered into the key protects the key, and identifies nobody to this machine.
An empty port is not a refusal. An Opener that finds nothing wraps its error with keyfactor.Unavailable, which marks it mfa.ErrUnavailable, and a policy counts could not be asked apart from said no.
What it cannot protect: the PIN’s hash reaches whatever device answers
CTAP has the platform hand the key LEFT(SHA-256(PIN), 16), encrypted under a secret agreed with the device itself, before anything is signed. A forged device is refused as a factor, but it has received that hash, and a short PIN falls to an offline search. That is the protocol. Use a long PIN, and do not type one into a key whose provenance is unknown.

data:
Is this Kerberos ticket good for this service? The acceptor half of Kerberos, and only that half: it holds a keytab, verifies the AP-REQ a client presents, answers with the AP-REP that proves the service is genuine, and then signs, verifies, seals and opens messages under the key that exchange established.
go get github.com/go-authn/krb5@v0.3.1 It never talks to a KDC and never issues a ticket, so whose tickets it accepts is somebody else’s decision. The issuing half is kdc, and this module does not depend on it — see why they are separate. Ticket decryption is gokrb5’s.
data.example#Example:
package main import ( "errors" "fmt" "log" "github.com/go-authn/krb5" "github.com/jcmturner/gokrb5/v8/keytab" ) // establish is one GSS-API exchange: the client's AP-REQ in, the AP-REP out. func establish(a *krb5.Acceptor, token []byte) (*krb5.Context, []byte, error) { ctx, apRep, err := a.Accept(token) if err != nil { return nil, nil, err // no context: refuse, never fall back to something weaker } // The client will not consider the context open until it has verified // apRep, so sending it back is not optional. log.Printf("%s (user %q, realm %q) until %s", ctx.Principal(), ctx.User(), ctx.Realm(), ctx.Expires()) return ctx, apRep, nil } func main() { // In a service: krb5.Load("/etc/krb5.keytab", krb5.Principal("nfs/files.example.org")). // Here, an empty keytab, so the refusals can be seen. a := krb5.New(keytab.New(), krb5.Principal("nfs/files.example.org")) _, _, err := establish(a, []byte("not a token")) fmt.Println(errors.Is(err, krb5.ErrNotAToken), err) _, err = krb5.Load("/nonexistent/krb5.keytab") fmt.Println(errors.Is(err, krb5.ErrNoKeytab), err) } true krb5: not a GSS-API krb5 token: asn1: structure error: explicitly tagged member didn't match true krb5: keytab "/nonexistent/krb5.keytab": open /nonexistent/krb5.keytab: no such file or directory It needs github.com/jcmturner/gokrb5/v8 for keytab.New, which krb5.New takes; krb5.Load reads a keytab from a path instead.
After Accept, a *Context says who: Principal() (alice@EXAMPLE.ORG), or User() and Realm() apart. Mapping a principal to a local account is the caller’s policy: alice@EXAMPLE.ORG and alice@PARTNER.ORG both answer to “alice”. Expires() is when the ticket behind it ends, past which a server holding a long-lived connection should stop honouring it. MIC/VerifyMIC and Wrap/Unwrap sign; Seal/Unseal add confidentiality (sec=krb5p). A Context is not safe for concurrent use; an Acceptor is.
data.what-it-is-checked-against#What it is ch:
A real MIT KDC and MIT’s own gss-client, against this package standing in for gss-server. test/kdc.sh builds a throwaway realm on loopback, unprivileged; the CI gets MIT Kerberos through pkgx (Ubuntu’s packages do not ship gss-client). The Linux test lane, the race detector and the coverage lane set KRB5_REQUIRE_JUDGE=1, so a missing fixture fails. A further step runs TestMITClientAgainstThisAcceptor and fails unless the log says authenticated as alice@ — a green lane whose judge silently stopped running is not accepted. TestMITClientSealed does the same with confidentiality on.
The macOS, Windows and cross-architecture lanes have no realm, and there the judge skips. The coverage lane’s floor is 90%.
data.what-it-refuses-and-why#What it refuses,:
A ticket this service will not accept — wrong service, wrong key, expired, replayed, a clock beyond ClockSkew (five minutes by default, MIT’s too) — is ErrRejected. Bytes that are not a GSS-API krb5 token are ErrNotAToken, and a token that is not an AP-REQ is ErrNotAPReq. The errors are deliberately coarse: a client learns that its ticket was refused, never which check refused it. An error means no context, and the returned token is empty.
A principal the acceptor does not answer for. With krb5.Principal("nfs/files.example.org"), a keytab holding several services answers for that one only.
A message whose signature does not match is ErrBadMIC, whichever of the length, the header, the sequence or the checksum disagreed. The acceptor signs with key usage 23 and verifies with 25, so a token this server produced cannot be replayed back at it as though the client had signed it.
A sealed token given to Unwrap is ErrSealed, distinct from a bad signature: a caller reading an integrity-only token must not be handed ciphertext that reads like a message. An unsealed token given to Unseal is ErrNotSealed: a protocol that promised confidentiality is not handed something that crossed the wire in the clear.
It asserts no acceptor subkey: the context key is the subkey the initiator put in its authenticator, or the ticket’s session key when it sent none (RFC 4121 §4.3).
A keytab is a secret at rest
Its path may come from a configuration file or from KRB5_KTNAME; the key inside it must never be logged, printed, or carried in an environment variable.
data.why-it-exists#Why it exists: gokrb5 is a client library. It verifies an AP-REQ and cannot build the AP-REP that answers one. Every GSS-API client asks for mutual authentication — MIT’s own gss-client sets GSS_C_MUTUAL_FLAG with no way to turn it off — so a service that cannot produce an AP-REP completes no context at all. Building it is most of what this module adds.

Is this SSH certificate or key revoked — as sshd would answer? The binary format of OpenSSH’s PROTOCOL.krl, the list sshd loads through RevokedKeys and ssh-keygen -k writes. golang.org/x/crypto/ssh has no support for it.
go get github.com/go-authn/krl@v0.6.1 IsRevoked follows ssh_krl_check_key in OpenSSH’s krl.c: a certificate is revoked when its serial or key ID is revoked under the CA that signed it or under any CA, when its CA key is revoked, or when its own key is revoked by blob or by SHA-1 or SHA-256 fingerprint. Serial 0 — what a CA writes when it names none — is never revoked by serial.
data.example#Example: package main import ( "crypto/ed25519" "crypto/rand" "fmt" "time" "github.com/go-authn/krl" "golang.org/x/crypto/ssh" ) func main() { ca := signer() user := signer() // The issuer: certificate 42 is revoked, and so is everything for key ID "alice". b := krl.NewBuilder(7, "revoked by the bridge") b.RevokeSerial(ca.PublicKey(), 42) b.RevokeKeyID(nil, "alice") // nil: under any CA b.SetExpires(time.Now().Add(time.Hour)) data, err := b.Marshal(time.Now()) if err != nil { panic(err) } // The server: parse the list, then ask about each certificate. k, err := krl.Parse(data) if err != nil { panic(err) } fmt.Println("version", k.Version, "signed", k.Signed, "expires set", !k.Expires.IsZero()) for _, c := range []struct { serial uint64 id string }{{42, "bob"}, {43, "bob"}, {44, "alice"}} { fmt.Println(c.serial, c.id, k.IsRevoked(certificate(ca, user.PublicKey(), c.serial, c.id))) } } func signer() ssh.Signer { _, priv, _ := ed25519.GenerateKey(rand.Reader) s, _ := ssh.NewSignerFromKey(priv) return s } func certificate(ca ssh.Signer, key ssh.PublicKey, serial uint64, id string) *ssh.Certificate { c := &ssh.Certificate{ Key: key, Serial: serial, KeyId: id, CertType: ssh.UserCert, ValidPrincipals: []string{id}, ValidBefore: ssh.CertTimeInfinity, } if err := c.SignCert(rand.Reader, ca); err != nil { panic(err) } return c } version 7 signed false expires set true 42 bob true 43 bob false 44 alice true The same list and certificates, written to files, get the same three answers from OpenSSH 10.3p1’s ssh-keygen -Q -f list.krl: REVOKED, ok, REVOKED.
data.expiry-expiresgo-authngithubio#Expiry: e:
A KRL has a generation date and a version, and nothing says when it stops being current, so a stale copy cannot be told from a fresh one. Builder.SetExpires writes that time in an extension section named ExtensionExpires, not critical, so sshd and ssh-keygen load the list and ignore it; Parse reads it into KRL.Expires.
No signatures
OpenSSH never exposed a way to write the KRL signature section and no longer verifies it. Parse skips one and sets Signed, which says nothing about authenticity; Builder never writes one. The list’s integrity, and so its expiry’s, comes from its transport — HTTPS from an authenticated server — or from a detached SSHSIG signature checked by the caller, which this package does not do.
data.merging-one-file-for-sshd#Merging: one f: sshd read a single RevokedKeys file until OpenSSH 10.3, so a server trusting several CAs needs their lists in one. Builder.Merge adds every revocation of a parsed list. Builder.MergeCA(k, ca, others...) keeps k’s section for ca, its any-CA sections re-scoped to ca, and its explicit keys and fingerprints, and leaves out — counting them — sections for another CA and keys or fingerprints that designate one of others. MergeCAWith with MergeOptions{DropKeys: true} also leaves out every explicit key except ca’s own, for a list not trusted with every CA’s users: a revoked user key locks that user out under every CA of the merged file, because sshd checks a certificate’s own key whoever signed it.
data.what-it-is-checked-against#What it is ch:
OpenSSH’s ssh-keygen, on the Linux and macOS lanes, where KRL_REQUIRE_SSHKEYGEN=1 makes a missing one a failure (Windows runs the pure-Go tests only):
a KRL written by ssh-keygen -k with every serial encoding, key IDs, three CAs plus “any CA”, explicit keys and a revoked CA key: IsRevoked answers like ssh-keygen -Q for 250 certificates, and Builder given the same revocations writes the same bytes; 40 random serial sets written by both: byte-identical, and the same answers for about 9000 certificates; every truncation and about 1400 single-byte corruptions: Parse refuses exactly what ssh-keygen refuses; the expiry extension loads in ssh-keygen, and the same section marked critical is refused; merged lists revoke exactly what one of their sources revokes. FuzzParse, seeded with KRLs ssh-keygen wrote, and FuzzBuilder run in CI. The coverage floor is 100%, measured on the Linux lane where ssh-keygen is present.
data.what-it-refuses-and-why#What it refuses,:
Parse refuses what ssh-keygen and sshd refuse: a bad magic or format version, truncated or trailing data, an unknown section or certificate subsection, an unknown extension marked critical, a CA key OpenSSH cannot parse, serial 0, an inverted serial range, a bitmap larger than OpenSSH reads or one that wraps past 2^64−1. It also refuses a malformed or repeated expiry: read as absent, it would turn a list meant to lapse into one that never does.
Builder refuses — at Marshal, which returns the first invalid request — serial 0, a range whose low end is 0 or above its high end, a key ID or comment containing a NUL, a certificate given where a CA key is expected, and an expiry before the generation date.
One deliberate difference. For many sparse serials close together, ssh-keygen -k writes a bitmap wider than its own reader accepts and then refuses its own file (bignum is too large). Parse refuses that file too, as sshd would; Builder starts a new section before a bitmap gets that wide, so what it writes is always readable.
Parse allocates in proportion to what the list revokes, as OpenSSH does: a KRL should come from a source trusted not to send an enormous one.

What are the bytes of an LDAP server? A library, not a daemon: the wire, the filter, the operations. authnd is the server that runs it and owns the configuration, the directory sources and the bind policy; this owns the bytes.
go get github.com/go-authn/ldap@v0.8.0 Written from RFC 4511 (the protocol), 4512 (the root DSE and the schema), 4513 (authentication), 4514 and 4515 (DN and filter string forms), 4517 and 4518 (syntaxes, matching rules, string preparation), 4526, 2696 (paged results), 3672 (subentries), 3673, 4527 (read entry controls), 4532 (whoami) and 3045.
A Server is a set of handlers, each an optional field: Bind, SASL, Search, Compare, Extended, Add, Modify, Delete, ModifyDN, Abandon. A nil one means this server does not do that, and the operation is answered unwillingToPerform — not insufficientAccessRights, which would start an argument about permissions that do not exist. The root DSE is answered by the server itself, and publishes exactly what it honours.
data.example#Example:
A server with one person who can bind and a search that writes what the filter matches:
package main import ( "context" "crypto/subtle" "log" "log/slog" "os" "github.com/go-authn/ldap" ) var people = []*ldap.Entry{ {DN: "uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org", Attributes: []*ldap.Attribute{ ldap.StringAttribute("objectClass", "posixAccount"), ldap.StringAttribute("uid", "dora")}}, {DN: "uid=svc-web-prod,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org", Attributes: []*ldap.Attribute{ ldap.StringAttribute("objectClass", "posixAccount"), ldap.StringAttribute("uid", "svc-web-prod")}}, {DN: "uid=svc-web-stage,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org", Attributes: []*ldap.Attribute{ ldap.StringAttribute("objectClass", "posixAccount"), ldap.StringAttribute("uid", "svc-web-stage")}}, } // binder checks one password. A real one asks a directory: see go-authn/directory. type binder struct{} func (binder) Bind(_ context.Context, _ ldap.Session, req *ldap.BindRequest) (ldap.Result, error) { if req.Name == "" && len(req.Simple) == 0 { return ldap.Result{Code: ldap.Success}, nil // anonymous: the connection stays unbound } // A name with an empty password is an UNAUTHENTICATED bind (RFC 4513 // 5.1.2). This package hands it to the handler, and the handler refuses it: // the comparison below does, since the password is never empty. ok := ldap.EqualDN(req.Name, "uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org") && subtle.ConstantTimeCompare(req.Simple, []byte("hunter2")) == 1 if !ok { return ldap.Refuse(ldap.InvalidCredentials, "invalid credentials"), nil } return ldap.Result{Code: ldap.Success}, nil } // searcher writes each entry in scope that the filter matches, as it finds it. type searcher struct{} func (searcher) Search(_ context.Context, s ldap.Session, req *ldap.SearchRequest, w ldap.EntryWriter) (ldap.Result, error) { if s.BoundDN() == "" { return ldap.Refuse(ldap.InsufficientAccessRights, "bind first"), nil } for _, e := range people { if ldap.InScope(e.DN, req.BaseObject, req.Scope) && req.Filter.Matches(e) { if err := w.Entry(e); err != nil { return ldap.Result{}, err // the client went away, or a limit was reached } } } return ldap.Result{Code: ldap.Success}, nil } func main() { srv := &ldap.Server{ Bind: binder{}, Search: searcher{}, NamingContexts: []string{"dc=example,dc=org"}, Log: slog.New(slog.NewTextHandler(os.Stderr, nil)), // On anything but loopback: TLSConfig, and RequireTLS so that a // client that never asks for StartTLS is refused rather than // sending its password in the clear. } log.Fatal(srv.ListenAndServe("127.0.0.1:3389")) } Asked by OpenLDAP’s ldapsearch (2.4.28, as macOS ships it), with dora’s password in a file:
$ ldapsearch -LLL -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3389 -D uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y dora.pw \ -b ou=people,dc=example,dc=org '(uid=svc-*-prod)' uid dn: uid=svc-web-prod,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org uid: svc-web-prod $ ldapsearch -LLL -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3389 -b ou=people,dc=example,dc=org '(uid=*)' uid Insufficient access (50) Additional information: bind first $ ldapsearch -LLL -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3389 -s base -b '' namingContexts supportedLDAPVersion supportedExtension dn: supportedLDAPVersion: 3 namingContexts: dc=example,dc=org supportedExtension: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.3 $ printf 'dn: uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
changetype: modify
replace: uid
uid: x
' | ldapmodify -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3389 -D uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y dora.pw ldap_modify: Server is unwilling to perform (53) additional info: this server does not modify entries modifying entry "uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org" (uid=svc-*-prod) returns svc-web-prod and not svc-web-stage. The library this one replaces evaluated that filter as (uid=svc-*) and returned svc-web-stage as well; that defect is why this library was written. The root DSE does not list StartTLS, because no TLSConfig was given.
data.the-schema#The schema:
From v0.8.0, package schema is the directory schema of RFC 4512 §4, and Server.Schema makes a server use it. Nil keeps a server exactly as it was.
schema.Standard() embeds the definitions of RFC 4512, 4517, 4519, 4524, 4523, 2798, 2307, 3672 and 3045, plus openssh-lpk’s ldapPublicKey and sshPublicKey and the two OpenLDAP definitions they need, copied from the RFC text; each file in schema/defs names its source and section. schema.Build(append(schema.StandardFiles(), mine)...) adds a deployment’s own, and refuses one whose SUP, rules, syntaxes, MUST or MAY do not resolve. (*ldap.Entry).Validate(s) checks one structural chain with every superclass listed, every MUST, nothing outside MUST and MAY, SINGLE-VALUE, known types, values of their syntax, and the RDN’s values in the entry — and names every problem, as a *schema.ValidationError. With a schema, the root DSE carries subschemaSubentry: cn=Subschema, and a base search of cn=Subschema (ldap.SubschemaDN) is answered by the library, like the root DSE (RFC 4512 §4.2). The definitions come only when asked for by name or with +. It is behind the RequireTLS gate. Filters are evaluated with the schema’s matching rules (RFC 4517 §4.2, with RFC 4518 string preparation) in RFC 4511’s three-valued logic: an unknown attribute, a type with no rule for the match asked, or an invalid assertion value is Undefined, never an error. The server re-checks every entry a handler sends and drops those the filter does not make TRUE; a handler filters with req.Matches(e), which uses the same schema. package main import ( "errors" "fmt" "github.com/go-authn/ldap" "github.com/go-authn/ldap/schema" ) func main() { s := schema.Standard() // RFC 4512, 4517, 4519, 4524, 2798, 2307, ... and openssh-lpk // An account with posixAccount, and no homeDirectory. eli := &ldap.Entry{DN: "uid=eli,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org", Attributes: []*ldap.Attribute{ ldap.StringAttribute("objectClass", "top", "account", "posixAccount"), ldap.StringAttribute("uid", "eli"), ldap.StringAttribute("cn", "eli"), ldap.StringAttribute("uidNumber", "1001"), ldap.StringAttribute("gidNumber", "1001"), ldap.StringAttribute("mail", "eli@example.org"), }} var v *schema.ValidationError if errors.As(eli.Validate(s), &v) { for _, p := range v.Problems { fmt.Println("-", p) } } // uidNumber orders as an integer: 1001 >= 999, which as strings it is not. for _, f := range []string{"(uidNumber>=999)", "(uid>=a)"} { filter, _ := ldap.ParseFilter(f) fmt.Println(f, ldap.Evaluate(filter, eli, s)) } } - mail is not allowed by any of the entry's object classes - homeDirectory is required by posixAccount and is missing (uidNumber>=999) TRUE (uid>=a) Undefined mail belongs to inetOrgPerson, not to account. uid has no ORDERING rule, so a range on it is Undefined.
One departure from RFC 2307: uidNumber and gidNumber order as integers
RFC 2307 gives uidNumber and gidNumber an EQUALITY rule and no ORDERING rule, which would make every range filter on them Undefined — including the one SSSD builds from ldap_min_id and ldap_max_id. slapd defines both types itself with ORDERING integerOrderingMatch (servers/slapd/schema_prep.c; its nis.schema comments them out as “builtin”), and so does draft-howard-rfc2307bis-02 §2.1, so the embedded definitions follow them. That, and allowing auxiliary classes without DIT content rules (RFC 4512 §2.4.3 strictly forbids them; every server in use allows them), are said rather than discovered.
Not there, deliberately: DIT content rules, DIT structure rules and name forms; changing the schema over LDAP; RFC 4523’s certificate matching rules and directoryStringFirstComponentMatch, which are defined and not implemented, so assertions using them are Undefined; collective attributes; options other than lang- and binary.
authnd serves this schema and holds every entry it publishes to it.
data.what-it-is-checked-against#What it is ch:
OpenLDAP’s ldapsearch, in CI, and required where it is installed: the Linux test lane, the race detector and the coverage lane set LDAP_REQUIRE_JUDGE=1, so a missing client fails rather than skips. Windows has none and skips those tests. ldaptest, this module’s own wire client, is deliberately not the judge: it asks only what ldapsearch cannot, about one connection’s state — two binds on one socket, a SASL bind with an arbitrary mechanism, StartTLS followed by more LDAP.
FuzzMessage runs every message a client may send through the frame, the decoders and the filter round trip. The coverage floor is 99.7%, with the three unreached lines named in the workflow.
data.what-it-refuses-and-why#What it refuses,:
A filter means one thing. It is parsed or decoded once into a tree, and String, EncodeFilter and Matches all read that tree. An attribute that is not an RFC 4512 §2.5 attribute description, or a matching rule that is not an OID, is refused by both ParseFilter and DecodeFilter: before v0.6.1, printed back, a “present” filter on the attribute !x read as a NOT.
Plaintext, when it was promised otherwise. StartTLS is asked for by the client, so a server that merely offers it has promised nothing. RequireTLS refuses every operation on a connection that is not protected, with confidentialityRequired.
A bind that failed keeps nothing. RFC 4511 §4.2.1: the connection is made anonymous when the bind request is received, and stays so unless the bind succeeds — so a re-bind with a wrong password does not keep the previous person’s rights. A simple bind with no Bind handler is answered authMethodNotSupported, and LDAPv2 is refused as a protocol error.
The handler decides what an empty password means
An unauthenticated bind — a name with an empty password, RFC 4513 §5.1.2 — is passed to the Bind handler like any other simple bind, and a handler that returns Success for it binds the connection as that name. Refuse it in the handler, as the example does. directory’s ldapdir refuses it on the client side.
A critical control it does not honour. ManageDsaIT (RFC 3296), password modify (RFC 3062) and cancel (RFC 3909) are named as constants because a client may send them, not because they are answered: nothing here follows aliases or referrals, so a critical ManageDsaIT is refused with unavailableCriticalExtension.
What an unauthenticated peer can hold:
default MaxMessageSize 4 MiB a five-byte header claiming four gigabytes is refused before anything is reserved MaxMessageElements 16384 BER elements counted before decoding: before v0.5.0, 4 MiB of empty strings held 373 MiB before any bind IdleTimeout 5 minutes the whole message must arrive in time, not its first byte; negative means never MaxPending, MaxPendingAuth 100, 1000 operations one connection may have in flight before it has bound (MaxPending) and after (MaxPendingAuth), as slapd’s conn_max_pending and conn_max_pending_auth; a connection that goes over is sent a notice of disconnection and closed MaxPagedSearches 4 paged searches open per connection, each a goroutine parked on its next entry Filter nesting is bounded as well: a stack overflow in Go kills the process. Nothing logs an assertion value — a filter carries what somebody typed — only the filter’s shape.
A paged search answers what was asked. Until v0.8.0 the page reader sent each entry as the handler wrote it: a paged search for cn alone came back with every attribute, operational ones included, and typesOnly was ignored, while the same search unpaged kept to the selection. ldapsearch -E pr=N is how a client pages, so the same question got two answers. From v0.8.0 both apply the selection, which ldapsearch itself checks in CI.
Without a schema — Server.Schema nil, the default — every comparison is case-insensitive on the value: the safer of the two for reading, since it never hides an entry an exact comparison would have found.

Did enough factors answer, of enough kinds — and which ones? Nothing here reaches a device, and there is no cryptography: a Factor is anything that can be asked is this person here, now?, and this package decides what the answers add up to.
go get github.com/go-authn/mfa@v0.5.0 It imports nothing outside the standard library.
data.example#Example: package main import ( "context" "errors" "fmt" "github.com/go-authn/mfa" ) // factor is the smallest mfa.Factor: a name, a kind, and an answer. type factor struct { name string kind mfa.Kind err error } func (f factor) Name() string { return f.name } func (f factor) Kind() mfa.Kind { return f.kind } func (f factor) Verify(context.Context) error { return f.err } func main() { ctx := context.Background() twoFactor := mfa.Policy{Count: 2, DistinctKinds: true} // Two things the person knows are one kind of proof. _, err := mfa.Verify(ctx, twoFactor, factor{"your passphrase", mfa.Knowledge, nil}, factor{"a recovery code", mfa.Knowledge, nil}, ) fmt.Println(err) // A key that is not plugged in has not refused anybody. r, err := mfa.Verify(ctx, twoFactor, factor{"your passphrase", mfa.Knowledge, nil}, factor{"your security key", mfa.Possession, mfa.Unavailable(errors.New("no key attached"))}, ) fmt.Println(err) fmt.Println(r.Answers[1].Unavailable()) // The zero Policy is refused, not guessed at. _, err = mfa.Verify(ctx, mfa.Policy{}, factor{"your passphrase", mfa.Knowledge, nil}) fmt.Println(err) } mfa: 2 factor(s) answered but only 1 kind(s) among them (knowledge); two of the same kind are not two factors mfa: 2 factor(s) needed, 1 answered: your security key (possession): not available true mfa: a policy that requires 0 factors accepts anyone The real factors live elsewhere: totp for a code from a phone, keyfactor for a security key.
data.two-of-the-same-thing-is-one-factor#Two:
A passphrase and a recovery code are both things the person knows: whoever learned one has usually learned the other from the same place. So a factor says what it proves — Knowledge, Possession or Inherence — and the policy that means what two-factor is normally taken to mean is Policy{Count: 2, DistinctKinds: true}. Policy{Count: 2} alone is also offered, for a caller who wants two keys of the same kind on purpose; it is a different request and is spelled differently.
A factor whose Kind() is Unknown counts towards the number satisfied, never towards the kinds: it cannot be shown to differ from anything.
data.what-it-is-checked-against#What it is ch: No external judge: the module holds no protocol to disagree with. Its CI requires 100% statement coverage on Linux, macOS and Windows, runs the race detector, and runs the tests on amd64, arm64, riscv64, loong64, ppc64le, s390x, 386 and arm.
data.what-it-refuses-and-why#What it refuses,:
Verify refuses before it asks anybody:
why a Policy whose Count is below one a policy that requires 0 factors accepts anyone. There is no default policy: how much proof is enough belongs to whoever protects the thing fewer factors offered than Count the policy cannot be met, whatever they answer a factor whose Kind() is outside the enumeration counted as a distinct kind, Kind(42) beside a passphrase would pass as two-factor the same factor twice before v0.3.0, one passphrase passed twice satisfied Count: 2, and before v0.4.0 so did any factor holding a function. “The same” is the same type holding the same values, functions included: a function is the same function when it runs the same code And it keeps three things apart while it asks:
Could not be asked is not a refusal. A factor that returns ErrUnavailable — wrapped by mfa.Unavailable(err), which keeps the reason — is reported as such (Answer.Unavailable()), and never ends an attempt even with StopOnFirstFailure. Every factor is asked by default, so a person can be told your key answered, your fingerprint did not in one attempt. StopOnFirstFailure is there when stopping early is wanted. A factor not reached has no entry in Result.Answers: reporting it as failed would send somebody after nothing. The Result is returned whether or not the policy was met, with the error naming what was missing in words a person can act on.

Who does this bearer token say is asking, and should it be believed? Discovery, the key set, and the checks a resource server must make — in pure Go, with no dependencies outside the standard library.
go get github.com/go-authn/oidc@v0.4.1 There is no login flow here: no redirect, no code exchange, no client secret, no cookies. This is the resource-server half — something arrives with a token, and this says who that is.
data.example#Example:
package main import ( "context" "fmt" "log" "net/http" "strings" "github.com/go-authn/oidc" ) func main() { // Discovery happens here, at startup: an issuer that does not answer is // a server that cannot authenticate anybody. v, err := oidc.New(context.Background(), oidc.Config{ Issuer: "https://login.example.org", Audience: "fileshare", Type: "at+jwt", // a resource server takes access tokens, not ID tokens }) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } http.HandleFunc("/", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { raw, ok := strings.CutPrefix(r.Header.Get("Authorization"), "Bearer ") if !ok { http.Error(w, "unauthorized", http.StatusUnauthorized) return } tok, err := v.Verify(r.Context(), raw) if err != nil { log.Print(err) // which check refused it: for this log only http.Error(w, "unauthorized", http.StatusUnauthorized) return } fmt.Fprintln(w, tok.Subject(), tok.Username(), tok.Groups()) }) log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil)) } A Verifier is safe for concurrent use and holds the key set: build one at startup and keep it. Verify’s error says which check refused the token, for the server’s log; the client gets one refusal whatever the check.
Three configurations New refuses before anything is fetched:
package main import ( "context" "fmt" "github.com/go-authn/oidc" ) func main() { ctx := context.Background() for _, cfg := range []oidc.Config{ {Issuer: "http://login.example.org", Audience: "fileshare"}, {Issuer: "https://login.example.org"}, {Audience: "fileshare"}, } { _, err := oidc.New(ctx, cfg) fmt.Println(err) } } oidc: http://login.example.org is not https: the key set decides every signature, and over cleartext so does anybody on the way oidc: no audience: a token minted for another service is a valid token, and a verifier that does not check accepts every one the issuer ever signed oidc: no issuer: a verifier without one accepts tokens from anybody The rest of Config is optional: JWKSURL skips discovery; UsernameClaim and GroupsClaim (default groups) name the claims; ClockSkew and MinRefresh default to one minute; Client is the HTTP client, for a proxy, a private CA or a timeout. A Token reads Subject, Issuer, Audience, Email, EmailVerified, Username, Groups, Expiry, NotBefore and IssuedAt; Claim(name, &v) decodes any other claim, and Has(name) says whether it is there.
data.what-it-accepts#What it accepts: Ten signature algorithms, as an allowlist: RS256 RS384 RS512, PS256 PS384 PS512, ES256 ES384 ES512, and EdDSA (Ed25519). A token whose alg is not one of these is refused before any key is fetched. alg: none and the HMAC family are refused by not being on the list, and the key must be of the algorithm’s kind: a token claiming RS256 is checked with an RSA key or refused.
data.what-it-is-checked-against#What it is ch: pyjwt signs every token in the test suite, so the verifier is never judged by a signer from the same hands. The HMAC-confusion token is forged by hand, because pyjwt refuses to produce it. testdata/fixed.json — tokens pyjwt signed once with a fixed key — lets the architecture lanes, s390x included, verify real signatures with the clock fixed. The Linux test lane, the race detector and the coverage lane install pyjwt and set OIDC_REQUIRE_JUDGE, so a missing pyjwt fails rather than skips. Accepting HMAC, comparing the issuer by prefix and skipping the audience check were each tried on purpose, and each turns a test red. The coverage lane’s floor is 90%.
data.what-it-refuses-and-why#What it refuses,:
why alg: none a token that says it is unsigned is a JSON object somebody typed HMAC against a public key HS256 takes a shared secret, and the issuer’s key is public: anybody could mint a token an issuer that merely starts with the right one iss is compared whole: https://login.example.org.evil.test starts with the right string a missing or wrong audience a token minted for another service is valid; it is not addressed to this one a token with no expiry it is a password somebody can copy once an issuer, a key set, or a redirect over cleartext HTTP, except to loopback the key set decides every signature an RSA key under 2048 bits, or with n or e not in shortest form; an EC point not on its curve signatures under a short key can be forged; before v0.2.2, a 1024-bit modulus padded with zero bytes passed as 2048 bits a key published with use other than sig a key set legitimately holds encryption keys too with Type set, a token of another typ; with it unset, a typ other than JWT or at+jwt (a token with no typ header passes) RFC 9068 §4: a resource server checks typ: at+jwt, or it takes an ID token for an access token whenever the audiences agree a part that is not canonical base64url a token verifies as one string ECDSA’s s and n − s both verify, as the algorithm allows. So a denylist or a replay cache keys on jti or sub, never on the token as sent.
Keys rotate, and an unknown key is not a way to hammer the issuer. A signature nothing held can verify is worth one refetch of the key set per MinRefresh, whether the kid is new or the same kid carries a new key. Tokens that need the key set while a fetch is under way wait for it, and a fetch that fails still counts.
Which name Username() gives. By default preferred_username, then email only when email_verified is true, then sub. An unverified email is a string the person typed (OIDC Core §5.1). A configured UsernameClaim is read as named, with no fallback.

What did this person’s identity provider say about them? A SAML 2.0 service provider for an identity federation such as RENATER’s Fédération Éducation-Recherche or eduGAIN: it reads the federation’s signed metadata, sends people to their own institution’s identity provider, and reads back what that provider says.
go get github.com/go-authn/saml@v0.4.1 It is the half of authn-bridge that faces the federation, and usable on its own by anything that wants to be a SAML SP. Not here: an IdP, Single Logout, the artifact binding, signed AuthnRequests, attribute queries, SAML 1.1.
Federation fetches the metadata, verifies it against a pinned certificate, and keeps it fresh with Run ParseMetadata the same verification, for a document already in hand DiscoveryURL, Chosen send the person to a discovery service, and read back the IdP it chose SP.Request the AuthnRequest, over HTTP-Redirect, and the Pending to keep SP.Accept the SAMLResponse posted to the ACS, read into an Assertion Assertion.Subject subject-id, then pairwise-id, then eduPersonPrincipalName, then eduPersonTargetedID, then a persistent NameID — never mail SP.Metadata the SP’s own metadata, to register with the federation
data.what-it-is-checked-against#What it is ch: RENATER’s own metadata, as RENATER signed it on 2026-09-29, in testdata/fer-idps.xml.gz, with its certificate checked against the SHA-256 fingerprint RENATER publishes. All 343 IdPs are read; rewriting the host of one Location is refused. The architecture lanes, s390x included, verify that signature too. xmlsec1 signs and encrypts every response in the suite, from templates: GCM and CBC, RSA-OAEP with SHA-1 and with SHA-256, Response signed, assertion signed, both. The Linux test lane, the race detector and the coverage lane install it and set SAML_REQUIRE_JUDGE. crewjam/saml’s IdP writes whole responses to this SP’s AuthnRequests in a separate CI job (interop/crewjam, a module of its own, not in the published module): RSA-SHA256 with AES-128-CBC and the Response signed is accepted; its default RSA-SHA1 is refused; the same CBC assertion with the Response signature removed is refused before decryption. The coverage lane’s floor is 92%.
data.what-it-refuses-and-why#What it refuses,:
Metadata:
why not signed by the pinned certificate the certificate is a parameter, never fetched alongside the metadata: a key that arrives over the same channel as the document vouches for nothing past its validUntil, or with none a signed document that never expires is a key compromise that never ends. A failed refresh keeps the last good copy, until that copy expires valid for more than 28 days from now Federation.MaxValidity changes the bound; a negative value removes it older than the copy in use a rollback: validly signed, and possibly carrying a key since revoked fetched over http:// from anywhere but loopback the signature would catch a change, but not a path that holds back the new document An IdP’s certificate in metadata is trusted because the federation’s signature names it; its dates are not looked at, since IdP certificates are often self-signed and expired.
Responses are checked at Accept. Each refusal below is returned to the caller as an error, for the server’s log:
why nothing signed, or signed with SHA-1 saml-profiles 4.1.4.5: over POST the assertion must be signed. A Shibboleth IdP signs the Response by default; either is accepted more than one assertion how a signed one and an unsigned one arrive together and the wrong one is read (CVE-2022-41912) anything outside what the signature covered it is never read: only the element rebuilt from the bytes the signature digested is a scoped identifier outside the IdP’s Scopes dropped: otherwise any IdP could assert alice@another-university.example AES-CBC ciphertext no verified signature covers not even decrypted: unauthenticated CBC is a padding oracle. RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 key transport is not accepted at all; AES-GCM and RSA-OAEP are another audience, ACS or request; an unsolicited response; a request more than an hour old saml-profiles 4.1.4.3 an assertion already used a bearer assertion is whoever holds it a condition it does not understand saml-core 2.5.1: the assertion is then Indeterminate a password returned when MFA was asked for (Options.AuthnContext) an IdP may ignore the request with ForceAuthn, an AuthnInstant from before the request the IdP reused a session it was asked not to The default replay cache is one process’s memory
SP.Replay defaults to NewMemoryReplay(). Several instances behind a load balancer would each accept the same assertion once, and a restart empties it. Implement Replay over shared storage; its Use must be atomic.

Who has the identity provider just created, changed or deleted? An identity provider (Entra ID, Okta, Keycloak, …) creates, updates and deletes people and groups in your application over HTTP; this package is that HTTP endpoint, for Users and Groups (RFC 7643, RFC 7644), over a Backend you write. Pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0, standard library only.
go get github.com/go-authn/scim@v0.1.0
data.example#Example:
srv := &scim.Server{ Backend: scim.NewMemory(), // or your database BaseURL: "https://app.example.org/scim/v2", // for meta.location } mux.Handle("/scim/v2/", http.StripPrefix("/scim/v2", scim.BearerAuth(token, srv))) The Server assigns ids, timestamps and versions, validates input and applies PATCH; the Backend keeps what it is given and enforces what only it can see: ErrConflict for a taken userName (409 uniqueness), InvalidValue for a member that does not exist (400 invalidValue), ErrPrecondition when the stored version is not the one that was read. NewMemory() is the reference implementation.
It serves /Users and /Groups (list with filter, startIndex, count, attributes, excludedAttributes; create; get, PUT, PATCH and DELETE by id with ETag and If-Match), /Users/.search and /Groups/.search, and the discovery endpoints /ServiceProviderConfig, /ResourceTypes and /Schemas. Filters cover the whole grammar of RFC 7644 §3.4.2.2; PATCH is atomic: an operation that fails leaves the resource as it was.
data.what-it-is-checked-against#What it is ch: What identity providers really send, tested with their payloads: Entra ID’s "Replace", its string booleans ("active": "False"), its member removal by value list, its filtered add that creates an email; Okta’s replace without a path that repeats the id. The filter, PATCH and the whole handler are fuzzed (FuzzFilter, FuzzPatch, FuzzServer), and the coverage lane’s floor is 92%.
data.what-it-refuses-and-why#What it refuses,:
Everything here comes from outside, so the limits are part of the API:
a body over MaxBodyBytes (1 MiB), a PATCH with more than MaxOperations (100), or one that grows the resource past the body limit 413 a group with more than MaxMembers (10 000) 400 invalidValue a filter over 4 KiB, nested deeper than 32, with an unknown operator, or gt on a boolean 400 invalidFilter writes to id, meta, schemas or a user’s groups 400 mutability a resource without its core schema, a userName that is empty, over 256 bytes or has control characters, two primary emails 400 a missing or wrong bearer token (BearerAuth, constant time; an empty token admits nobody) 401 any Backend error that is not one of the sentinels 500 with a body that says nothing; the error goes to ErrorLog Not supported: bulk operations, sorting, password changes, /Me (announced as such in /ServiceProviderConfig).
