Where does a daemon’s TLS server certificate come from? A certificate and key on disk, re-read when they change, or an ACME CA through autocert, External Account Binding included.
go get github.com/go-authn/servercert@v0.5.2 A Config names exactly one source — CertFile and KeyFile, or ACME — and New returns a *Source whose TLSConfig() serves it, with MinVersion TLS 1.2.
data.acme#ACME:
autocert answers two challenge types and no other: tls-alpn-01 (RFC 8737, port 443, ALPN acme-tls/1) and, with HTTPChallenge, http-01 (RFC 8555 §8.3, port 80, served by Source.HTTPHandler). There is no dns-01, hence no wildcard and no IP-address certificate.
Certificates are obtained at the first handshake whose SNI names one of Domains, or before any client by Source.Prefetch, and renewed by autocert before they expire. A client that connects by IP address sends no SNI and is served the first domain’s certificate.
Append to NextProtos, never replace it
With ACME, TLSConfig().NextProtos holds acme-tls/1, without which the CA’s tls-alpn-01 validation fails. And append you must: a Go TLS server that advertises ALPN protocols refuses a client whose offer shares none, so an NFS-over-TLS server adds sunrpc (RFC 9289). net/http adds http/1.1 and h2 itself.
A CA that needs no challenge. autocert returns at once when a new order is already ready, which is what a CA with pre-validated domains answers: GÉANT TCS, served by HARICA, for an Enterprise Admin account. An internal server reachable on neither port 80 nor 443 from the Internet can still get a publicly trusted certificate. The EAB HMAC key is a secret, so the configuration names a file holding it (EABHMACKeyFile), never the key.
One defect of x/crypto/acme is worked around (golang/go#77704): after finalizing an order the CA is still processing, the client polls the URL in the finalize response’s Location header, which RFC 8555 does not put there. servercert gives the ACME client a transport that adds that header, with the order’s URL from the earlier newOrder response.
data.example#Example:
From files:
package main import ( "log" "net/http" "github.com/go-authn/servercert" ) func main() { src, err := servercert.New(servercert.Config{ CertFile: "/etc/fileshare/tls/fullchain.pem", KeyFile: "/etc/fileshare/tls/privkey.pem", OnError: func(err error) { log.Print(err) }, // a renewal that did not load }) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) // unreadable, unparsable, or a key that is not the certificate's } srv := &http.Server{Addr: ":443", TLSConfig: src.TLSConfig()} log.Fatal(srv.ListenAndServeTLS("", "")) } Config.Check refuses a configuration that cannot work, and touches nothing — no file read, no directory created:
package main import ( "fmt" "github.com/go-authn/servercert" ) func main() { // Check touches nothing: no file is read, no directory created. for _, c := range []servercert.Config{ {ACME: &servercert.ACME{Domains: []string{"*.example.org"}, CacheDir: "/var/lib/fileshare/acme"}}, {ACME: &servercert.ACME{Domains: []string{"192.0.2.10"}, CacheDir: "/var/lib/fileshare/acme"}}, {ACME: &servercert.ACME{Domains: []string{"files.example.org"}, CacheDir: "acme"}}, {CertFile: "/etc/fileshare/tls/fullchain.pem"}, {ACME: &servercert.ACME{Domains: []string{"files.example.org"}, CacheDir: "/var/lib/fileshare/acme", DirectoryURL: "http://acme.example.org/directory"}}, {ACME: &servercert.ACME{Domains: []string{"files.example.org"}, CacheDir: "/var/lib/fileshare/acme"}}, } { fmt.Println(c.Check()) } } servercert: ACME domain "*.example.org" is a wildcard; that needs dns-01, which autocert does not do servercert: ACME domain "192.0.2.10" is an IP address; autocert issues only for DNS names servercert: ACME.CacheDir "acme" is not an absolute path servercert: CertFile and KeyFile go together; one of them is empty servercert: ACME.DirectoryURL "http://acme.example.org/directory" is not an https URL (RFC 8555 §6.1) The last one is Let’s Encrypt production: DirectoryURL empty.
data.files#Files: New reads the pair and fails now on one that is unreadable, does not parse, or whose key is not the certificate’s. After that, at most once every 10 seconds and during a handshake, the files are read again; a changed pair is parsed without holding a lock and swapped in. A changed pair that does not load — the certificate written before its key, a truncated file — is reported once to OnError, and the last good pair stays in service, so a renewal job that writes the two files one after the other never takes the server down.
data.what-it-is-checked-against#What it is ch: pebble, Let’s Encrypt’s test CA, run in-process from its ca, db, va and wfe packages with a DNS stub, issuing real certificates that crypto/tls verifies against pebble’s root: tls-alpn-01; http-01 through HTTPHandler and its control with HTTPChallenge off; EAB required, absent, wrong, then right; a pre-validated domain issued with no challenge port open, and its control. A test runs the same issuance without the golang/go#77704 workaround and requires it to fail. The coverage floor is 100%.
data.what-it-refuses-and-why#What it refuses,:
Check refuses: neither or both sources; half a file pair; ACME without domains or cache directory; a relative path; half an EAB; a domain that is an IP address, a wildcard, a single label, ends with a dot, or is not a valid host name; a directory URL that is not https (RFC 8555 §6.1).
New also refuses a cache directory — it holds private keys — that is a symbolic link, is accessible by group or others, is owned by a user other than the process’s effective user, or cannot be written; a missing one is created 0700 and checked after. Every directory above it must be changeable only by root or the effective user, as sshd’s StrictModes asks of the path to authorized_keys, and a symbolic link above it is refused unless root owns it. On Windows, mode and owner are not checked — ACLs decide both, and restricting them is yours — and a symbolic link anywhere in the path is refused.

data:
Is this six-digit code right — and has it been used before? Time-based one-time passwords (RFC 6238); a Verifier that remembers what a server has to, the codes already used and the wrong ones; and a factor that an mfa policy can ask for.
go get github.com/go-authn/totp@v0.4.2 Its one dependency is go-authn/mfa.
The defaults are what every phone assumes: six digits, every 30 seconds, HMAC-SHA1, one step of tolerance either side. Options changes Digits, Period, Algorithm (SHA1, SHA256, SHA512) and Window.
data.example#Example:
package main import ( "fmt" "time" "github.com/go-authn/totp" ) func main() { secret, err := totp.ParseSecret("JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXPJBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP") if err != nil { panic(err) } now := time.Date(2026, 10, 10, 12, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC) o := totp.Options{Now: func() time.Time { return now }} code, _ := totp.At(secret, now, o) // what the phone shows fmt.Println(code) v := &totp.Verifier{Options: o} fmt.Println(v.Verify("dora", secret, []byte(code))) // accepted fmt.Println(v.Verify("dora", secret, []byte(code))) // the same code again fmt.Println(v.Verify("Dora", secret, []byte(code))) // another spelling, same secret // A secret shorter than 128 bits makes no code. short, _ := totp.ParseSecret("JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP") _, err = totp.At(short, now, o) fmt.Println(err) } 395621 totp: that code has already been used totp: that code has already been used totp: a secret of 80 bits; RFC 4226 requires at least 128 In a policy, the code becomes a factor of kind Possession, next to whatever checks the password:
package main import ( "context" "fmt" "github.com/go-authn/mfa" "github.com/go-authn/totp" ) // knows stands in for whatever checks the password. type knows struct{} func (knows) Name() string { return "your password" } func (knows) Kind() mfa.Kind { return mfa.Knowledge } func (knows) Verify(context.Context) error { return nil } func main() { ctx := context.Background() secret, _ := totp.ParseSecret("JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXPJBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP") verifier := &totp.Verifier{} // one per server, kept: it remembers used codes code := []byte("123456") // what the person typed _, err := mfa.Verify(ctx, mfa.Policy{Count: 2, DistinctKinds: true}, knows{}, totp.Factor("dora", secret, code, verifier), ) fmt.Println(err) } mfa: 2 factor(s) needed, 1 answered: your authenticator app (possession): totp: that code is not right A code read aloud over the telephone is possession no longer; the classification is what DistinctKinds relies on.
data.what-it-is-checked-against#What it is ch: pyotp, a Python implementation: 200 random cases across secret lengths from 16 bytes, 6 to 10 digits, four periods and all three algorithms (differential_test.go). The Linux test lane, the race detector and the coverage lane install it, and there TOTP_REQUIRE_JUDGE turns a missing pyotp into a failure rather than a skip. RFC 6238 Appendix B, all six times and all three algorithms, and RFC 4226 Appendix D, counters 0 to 9. Every digit count over 1000 steps per algorithm, against RFC 4226 §5.3 recomputed in arbitrary precision. The coverage lane fails below 95% (its stated standard is 100%), and the tests run on eight architectures.
data.what-it-refuses-and-why#What it refuses,:
A code already accepted. RFC 6238 §5.2: the verifier MUST NOT accept a second attempt of an OTP that already succeeded. The stateless totp.Verify cannot — it holds nothing between calls — so a server uses a *Verifier, which refuses with ErrUsed every step up to and including the last one it accepted: a code from thirty seconds ago is still inside the default window.
A Factor without a Verifier. totp.Factor with a nil *Verifier refuses every code, saying a Verifier is missing. It is not reported as unavailable, so a policy cannot pass on the other factors and hide the mistake.
Guessing, per secret. A Verifier counts wrong codes per credential — the secret, held only as its SHA-256 — not per name, because the name is whatever string the caller passes, and before v0.3.0 dora, Dora and DORA were three counters for one secret.
field default Throttle DefaultThrottle = 5 wrong codes in a row before ErrThrottled; the code sent meanwhile is not looked at, so not even the right one passes Pause DefaultPause = 15 minutes how long that lasts Lockout DefaultLockout = 100 wrong codes in a row, however spread out, before ErrLockedOut, which only Forget lifts (NIST SP 800-63B §5.2.2) Only a wrong code counts; a replay, a code of the wrong length or a refused parameter does not bring a pause nearer. The whole check is made under one lock, so guesses sent at the same moment are counted one by one. ErrLockedOut wraps ErrThrottled, so errors.Is(err, totp.ErrThrottled) is true for both refusals, and errors.Is(err, totp.ErrLockedOut) only for the lockout.
Parameters that cannot be right:
a secret under 128 bits (MinSecret = 16 bytes, RFC 4226 R6), in Generate, At, Verify and Verifier.Verify. ParseSecret still reads one: it is a parser; a period that is not a whole number of seconds, or under one second; fewer than 6 or more than 10 digits (RFC 4226 §5.3); a window wider than MaxWindow = 10 steps either side. 0 means the default of one step; NoWindow accepts only the current step. Every step in the window is tried without stopping early, and the comparison is constant-time. ErrWrongCode is the same error for “wrong” and “too old”.
The secret is the credential
Whoever holds it produces every future code. No error message here quotes a code or a secret, and URI — the otpauth:// string an authenticator reads from a QR code — carries the secret by construction: it is for the person enrolling, and nobody else.
The Verifier’s memory is this process’s. Two servers behind a load balancer each refuse their own replays and count their own guesses; a deployment that needs one answer puts a shared store behind the same interface.

data:
May this WireGuard key connect, and whose is it? WireGuard authenticates a peer by its static public key and by nothing else: no certificates, no expiry, no revocation. So the question is answered outside the protocol, and answered again whenever the answer changes. A provider — authn-bridge — answers it; this module is what the provider and a gateway agree on.
go get github.com/go-authn/wireguard@v0.1.1 Its one dependency is oidc v0.4.0, which verifies the list.
It does two things: ParseKey says what a public key is, and Source.Fetch gets the provider’s signed List of the keys people registered, each a Peer with its Key, Subject, Username, Device and the end of its lease.
Only public keys pass through here
A private key is generated on the device and never leaves it; nothing in this package has a place for one.
data.example#Example:
package main import ( "crypto/ecdh" "encoding/base64" "fmt" "strings" "github.com/go-authn/wireguard" ) func main() { // A public key as wg(8) prints it. Here it is derived from a fixed // private key; on a device, `wg genkey | wg pubkey` makes one, and the // private half never leaves it. priv, _ := ecdh.X25519().NewPrivateKey([]byte(strings.Repeat("\x2a", 32))) text := base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(priv.PublicKey().Bytes()) k, err := wireguard.ParseKey(text) fmt.Println(k, err) // The all-zero key authenticates nobody. _, err = wireguard.ParseKey(base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(make([]byte, 32))) fmt.Println(err) // Unpadded is another spelling of the same bytes, and is refused. _, err = wireguard.ParseKey(strings.TrimRight(text, "=")) fmt.Println(err) } B6r/Pp/BZydVRPTDpqF82Dfy7G54zYpXsePfs8wDWnY= wireguard: the key is a point of low order, which authenticates nobody wireguard: the key is not base64: illegal base64 data at input byte 40 A gateway keeps one Source and fetches the list:
package main import ( "context" "log" "os" "time" "github.com/go-authn/wireguard" ) func main() { ctx := context.Background() src, err := wireguard.NewSource(ctx, wireguard.SourceConfig{ Issuer: "https://bridge.example.org", ClientID: "gateway-1", ClientSecret: readSecret("/etc/gateway/client-secret"), }) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } for { l, err := src.Fetch(ctx) // signed, typ wireguard-peers+jwt, for this gateway, not older if err != nil { log.Print(err) } else { for _, p := range l.Peers { log.Printf("peer %s is %s (%s) until %s", p.Key, p.Subject, p.Username, p.Expires) } } time.Sleep(time.Minute) } } // readSecret reads the client secret from a file: never from the command // line or the environment. func readSecret(path string) string { b, err := os.ReadFile(path) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } return string(b) } NewSource reads the provider’s configuration at startup. Fetch gets a token for the gateway itself (client_credentials, scope wireguard_peers), fetches the list from /wireguard/peers under the issuer, and verifies it with go-authn/oidc: the signature against the provider’s key set, the issuer, the audience (this gateway’s ClientID), the expiry, and the typ wireguard-peers+jwt (ListType) — so neither an access token nor an ID token can pass for a list, nor a list for a token.
data.what-it-is-checked-against#What it is ch: wg(8) itself, from wireguard-tools, makes the keys ParseKey must accept. It is installed in the Linux test lane, the race detector and the coverage lane, which set WIREGUARD_REQUIRE_JUDGE=1 so a missing wg fails rather than skips. The low-order test checks the seven points libsodium lists, each with and without the top bit. The coverage floor is 100%.
data.what-it-refuses-and-why#What it refuses,:
A key (ParseKey):
any other spelling of the same bytes. The decoding is strict and the text must print back exactly as it came, so a store keyed on the text cannot hold one key twice under two names; a point of low order, the all-zero key among them. Every exchange with one gives the same shared secret whatever the other side’s key (RFC 7748 §6.1), so it authenticates nobody. crypto/ecdh decides it by computing an exchange, so the top-bit variants are refused too. A list (Fetch):
why a list with a lower version than one this Source has taken an old list is signed too, and may list a key taken back since a key listed twice whichever a gateway kept, the other person’s traffic would arrive under the wrong name a peer with no subject it belongs to nobody a key that is not one see above an issuer or token endpoint in the clear, except loopback the gateway’s secret and the list would cross a link anybody can read a SourceConfig without ClientID and ClientSecret a gateway reads the list as a client of its own A list carries exp: a gateway that cannot fetch a newer one by then has no list, rather than a stale one. Peer.Subject is the person’s sub as the client that registered the key sees it, public or pairwise — the value a gateway also finds in that person’s access tokens.

data: go-authn is asked to prove people, so its refusals are the design rather than the exceptions. This section gathers the ones that cross program boundaries; each program’s own pages say what it refuses on its own.
data.a-revocation-end-to-end#A revocation, en: authn-bridge signs and dates a KRL (for SSH certificates) and a CRL (for X.509 client certificates), and publishes them. authn-revokd fetches each list, verifies its signature and dates, refuses one older than the list it holds (across a restart too), and only then writes it where the server reads it. sshd (RevokedKeys), go-fileshare and anything else read a file that has already been verified. A CAEP session-revoked event, through the provider’s Shared Signals transmitter, voids what no list can name: everything issued to a person before a given moment. go-fileshare’s documentation describes the receiving side: revocation lists, shared signals.
data.releases#Releases: Every binary is built by the release workflow from a tagged commit and can be checked three ways: verifying a download.
data.the-refusals-that-matter-most#The refusa: what is refused why authnd a search by anyone but a declared reader a bind proves who somebody is; it is not permission to list everybody authnd a Kerberos ticket for a person whose source holds no password a KDC needs a key derived from the password; an NT hash or a password check cannot produce one (why) authnd a kerberos block beside an mfa block a kinit carries the password and nothing else, so the realm would issue tickets on one factor to people the mfa block says need two authn-bridge an assertion nobody signed, an identifier from outside the institution’s own scope every member of a federation is trusted, so each must be held to its own people: otherwise any one institution could name anybody authn-revokd a list that is unsigned, expired, or older than the one it holds a mirror in between may delay a list, never forge it or roll it back authn-revokd trusting a list that has lapsed it writes one that revokes the CA itself, so sshd refuses rather than trusting a stale list sshcert-authorize a certificate whose domain grant does not name this host a certificate from a federation CA is not, by itself, permission for every host that trusts that CA

data:
Each release of authnd, authn-bridge, authn-revokd and sshcert publishes six static binaries (CGO_ENABLED=0: linux, darwin and windows, on amd64 and arm64), a SHA256SUMS file, and a build-provenance attestation for every binary. The examples below use authn-bridge v0.23.1; the other programs work the same way with their own repository and name.
gh release download v0.23.1 --repo go-authn/bridge
data.1-the-checksum#1. The checksum: sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing # macOS: shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS authn-bridge-darwin-amd64: OK authn-bridge-darwin-arm64: OK authn-bridge-linux-amd64: OK authn-bridge-linux-arm64: OK authn-bridge-windows-amd64.exe: OK authn-bridge-windows-arm64.exe: OK This proves the file is the one the release lists, and nothing more: whoever could replace a binary on the release page could replace SHA256SUMS beside it.
data.2-the-provenance#2. The provenance:
gh attestation verify authn-bridge-linux-amd64 --repo go-authn/bridge echo $? The attestation is signed by GitHub for the workflow run that built the file, so it names the repository and the workflow, not a key somebody holds.
Read the exit status, not the output. Without a terminal, some versions of gh print nothing at all when the verification succeeds: measured with gh 2.65.0 on authnd, a genuine binary gave exit status 0 and an empty output. A binary with one byte appended gave exit status 1 and Error: failed to fetch attestations from go-authn/authnd: HTTP 404: Not Found, because no attestation exists for its digest. Silence is not the failure; a non-zero status is.
data.3-what-the-binary-says-about-itself#3. W:
go version -m authn-bridge-linux-amd64 path	github.com/go-authn/bridge/cmd/authn-bridge mod	github.com/go-authn/bridge	v0.23.1	build	-trimpath=true build	CGO_ENABLED=0 build	vcs.revision=9a51e5e9839f879d44c09b8b4e71f823e72ee0aa build	vcs.modified=false (lines shortened to the ones that matter). The mod line must be the tag exactly, and vcs.modified must be false: a build from a tree with uncommitted changes says true, and its version reads v0.23.1+dirty. The release workflow refuses to publish unless every one of the six binaries passes both checks, and unless the program prints the tag as the last word of its version line:
$ authnd --version authnd version v0.11.1 $ authn-bridge --version authn-bridge version v0.23.1 $ authn-revokd -version authn-revokd v0.6.4 authnd and authn-bridge take --version; authn-revokd takes -version, Go’s standard flag syntax. From v0.6.1 it prints on standard output, like the other two, so v=$(authn-revokd -version) captures it.
data.which-releases-have-binaries#Which relea: Binaries, sums and attestations are published from authnd v0.9.2, authn-bridge v0.19.3, authn-revokd v0.5.0 and sshcert v0.1.2. The first release of each built its binaries inside the checkout and reported +dirty; that was fixed in the next one, and the per-binary check came after that. Earlier tags are source-only: build them with go install …@, which records the tag in the build information that go version -m reads. What the program prints is not always that: sshcert-authorize printed dev for a go install build until v0.1.5, and revokd has no -version before v0.5.0.

data:
A certificate from a federation’s CA is not, by itself, permission for every host that trusts that CA. The EuroHPC Federation Platform’s SSH CA writes the hosts a certificate is meant for into an extension, ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org, and sshd ignores it. go-authn/sshcert reads and writes that extension, and its command, sshcert-authorize, is what sshd runs to enforce it. Pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0. These pages describe v0.1.7.
$ go install github.com/go-authn/sshcert/cmd/sshcert-authorize@v0.1.7 $ sshcert-authorize -version sshcert-authorize v0.1.7 sshcert-authorize the AuthorizedPrincipalsCommand: what it checks, what it refuses, and how sshd calls it
data.the-extension#The extension:
Its data is a compact JSON array of host patterns, ["login.example.org"]. A * matches one or more characters within a single label, and names compare without case:
pattern matches does not match login.example.org login.example.org, LOGIN.example.org www.login.example.org *.example.org a.example.org example.org, a.b.example.org prod-*.example.org prod-1.example.org prod-.example.org *.*.example.org a.b.example.org a.example.org The reading is strict: only what the encoder writes is accepted. No whitespace, nothing after ], no JSON escapes, no duplicates, at most 64 patterns, each made of letters, digits, hyphens and *, in labels of 1 to 63 bytes, at most 253 bytes, and no * in the rightmost label. null, objects, numbers and nested arrays are refused. [] is accepted, and grants no host.
A grant that is present and malformed is never reported as absent. That difference is the whole point of the command.
data.who-uses-it#Who uses it: authn-bridge writes the extension for a client’s ssh_domain_grants, after checking each pattern with this package’s ValidatePattern. go-fileshare’s SFTP server reads it with ssh_domains, and refuses a certificate with no grant unless ssh_accept_ungranted is set. sshcert-authorize is the same check for a plain sshd.

data: sshd asks it, for each certificate login, which principals may log into the account. It answers with the account’s principals only if the certificate’s domain grant names this host; otherwise it answers nothing, and sshd refuses the certificate. It takes the arguments, flags, output and log format of GÉANT’s ssh-cert-authorize, and differs in what it refuses.
data.flags#Flags:
$ sshcert-authorize -help usage: sshcert-authorize [flags] USER [CERTIFICATE [KEYTYPE]] An sshd AuthorizedPrincipalsCommand (%u %k) that refuses a certificate whose ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org extension does not grant this host, or that has none. -allow-no-grant let in a certificate with no domain grant (GÉANT's behaviour); a malformed grant is still refused -debug log details -domain string the host's domain (overrides --domain-env and --domain-file) -domain-env string environment variable holding the host's domain -domain-file string file holding the host's domain, one name per line (default "/etc/ssh/cert-allowed-domain.conf") -extension string name of the domain-grant extension (default "ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org") -krl string refuse certificates this OpenSSH KRL revokes, and every certificate once it has expired or cannot be read -principals-dir string directory of principals files, one per user (default "/etc/ssh/auth_principals") -syslog log to syslog, facility AUTH (--syslog=false: to stderr) (default true) -version print the version and exit Logs are key=value lines (action=cert_processed, action=denied, action=authorized, with serial and ca_fingerprint), to syslog, facility AUTH, by default. sshd discards the command’s standard error, so keep syslog on in production; --debug also writes everything to standard error. A value that comes from the client, such as the account name, is quoted when it holds a space, =, a quote or a control character, so it cannot forge a log field.
-version prints the module version, in a release binary and in one built by go install alike:
$ go install github.com/go-authn/sshcert/cmd/sshcert-authorize@v0.1.7 $ sshcert-authorize -version sshcert-authorize v0.1.7 Before v0.1.5, a binary from go install printed sshcert-authorize dev.
data.how-sshd-calls-it#How sshd calls it:
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config TrustedUserCAKeys /etc/ssh/efp-ssh-ca.pub AuthorizedPrincipalsCommand /usr/local/bin/sshcert-authorize %u %k AuthorizedPrincipalsCommandUser nobody install -o root -g root -m 0755 sshcert-authorize /usr/local/bin/ echo login.example.org > /etc/ssh/cert-allowed-domain.conf and, for each local account, the principals that may log into it, one per line, in /etc/ssh/auth_principals/. sshd runs the command only from a path owned by root and writable by nobody else.
%u is the account being logged into. %k is the certificate, base64; a whole ssh-...-cert-v01@openssh.com BASE64 line is read too, and when the argument is absent the certificate is read from standard input. A third argument, when one is given (sshd’s %t), must be the certificate’s type, or the certificate is refused.
exit prints sshd 0 the account’s principals, one per line lets the certificate in if one of its principals is among them 1 nothing refuses it 2 nothing refuses it: the arguments were wrong It does not check the signature, the CA or the validity dates
Nothing in the command verifies the certificate’s signature or its validity window: sshd, which trusts the CA through TrustedUserCAKeys, does that. The command decides one question, whether the certificate is meant for this host and this account.
data.krl#--krl:
RevokedKeys is sshd’s own check, made before the command runs, for every key and certificate, and it also revokes a CA key; prefer it. --krl FILE checks an OpenSSH KRL inside the command, and adds what sshd does not do: it refuses every certificate once the list has expired (its expires@go-authn.github.io extension, which sshd ignores), and every certificate when the list cannot be read. A list with no expiry is used without one.
Three runs: with the KRL authn-revokd writes, first a current one, then the fail-closed one it writes when the issuer’s list lapses; and last with --krl naming a file that does not exist:
$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --krl ../revokd/out/sshd.krl --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-cert.pub)" INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1001 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.example granted" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q INFO: action=authorized user=alice cert_principals=["a1b2c3@univ-example.example"] server_principals=["a1b2c3@univ-example.example"] domain=login.hpc.example.org serial=1001 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q a1b2c3@univ-example.example $ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --krl ../revokd/out/sshd.krl --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-cert.pub)" INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1001 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.example granted" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q WARNING: action=denied user=alice domain=login.hpc.example.org reason="certificate revoked" serial=1001 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q $ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --krl missing.krl --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-cert.pub)" INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1001 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.example granted" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q WARNING: action=denied user=alice domain=login.hpc.example.org reason="KRL unreadable: open missing.krl: no such file or directory" serial=1001 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q The second run is refused because the fail-closed list revokes the certificate’s CA key: the check covers the certificate’s own key, its serial and key ID, and the key that signed it. The third is refused because the list cannot be read: no list is not taken to mean nothing revoked.
data.what-it-refuses#What it refuses:
In the order it checks:
an account name that is empty, ., .., or holds /, \ or a NUL; a host with no domain configured, or one that is not a valid host name; a certificate that does not parse, a plain key, or a host certificate; a %t that is not the certificate’s type; with --krl, a certificate the list revokes, or every certificate when the list cannot be read or has expired; a domain grant that is present and malformed, whatever the flags; no domain grant at all, unless --allow-no-grant; a grant none of whose patterns matches any of the host’s names; an account with no principals file, or an empty one. The host’s names are --domain, or the variable --domain-env names, or the lines of --domain-file (blank lines and # comments ignored; several lines are several names, any of which may match).
Against certificates signed by a test CA for the account alice, whose principals file lists a1b2c3@univ-example.example, on a host called login.hpc.example.org:
$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-cert.pub)" INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1001 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.example granted" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q INFO: action=authorized user=alice cert_principals=["a1b2c3@univ-example.example"] server_principals=["a1b2c3@univ-example.example"] domain=login.hpc.example.org serial=1001 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q a1b2c3@univ-example.example The last line is the answer sshd reads; the lines before it are the log, here on standard error. A certificate granted other hosts:
$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-other-cert.pub)" INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1003 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.example other host" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q WARNING: action=denied user=alice domain=login.hpc.example.org reason="domain not granted" grant=["*.elsewhere.example.net"] serial=1003 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q A certificate with no grant:
$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-nogrant-cert.pub)" INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1002 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.example no grant" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q WARNING: action=denied user=alice domain=login.hpc.example.org reason="no domain grant" serial=1002 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q An account with no principals file, and a plain key:
$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals bob "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-cert.pub)" INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1001 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.example granted" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q WARNING: action=denied user=bob domain=login.hpc.example.org reason="no principals file for the user" serial=1001 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q $ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice.pub)" WARNING: action=denied user=alice domain=login.hpc.example.org reason="a ssh-ed25519 key, not a certificate" Each of these exited 1, and printed nothing on standard output.
data.why-a-certificate-with-no-grant-is-refus:
GÉANT’s ssh-cert-authorize lets a certificate with no domain grant through (“might be valid for non-domain-based auth”), and one whose grant it cannot parse, or that is empty. Then a site that trusts two CAs in TrustedUserCAKeys (the federation’s, and its own for staff, or a test CA) lets a certificate from the second CA in on every host, for any principal in a principals file, with no domain check at all. The domain filter is only a filter if a certificate that does not say where it may be used is refused.
A site that really wants GÉANT’s behaviour says so, and the command logs each time it applies it:
$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --allow-no-grant --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-nogrant-cert.pub)" INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1002 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.example no grant" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q WARNING: action=no_grant_allowed user=alice domain=login.hpc.example.org serial=1002 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q INFO: action=authorized user=alice cert_principals=["a1b2c3@univ-example.example"] server_principals=["a1b2c3@univ-example.example"] domain=login.hpc.example.org serial=1002 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:Fpa/Ku2Wv1EDCR+KSsqZ2eECTM1zftiBWj01Lr+NO2Q a1b2c3@univ-example.example Even then, a grant that is present but malformed is refused.

data.not-implemented-yet#Not implemented yet: Writes through LDAP, beyond a person changing their own password. authnd answers a modify of one’s own userPassword and the RFC 3062 password modify operation (what ldappasswd sends), both only with the current password, and nothing else: add, delete and modifyDN exist in go-authn/ldap and are deliberately not wired (server.go). The library carries a modify as an ordered list (RFC 4511 4.6) and answers the read entry controls (RFC 4527), so the shape is there; what is missing is the policy of who may write what. A second factor inside Kerberos: OTP pre-authentication (RFC 6560) in FAST (RFC 6113). Until it exists, a kerberos block and an mfa block cannot both be configured. RC4-HMAC: the realm issues aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 only, so a person known only by an NT hash cannot be issued a ticket. This is a choice (RC4 is deprecated by RFC 8429), not a gap waiting to be filled.
